- Director of the Rreenbank Alkali Wiks Company COMPArY (LIMITED) St. Helene). LANCASHIRE, EDWARD MILNER, J.P. (Springfield, - ' -.doh)
REGISTERED OFFICE AT THE MILL, CHORLEY.

CAPITAL, £BO,OOO, in 16,000 Shares of £5 each. Is. per Share to be paid on Application, and 103. per Share on Allotment; subseqwmt Calls not to exceed 10s. per share, and subject to twenty-eight days' notice. Directors. FRED. J. LIGIITOLLER (R. .4; G. Lightoller, Cotton Spinners; Tbos. Barton IC Sons, Spinners and Manufacturers), Chorley and Manchester. JAMES SCHOLEFIELD, Park Side Spinning Company, Royton. OSWELD E. PART (John Lancaster & Co.), Liverpool. WILLIAM WILSON, Agent, 24, Belmont Street, Oldham. C. WOOD LIGIITOLLER, Imperial Buildings, Manchester. PETER WIDDOWS (W. & C. Widdows, Cotton Spinners; Withlows Brothers, Cotton Spinners). Chorley and Adlington. If. PERCY DODSON, 9, The Albany, Liverpool. With power to add to their number.

Solicitors. Messrs. SIMPSON a NORTH. L verpo Auditors. Messrs. P. 8; J. KEVAN. Bolton, Chartered Accountants. Bankers Messrs. CIINTAFFES BROOKS & Co., Manchester. Messrs. BROOKS ,Sc Co., London. Secretary (pro tern.) M. F. WADDELL, Victoria Mills, Chorley.

This Company is formed to acquire that portion cf the Mills and Property of Messrs. R. and G. Light°ller called the Vic- toria Mills, which were partially dertroyed by fire rI e time since. The Estate consists of 8,612 square yards of freehold land, at the low rental of £lO7 13s per annum. The Property has recently been valued in its present state by Mr. John Hoyle, the well-known mill valuer, at £11,840. A Provisional Agreement has been made between Mr. Fred. J. Lightoller on the one part, as repretenting Messrs. It. & G. Liahtoller, and the Directors for the Company, by which the whole of this property has been agreed to be sold to the Com- pany at the low price of £7,000, including the right to use the Trade Mark and Tickets of Messrs. R. and G. Lightoller, whose Yarns have for the past century been well known in the Man- chester and Eastern Markets. The Mill when rebuilt will be entirely fireproof, five storeys high, with cenar ; will hold about 69,000 spindles, viz :--32,400 twist and 36,600 welt (with preparation), calculated to produce 51,0001b5. of Yarn per week. The Yarns which the Mill will be laid out to spin are (average) 32's Twist and 38's Weft. Mr. Fred. J. Lightoller has agreed to take £lO,OOO worth of shares in the new Company, and to allow the purchase money to be paid one-third each year, so as to complete in three years; also to give his services for three years at least to the Company as Managing Director. Messrs. Platt, of Oldham. and others have given estimates for the Machinery: 36,600 weft spindles. 32,400 twist spindles, 1 6,272 roving spindles. 1,792 intermediate spindles, 751 slub spindles, 10 drawing frames, 60 double cards; scutching-room machinery in proportion. Messrs. J. Clayton and Co •of Preston, have given estimates for the rebuilding of the mills, new gearing, eNgines, and new boilers. ac. After carefully going into the estimates of sundry well-known firms, including the above mentioned, the Directors conclude that a Mill ofthe most modern proportions. entirely fireproof, and fitted with the best machinery and engines, will be built at a cost (estimated) of 225. per spindle—a lower price than any such Mill has been put up for in Lancashire for many years. These advantageous terms, and the excellent position of the Mill for obtaining good hands and convenience of carriage (being within 200 yards of the Lancashire and Yorkshire and London and North-Westerd Railway Companies' Goods Sta- tions), will, the Directors feel sure, secure a profitable working (pro oe espryoptaatsacria eppi reepsorae): greattti, aasnrttrTe: of the concern. fin- os hi at iriee etas pditaesilriasballeready subscribed for, an For tu he particulars apply to M. div.head: VICTORIA MILL CRORLEY,
div.p: VICTORIA MILL CRORLEY,

The Ordinary Shares having all been applied for, the directors cannot aow entertain applications for any other than Prefer- ence Shares. BRUNNER, MOND AND CO., LIMITED. Incorporated under the Companies' Acts, 1862 to 1880. CAPITAL-1600,000, IN 60,000 SHARES OF 1.0 EACH. First Isme-4360 000, in 36,000 Shares of £lO each, on which the sum of £5 per Share will be at first called up. Directors. JOHN CROSPIELD, J.p., Chairman Oomph Oros&Id and Sons, Soap Vaaufacturers, Warrington) JOHN TOMLINSON BRUNNER, Managing Director (Win- nlngton, Northwich.) LUDWIG MOND, Managing Director (Wlnnington, North- wieh). CHARLES MENZIES HOLLAND (Field House, Chester, blr-‘r of t y, Ltri Led. _ .r. .nsite Warrington, Salt Manufacturer, Marston, Norlhwich). Bankers. PARR'S BANKING COMPANY (Limited), Warrington and Branches.
Solicitors.
H. FORSHAW & HAWKINS, 2, Harrington-street, Liver-
. pool. A. A J. E. FLLTCHER, Northwich, Cheshire.
Auditor. THOMAS WILLIAM BEAD, 30, Castle-street, Liverpool.
Secretary. THOMAS lIUNGERFORD FORGAN. Offices. WINNINGTON, NEAR NORTH WICH. ABRIDGED PROSPECTUS..

- - - This Company has been registered with a Capital ef £OOO,OOO, divided into 60,000 Shares of £lO each. It is no intended in the first instance to issue snore than 36,000 shares, of which 18,000 will be :Preference Shares. entitling to a first charge upon the profits limited to seven pounds per centum per annum. .

The Company is formed for the purpose of carrying on the manufacture of Alkali by the Ammonia Process on a very ex- tensive, scale, and with this object to purchase and to largely extend the business of Messrs. Brunner, Mond and Co., of Witi- nington and Sandbach, the only Manufacturers in the United Kingdom working this process. The put hese will include two Alkali Works, a valuable Free- hold Estate of 140 acres, very valuable Patent Rights, and other property. The business will be taken to as a going concern as on the Ist January, 1881. The vendors will receive and pay all trade debts due to and owing by them on that day, and the profits there- after will belong to the Company, the Venders receiving in- terest at the rate of £5 per cent. per annum thence up to the completion of the purchase. The price to be paid to the Vendors for the several properties enumerated above is £200,000, from which sum will be deducted the amount of a certain mortgage affecting the property (No. 2) for £s,7oo,—the liability thereunder being taken over by the Company—and the net amount will be paid by the allotment to the Vd Mors at par of 12,000 fully paid up .210 Ordinary Snares and the balance in cash.

The Company acquires these properties on very favourable terms, and obtains full value for the price paid, as will be readily seen from the following statement as to how the main items have been dealt with. The works have been put down at their cost to the Vendors, the 129 acres at Winnington have been taken at a recent valuation by Messrs. Picton, Chambers, and Bradley, of Liverpool, and the sum of £lO,OOO only has been added for Patent Bights, Trade Mark. and Goodwill. No promotion money has been or will be paid, and the Vendors will defray all the expenses up to and including the formation of the Company. Arrangements have been made with Messrs. Brunner and Mend under which they are to act as Managing Directors at salaries of £1,500 per annum each. The Company will take over the stocks paying for them the amount at which they stand in the books on the Ist January, 1881. The Company will also have the benefit of advantageous forward contracts for the purchase of raw materials, and for the sale of finished products. The Vendors have during a very few years. developed their business at so rapid a rate that they rank to-day amongst the largest Alkali Manufacturers in the world ;—during 1875 their total snake was only 2,500 tons, whilst last year it reached 18,800 tons. They have step by step brought their special manufacture to great perfection, and they TOW produce their Pure Alkali for considerably less money than the cost of the common Boaa Ash made by their competitors. Their brand stands first in the market, and commands a higher price than any other. The Vendors have decided to convert their business into a Limited Company, for the reason that in their opinion the re- sults achieved and the prospects before them now warrant an enlargement of their operations to an extent beyond the power of private means. Already a large amount of capital has been expended in preparations for extending the Winnington Works, and it is calculated that the first issue of Capital need only be partially called up to enable the Company to complete exten- sions of these Works sufficient to treble their production. The extraordinary success attained by the Vendors•during a prolonged period of severe depression in trade is ample proof of the great dividend-earning power of the business acquired by the Company, and the intended increase of the make will ren- der it still more profitable in the future. The Directors have no hesitation in expressing their opinion that the Ordinary Share Capital of the Company will ler years to come earn a minimum profit of Fifteen per cent, per annum, a figure which in every year of fairly good trade will be largely exceeded, and they confidently recommend the Shares as an un- usually sound and profitable investment. The Directors now offer to the public a portion of the Ordin- ary and of the Preference Shares of the Company. Application tor Shares are to be made to the Bankers of the Company. Applications may be made either for Preference Shares alone, —or to? Ordinary Shares and Preference Shares together,—but every application for Ordinary Shares is to be coupled with an application for at the least an equal number of Preference Shares. The sum of £1 to be paid on application; £3 on allot- ment; and 21 on the Ist of July. The Call due in July upon the Preference Shares may be paid up in advance on allot- 'Die Directors do not contemplate making any further Call during the year 1881. The only Agreement entered into by or on behalf of the Company is ene dated the 25th day of February, 1881, made between John Tomlinson Brunner and Ludwig Mond of the one part and the Company of the other part, being the Agreement for Bale and Purchase of the before-mentioned Estates and Business. copy of this Agreement and of the Memorandum and Articles of Association of the Company may be seen at the Ofilces of the Solicitors. Prospectuses and Forms of Appli- cation may be obtained from the Secretary, from the Bankers, or from the Solicitors.

ONLY. Only a curl of brightest gold, Laid by with the fondest care, That soitly slept, in the long ago, On a forehead white and tair. Only a dream that is past and gone, Too lovely and dear to be. Oh sad to-day, In their memories sweet, '

Are the visions it brings to me. Only a curl of golden hair! Ah ! why do the tear-drops fall As I muse on a dream that was once so fair? It is all that is left me—all. Gone are the smiles from the winsome face That only now in dreams I see: Gone are the kisses whose tender grace Made music and song for me. Shut is the light from the laughing eyes, Silent the pattering feet; Cold are the lips that will smile no more, And 'taken their music sweet; And my soul grows sick as a snowy grave Through the mist of tears I see. And fondly press to my throbbing lips All that remains for me. I know that the roses will come again, And brighten the sleeping bill; Bet nevermore shall their balm and bloom My heart with their rapture till. Though the daises smile on the summer hMs, And the sunlight sleep rm the sea; For this little curl of golden hair Is all that is left to me.

BL—LIBITESSees. t thou her blushes, that like shadows sweet Pass upward from the silence of the heart, Avowing its fond dream by token meet— Their crimson traits dissolve, but. not depart The hopes they usher to the lover's breast; The signature has melted from the bond, But he doth trust it, asking nought beyond What promise all so briefly hath imprest ; Deep in her virgin heart hath sunk the glow— But thou hast culled its promise, and to thee If lapse of faith or dark misdoubt should be, 'Twill steal into the blenching face of woe, Chide back thy pulse to its remitted flow, • And tinge despondent thought and misery. —Rev. C. Tennyson Turner.

A boy of four, taken to church for the first time, to the organ a few moments,and then said: a Whenwill the organ man let the monkey out?" Every young man who communes with nature in solitude longs for the presence of somebody's sister that he may tell her what a beautiful thing solitude is. Professor Huxley calls it a "corrollifloral dicotyledonous oxogen, with a monopetalous corolla and a central placen- tation." If you are in a hurry, you can call it a primrose, instead. There is only now and then an opportunity of displaying great courage, or even great wisdom; but every hour in the day oilers a chance to show our good nature, charity, and kindness of heart. The fair daughters of this land! May they add virtue to beauty, subtract envy from friendship, multiply amiable accomplishments by sweetnes of temper, divide time by sociability and economy, and reduce scandal to its lowest

denomination. The philosophic Billings graphically illustrates the dif- ference between a blunder and a mistake. "When a man puts down a bad umbrella and takes up a good one," saith Josh, "he makes a mistake, but, when he puts down a good one and takes up a bad one, he commits a blunder." The peril of employing highly educated young men as clerks was again illustrated yesterday. A woman stopped and asked : "Is them lettuce fresh ? " "You mean that lettuce," suggested the clerk, " and it is fresh." " Then you'd better eat it," she snapped, as she walked on. A Texas landlord has adopted a novel way to make money. He requires his guests to pay for their dinner in advance, and then, just as they get seated, two big fellows, rigged up as desperadoes, jump up, get into a fight, and begin to fire blank-cartridged revolvers in a reckless and promiscuous manner. The guests climb out of the windows and rush for the doors in a wild scramble for life, and few of them come back to en the dinner they have paid for. A young mother, in despair at ever teaching her little girl, aged four, her letters, and thinking that perhaps the child knew more than she would admit, said, "Now, Katie, I won't try to teach you to-day; you shall be mother, and teach me my letters." "May I really and truly be mother?" said Kate. " Yes, my darling." "Let's begin, then," was the response. "You have been a very good child to-day, and you may have a whole holiday." And Katie shut up the book and ran off laughing. - A smEws WARNO7O.—" Yaas, there's money made in socks, no doubt," said the old man, as he removed his hat and ran his flugers through his gray locks, " but's it's a reesky bizness ; it' suthin' like betting on where lightning's going to strike, with the odds in favour of hitting the tree you stand under." "Then you never speculate ?" "Never. I dig along on the old farm, taking one crop with another, and pulling out stumps when I've nothing else to do; and if I don't make any great shakes, I haven't anything to worry over. I had a party solemn warning during the coal-ile excitement, and it cured me o' speculatin'." " How was that ?" "Waal, I was a widower then; wife fell down the well, and was drawed out as stiff as a poker. I had a big farm, lots of stock, and was called party solid. We all got excited about lie, and all of us dug more or less holes in search of the stuff. All of a sudden a widder livin' about about two miles from nue found ile in a dozen places on her farm. She was a widder with a bad nose, freckles all over her face eyes on the squint, and built up like a camel. Btd when she strack lie that was a different thing. Old Deacon Spooner, wh ) was a widower, got smashed right away. Our preacher, who had lost his third wife, saw the spec. I tholght it over, and concluded she was an angel. I guess some six or seven of us begun courting that widder within 16 hours after the first sight of ile. I know the procession reached from the gate to the house." " And you got her?" "Not much I didn't, and that's what I'm thankful for. Somehow or other I couldn't work up to the pint. That nose kinder stood in the way every time I was ready to pop the question. She acted like she wanted me,but Deacon Spooner got the best of us all, and they made a hitch." "And then what ?" "Nothing, except she had dosed that farm with a barrel of lie, and thus got a husband for herself and a home for her five children. When the news came out, I was so cold along the backbone that they had to kiver me up with a hoss-blanket ; and since that time I haven't had the nerve to buy eggs at seven cents a dozen and hold 'em for a

rise." MR. CARLYLE ON STATUES.—Everyone must sympathise with the desire to do honour to Mr. Carlyle which has led the people of Chelsea to propose to raise a memorial to the "writer of books" who lived amongst them for so many years. But is the erection of a statue on Chelsea Embank- ment, opposite Cheyne-row, the most appropriate method of commemorating Thomas Carlyle? In one of the most famous of his "Latter-day Pamphlets" Mr. Carlyle ex- presses himself somewhat strongly on the subject of statues. After observing that the first question to be decided by "a company of persons who have decided to set up a brazen image" was whether the hero's memory is worthy a statue, Mr. Carlyle said the next question to be decided was whether the statue would be worthy the hero :—" Is it so excellent in point of art as to be a respectable approach to the Ideal? Or, alas! is it not such an amorphous brazen sooterkin, bred of prurient heat and darkness, as fall, if well seen into, far below the Real? Can you, my misguided friends, think it humane to set up in its present uncomfortable form this blotch of mismolten copper and zinc, out of which good warming-pans might be made? Cannot the Woods and , Forests, in the name of sense and common decency, inter- ' fere at least thus far? Namely,to admonish the misguided citizens, subscribers to the next Brazen Monster of sad sculptural solecism, and exhort them three successive times to make warming-pans of it and repent; or failing that, finding them obstinate, to say with authority, Well, then, persist. Set up your Brazen Calf, ye misguided citizens, and worship it, you, since you will and can. But observe, let it be done in secret, not in public; we say in secret at your peril! Observe, therefore. Build a high enough brick case or joss-house for your Brazen Calf, with undia- phanous walls, and lighted by sky windows only; put your Monster into that and keep him there. Thither go at your pleasure and worship your belly-ful ; ruin your own soul s. only, and leave the poor population alone; the poor, speech less, unconscious population whom we are bound to protect, and will!' "—Pall Mall Ga:ette. Qulcx Wonx.—Thirty years ago Michigan people were a frank and truthful set. Strangers could go there and trade horses with their eyes shut, and breach of promise cases were unknown. Folks meant what they said, and when they gave their word stuck to it. Exactly thirty years ago this month a widower from New York State appeared in Lansig on business. The same business carried him over to De Witt, eight miles away. While en route he stopped at a log farm-house to warm his cold fingers. He was warmly welcomed by the pioneer and his wife, both of whom were well along in years, and after some general talk the woman queried—" Ana I right in thinking you are a widower?' "Yes." "Did you come here to find a wife?" "Partly." "Did anybody tell you of our Susie ?" "No." "Well, we've got as bouncing a girl of 22 as you ever set eyes on. She's good-looking, healthy, and good-tempered, and I think she'll like your looks." "Where is she?" "Over in the woods, here, chopping down a 'coon tree. Shall I blew the horn for her ?" "No. If you'll keep an eye on my horse I'll find." "Well, there's nothing stuck up or affected about Susie. She'll say yes or no as soon as she looks you over. If you want her, don't be afraid to say so." The stranger heard the sound of her axe, and followed it. He found her just as the tree was ready to fall. She was a stout, good- looking girl, swinging the axe like a man, and in two minutes he had decided to say :—" Susie, I'm a widower from New York States; I'm 39 years old, have one child, own a good farm, and want a wife. Will you go back home with me?" She leaned on the axe and looked at him for half a minute, and then replied—" Can't say for certain. Just wait till I get these coons off my mind." She sent the tree crashing to earth, and with his help killed five coons which were stowed away in a hollow. "Well, what do you say ?" he asked, as the last coon stopped kicking. "I'm you'ru," was the reply, "and by the time you get back from De Witt I'll have these pelts off and tacked up and be ready for the preacher." He returned to the house, told the old folks that he should bring a preacher back with him, and at dusk that evening the twain were married. Hardly an hour had been wasted in courting, and yet he took home one of the lest girls in the State of Michigan.--.Derreit Free Tress.
NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CULTURE, &c.

M. Leon Say has strongly pressed on the French Govern- I ment the necessity of relieving agriculture by reverting to the distinction made till 1821, between land and buildings. Theland-tax now yields 120 millions levied on the former and 50 millions on the latter. M. Say thinks the former should be reduced by one-third, the remission being secured to the tenants in the case of land not cultivated by the

owner. A STABLE ow TTIE HOUSE TOP.—It must be confessedthat the building of a stable for 20 horses on the top of a private mansion, access to which is obtained by means of a lift, is calculated to awaken a feeling of astonishment even in these days of marvels. Yet this is the case of a hone just erec-1 ted in Belgraye-square, by Mr. Sassoon. Ground is, of course, very valuable in Belgrave-square and by relegating the horse to the top of the house two birds are killed with one stone; for space is saved and the smell of the stables avoided. The horses do not seem by any means to object to the anode of ascent; possibly they are unconscious of it on account of the closed shutters of the lift. GOOSEBERRIES.—The frequent failure of the larger fruits of the orchard and garden enhances by comparison the value I of those smaller fruits that rarely fail, even in part, and may be said with truth never to fail utterly. The Goose- berry is an important member of this section of small fruits; it is greatly valued in a green state for tarts; it is a good family fruit for pies and puddings when full grown and half-ripe; it may be preserved whole when green in bottles, and may when ripe be converted into a very useful jam- Not many who are enthusiasts in fruit culture are familiar with the delicious flavour of such gooseberries as Pitmaston Greengage, Bright Venus, Goldfinder, and Irish plum, all of which are as useful for ,culinary purposes as commoner sorts, and, therefore, if not wanted as table fruits, will pay their rent in another way. As any good soil will grow gooseberries, there can be no difficulty in securing sup- plies, provided the sorts are suitable for the purposes for which they are cultivated Those grown to produce hand- some high-flavoured fruit will require systematic pruning, and should not'be allowed to bear heavy crops; but for the production of a large bulk of useful family or market fruit there is no necessity for pruning. Put the trees at proper distances and leave them to grow as they may, taking care, however, to assist them with a heavy mulch of fat dung every alternate year in the mouth of November.—G' dener's Magazine. DRESSING STRKWBERRIES.—WheneTer the ground is crisp with frost no labour will be more profitable than cover- ing the soil two or three inches thick with manure between the rows and plants of this delicious, wholesome, and highly esteemed fruit. It is not necessary to dig the ground, but any weeds that exist should be removed before the manure is spread ; the old leaves of the strawberries, however, should not be removed, as they afford shelter to the crowns. The manure for this purpose should net be too short and rotten; it is best when about half decayed, as it then serves two or three important purposes—its virtues are washed down by the rains for the support of the plants, and the straw particles on the surface become clean, sweet, and bleached, forming an excellent medium for keeping the fruit clean, much of which is often spoiled when in direct contact with the soil. By adopting the practice recom- mended, there is no need for placing straw under the fruit in summer, while the manurial covering prevents the evaporation of moisture from the soil during dry weather in spring, thus keeping the roots regularly moist. This is the beat of all modes of enriching strawberry beds, and is infinitely superior to digging the manure into the soil, thus injuring the roots and exposing them to frost in winter and drought in summer, which seriously impair the productive- ness of the plants. FOOT AND MOUTH DISEASE.—A well-known London practitioner, Mr. Priestman, writes as follows respecting remedies i—To the 12th of January I had attended eight hundred head of cattle in sixteen dairies, with uniform re- sults, not having to slaughter one animal through the bad condition of the feet. A few have been killed with swollen udders, on account of not yielding a paying quantity of milk before they were affected. I think I may safely say one- third of the entire number escaped without showing any signs of the disease; another third showed but slight symp- toms; and the remainder in the ordinary form, but recover- ing quicker than when left to take their chance. A most important feature is that none of them appear to lose flesh, and in about three weeks from the commencement of the outbreak it is difficult to discover any signs of its ravages. It is also evident to inc that the earlier in the disease the herd is treated, the less virulent is the attack; and L feel confident that if carbolic acid could be universally used (with other precautionary measures) it would tend materi- ally to rid us of the infection. My mode of treatment is as follows :—As soon as the disease is observed in the herd, I administer to every animal four drachms of carbolic mix- ture in a quart of cold water daily for four consecutive days, giving cold wet bran and pulped wurzel only to those affected. When requisite, the feet are dressed with the same mixture. As a caution to tenants, a correspondent writes to de- scribe the very extraordinary treatment to which he has been subjected by the combined action of a rapacious land- lord and a blundering set of lawyers. The story is a long one; but the gist of it may be briefly given. My corre- spondent hired a farm in Essex on lease in 1858, and occu- pied it for three years, when he left it to take a larger fermi. transferring it to a younger brother, apparently with the landlord's tacit consent, as the rent was demanded of and received from the younger brother after 1861. This second tenant died, and his father then took up the lease, and farmed the land to the end of the term of twenty-one years. All this time the original tenant had not the slightest inter- est in the farm, and he naturally supposed that all liability on , his part ceased when he transferred the lease to his brother. At the end of the term, in 1379, the farm was offered for sale; bet, as it was not sold, the father of the original lessee was requested to keep in the farm as yearly tenant. This he did until the beginning of 1880, when the farm was sold to a London merchant. It seems that the -vendor, in selling it, represented that a considerable sum for breach of covenants and dilapidations might be obtained from the lessee, and, after the sale had been completed, the new landlord put in a claim against the original lessee for £l,OOO. This outrageous demand was made upon a man who had left the farm more than eighteen years previously, and who could not be morally accountable for the manner in which it had been farmed since. It appears, however, that he had not legally protected himself against liability. An action was brought in the Court of Queen's Bench for £1,050, for breaches of covenants and dilapidations, in the name of the old landlord, and, as the jury was composed of London men, who knew nothing about farming, the judge appointed a barrister to settle the claim. He knew no more of farming than the jury, and as a kind of simple compro- mise, apparently, he cut down the claim to £514, and this, with costs, which the unfortunate • lessee had to pay, amounted to £l,OOO. During the recent years of loss—and the land is a heavy clay—the rent had been paid punctually without a shilling of reduction. The landlord, moreover. had neglected to perform his covenants in providing timber, bricks, ftc., for repairs. A valuer of great experience, who went over the farm declared that it was in fair condition, considering the difficulties of recent seasons. This tale speaks for itself, as one related last week from a different part of the country did also. The obvious moral is, Put not your trust in landlords. Take care that you have the law on your side, and do not give an unscrupulous ex- tortioner any chance of taking his "pound of flesh." Several recent instances have shown that Shylocks still abound.—Mark-lane Express.

How A CHILD ALARMED AN ARMY.—You have perhaps heard of the Waldenses, a Christian people living in the Italian Alps? Many many years ago they were subjected to repeated persecutions because et their religion and on one occasion the army of the Piedmontese, which' had en-, tered the Waldensian territory to murder and rob the inno- cent inhabitants, was totally defeated mainly through the instrumentality of a child. After a day of skirmishes be- wn eunpt ht heel two on faotei vs ,e thne,oWu mountains, iatnhse were gmroandtneaslel yp ur er rueiantg- them as rapidly as they could. Suddenly a loud scoffing was raised by the latter, who saw in the distance the Wal- densians kneeling in worship. Hardly had the derision ceased when a drum was heard to beat in a side valley. The Piedmontese paused at this unlooked-for sound in an unex- pected quarter, and fearing lest a Waldensian force might be lying in ambush, the army began to grow disordered; whereupon the Waldensians, taking advantage of the panic, at once swooped down upon their enemies and put them ut- terly to flight. This invading force was routed because it gave way to panic; and the panic arose because a child in a neighbouring valley was beating a drum in play !—Fronzi "Little Folks" Magazine for March. A COCE•AND-SULL STORY BY NAPOLEON.—NapoIeon I would not allow VilenenYe to approach Paris after his defeat at Trafalgar, and this is his account of the end of the admiral At Rennes, on the 26th of April, 1806, on his wav from England, Villlenenve put an end to himself! When taken prisoner, and conveyed to England, he was so mach grieved at his defeat that he studied anatomy in order to destroy himself. For this purpose, he bought some . Anatomical plates of the heart, arid compared them with his own body, in order to ascertain the exact situation of that organ. On his arrival in France, I ordered that he should I remain at Rennes, and not proceed to Paris. Villeneuve, I afraid of being tried by a court-martial, determined to destroy himself, and accordingly took his plates of the heart, and compared them with his breast. Exactly in the centre of the plate he made a mark with a large pin, then fixed the pin, as near as he could judge, in the same spot in his own breast, shoved it in to the head, penetrated his heart, and expired. He need not have done it, as he was a brave man, though possessed of no talent." This story is altogether too absurd. A man accustomed to battles and death was under no necessity to study anatomv in order to destroy himself. • A pistol bnllet through his head was a much likelier means • of suicide than a pin and all this adaptation. Accordingly, the public, bearing in mind the deaths of Pichegnt and ;Captain Wright, formed its own conclusions about the • matter.—Cassell's Illustrated History of Englaud." ---• MICA SOLES.—The flaky, transparent substance known as mica, has been applied by an ingenious American to keep the damp away from the feet, by fashioning it into a middle sole for boots and shoes. Sheets of it are covered with thin coatings of cement to hold to the leather, and inserted be- tween the upper and under layers of the sole. A FROST TELL-zarE.—Amateur gardeners can easily con- struct a frost-alarm, which will ring an electric bell when frost makes itself felt during the night in the greenhouse or conservatory. An iron wire, 10 or 20 feet long, hung so that its lower end is free to contract by the cold, and in so doing complete the circuit of an electric battery in circuit with the bell, is all that is necessary, and can be readily arranged. A little more ingenuity, and the wire can be ad- justed to drop a weight and strike a match, which will set fire to some light combustible capable of defeating the rigours panes by of Theeth c co ludr iboyu st h:r acbl oesuciduoefs smp roodk eu cwehdi cohnwwi l li nadroi awe: ' frost have suggested to a French inventor a systedi of ob- taining designs for printed stuffs by crystallisation. He has made experiments with solutions of the sulphates of zinc, copper, iron, alumina, and magnesia, with which'plates of glass were covered, and then allowed to dry slowly at different temperatures. The crystals thus deposited form a great variety of fanciful figures—flowers, feathers, stars, dtc. These may be fixed by the addition of albumen or gelatine. If copper plates are used, the designs thus obtained may also be made permanent by electrotyping. The great diffi- culty is to obtain continuous patterns to be reproduced on the cylinders used for printing; but that may be overcome by using cylindrical plates of copper, and turning them on their axles while the evaporotion is going on. The crystal- lisation is, however, frequently irregular, anlleaves blank ; spaces, which spoil the harmony of the design; but that , ciefect will probably be overcome by experience. ' A WONDERFUL THEORY.—A reader of the Scientific American, who has been trying certain experiments on the value of charcoal as a convenient means of storing oxygen', reports favourably as to the results. In a box or case con- taining one cubic foot of charcoal may be stored, without mechanical compression, a little over nine cubic feet of oxygen, representing a mechanical pressure of a hundred and twenty-six pounds on the square inch. From the store thus preserved the oxygen, he says, can be drawn by a small hand pump. From the fact of the charcoal absorbing oxygen in so much greater proportion than nitrogen, we have here, says the editor of that journal, a means of utilising its dis- criminative powers of selection in obtaining unlimited sup- plies of oxygen from the atmosphere, which contains nitrogen five times in excess of its oxygen,, or twenty per cent.; whereas by the separating or selective powers of the charcoal the mixed gases capable of being extracted from it contain over sixty per cent, of oxygen. It only suffices to withdraw this now highly oxygenised air into another vessel of charcoal, by the further exposure to which the propor- tion of oxygen will be increased to a still greater extent.— Design and Work. THE PHILOSOPHY OF SmaLLING.—The sense of smell occupies itself with gases; for these alone can gain access to the organ, or cause the sensation of smell. Lest the reader should suppose this statement opposed to the testi- mony of his experience' from the well-known fact that solids, such as cedar-wood, camphor, and musk, excite the sensation of smell, while ordinary scents are preserved and carried about in a liquid form, it must be explained that these substances contain volatile essentiai principles, which, on free exposure to the air, are slowly given off in a state of vapour. Some solids give off particles of their substance in a state of vapour without first becoming liquid, as is ordi- narily the case. Thus snow, which coats the earth in winter, will diminish daily, even though the air is frosty, and there is no melting process going on. In other cases, as in cedar-wood, oils naturally volatile seem to be long entangled in the solid matter, and but slowly rendcred to the air; but their odoriferous power is so great that very small portions of them produce strong perfumes. This is sometimes truly wonderful. Dr. Carpenter states that a grain of musk may be freely exposed to the air for ten years, during which time it perfumes the whole surround- ing air; yet when weighed, there is no perceptible loss ob- served. Matters which exhale odorous emanations are de- tected at a great distance, from the tendency of gases to pass through and diffuse themselves equably throughout all other gases. Thus, though there be but a very small escape of coal gas in one part of the room, it soon announces itself to the nose in every corner of the apartment. This is a faculty peculiar to gases, and produces many interesting results, which, however, cannot now be dwelt upon.—Cas- sell's Popular Educator. THE POSSIBILITY or A CHANNEL TUNNEL—By engineers and geologists the construction of a tunnel is thus con- sidered practicable, although they do not quite agree as to the choice of the strata. The problem seems to resolve itself into three alternatives. Firstly. The tunnel through the Lower Chalk would involve the least expenditure•of capital and time, as the distance between the two coasts is only 21 miles, and the tunnel in its entire length could be carried continuously through the one formation. Secondly. Al- though the Kimmeridge Clay would necessitate a longer route, still, if the Portland Sands upon further examination should prove to be absent on the English coast, so as to admit of the tunnel being carried direct into the Wealden Clays, the scheme would have its advantage in the thickness and impermeability of the argillaceous strata. It might be possible also to have a shaft midway at the Varne Shoal, which is concealed at low tide by only some three feet of water. Finally. There would remain the old Paleozoic rocks advocated by Professor Prestwich, which, although in his opinion safe and certain, would entail vast cost, from the depth at which they lie, their hardness, and from the many miles of underground railway needed on either coast to con- nect the Channel tunnel with the surface lines. It is, how- ever, within the range of probabilities that the enterprise which has enabled the French engineers successfully to fol- low the coal measures from Hardingen to near Marquise, may enable them to follow these strata further towards the coast; and as the strike of the "measures" trends to the Eng- lish coast between Folkestone and Dover, it is within the range of possibilities that a coal gallery under the Channel may prove the pioneer of the greater and more important work under consideration. Under any circumstances it is evident that the difficulties are formidable. Whether or not they are insuperable are questions which may safely be left to our engineers. The mommy and great obstacles over- come by engineering science of late years, lead us to expect that should the occasion arise, and the attempt be considered worth the cost, the ability to carry it out would not be want- in.—Good Words for March.

Owing to the late heavy rains part of a large tunnel on the Carrickfergus and Larne Railway has fallen in, and com- pletely blocked the line. . A correspondent writes from Falmouth :—The swallows have arrived on the Cornwall coast, betokening an early spring. The Rev. Mr. Enraght has been served with notice of motion, to be made before Lord Penzance, on the 26th inst., to order his se-commitment to prison. The Crown Prince of Sweden is engaged to the Princess Victoria of Baden, granddaughter of the German Emperor by his only daughter, Louise Marie Elizabeth. A boat belonging to the Qneenstown firm of clothiers was capsized off the harbour on Monday evening, and seven men were drowned. At Pontesbury, on Sunday, John Humphreys, cowkeeper, was accidehtally choked by a piece of meat lodging in his windpipe as he was eating his dinner. It is stated that in consequence of the depressed condition of agriculture considerable difficulty has been experienced in obtaining a gentleman to undertake the duties of high sheriff of Leicestershire. ' A fire at the malt kilns of Messre. T. Berry and Co., Worksop, near Sheffield, has entirely destroyed 6,000 bushels of dry malt and gutted the entire west portion of the build- ing. The damage is estimated at £12,000. In the hearing of a case of assault at the, Marylebone Police Court, on Monday, it was stated that the Salvation Army had, at great expense, established Isranches all over Louden'. We have a long list of wrecks on the Scotch coast. Many of them were accompanied by loss of life, and it is stated that on the coast between Montrose and Wick alone 150 seamen perished in the gales of Saturday and Sunday. At Derby, on Tuesday, Robert Ruff, a young man em- ployed at the railway works, was remanded on a charge of administering poison to his wife with intent to murder her. . Considerable excitement prevailed in Portsmouth on Monday and Tuesday by the desertion of soldiers ordered to India. Ills said that two hundred of them broke out of the barracks on Monday night. FRIENDLY SOCIE rms. A REPORT OF THE CHIEF REGISTRAR. A report, just issued, of the Chief Registrar of Friendly societies for the year ending 31st December, 1879, and ordered by the House of Commons in August last to be printed, gives some most valuable and interesting informa- tion regarding the returns of friendly and industrial socie- ties, trades unions, and the like. The figures given as to Societies registering rules, and the outcomu of the various returns made under the Act of 1874, tell withal a very satis- factory tale, and the Blue Book generally is full of encou- ragement to the advocates of thrift and prudence. The Chief Registrar has to report that in the year under review there was again an increase in the business of the Central Office. The total number of new societies or branches registered or certified amounted to 1,044, as against 786 in 1878; of amendments of rules 3,445, as against 2,848. Of these latter no fewer than 2,014 were complete amendments, which, added to the rules of the 1,044 new societies or branches, made a total of 3,058 complete sets of rules registered; a larger number, it is believed, than at any time during the previous experience of the Office. The increase was mainly in the number of new and converted branches of Friendly , Societies. The whole group of bodies registered under the . . _

Friendly Societies Acts showed an increase under every head, while there was a falling off in every other class of society registered. Co-operative societies dropped from 43 to 39; building societies from 132 to 123; trade unions from 22 to 17; and loan societies from 34 to 28. The inference that was derived from this increase in the formation of
bodies of a purely provideat character, accompanied by a decrease in those which demanded an outlay of capital, ap- .
peared obionsly to be that the continuance of the. commer- cial distress that year had seriously impaired the resources of the working classes without at all affecting their provi- dence. _ _ .

The annual returns sent into the office for the year 1878 spoke well for the attention given to them in the two pre- ceding years. The total nurtiber of returns received was 12,300, showing a slight increase (of 30) over the previous year,and they were better and more accurately filled up than on any previous occasion. The number of members returned rose from 4,603,794 to 4,692,175, or an increase of 83,381; and the funds from £11,109,571 to £12,148,609, or an in- crease of £1,039,033. Deducting all other classes of socie- ties, this would leave, for Friendly Societies proper, 4,643,336 members, and £11,988,350. In 1879, nine sum- monses were taken out by the Chief Clerk against Friendly Societies' secretaries for neglect in making and sending their annual returns; three of these belonging to Preston. Re- turns were received from 28 out of 31 collecting societies, within section 30 of the Act of 1875, showing a total of 2,091,251 members, £1,195,447 funds, £708,891 members' contributions received, and £287,894 expenses of manage- ment. This represented an increase over 1877 of 93,426 members and £162,695 in funds. Five of these collecting societies had over 100,000 members each, one of them being the Blackburn Philanthropic Burial Society. Of the 49 societies that registered in all during the year 1879 2,594 branches, the Manchester Unity maintained the lead it .had gained in the pre % ions year over the Ancient

Order of Foresters. As regards the Industrial Co-operative Societies, the Re- port has to state that the 39 registries in 1879 comprised a grocers' association, a mutual pianoforte society, and an industrial nail manufacturing society. The returns sent in for 1878 were very satisfactory in point of number, amount- ing to 963, against 896. They also showed a growth in membership, viz., 490,584 members, as compared with 461,666, while the share capital had increased from £5,142,958 to £5,347,199. On the other hand, the loan and deposit capital had t,,llen (probably, in a great measure, through withdrawal of deposits) from £916,955 to £692,478. The sales of g00(1,3 had also Wien off from £18,697,788 to £18,461,753, .ares which while they speak of the privations of the working clan during a period of distress, a,,1 of the drafts which they had to make on their savings, are not less eloquent as to the confidence which _ . .

the societies' inspired. In obedience to an order of the House of Commons, dated 23rd of June, 1879, a return was presented of the Build- ing Societies incorporated up the December previously, with an abstract of the last annual account forwarded by each. The return (so far as related to England and Wales) con- tained the names of 987 societies, of which 826 stated the annual income, and 830 furnished accounts of liabilities and assets. From the greater part of the remaining societies no return was due, a complete financial year not having expired since the incorporation; 767 societies stated the number of their members, being 275,450 in the aggregate, or an average of 359 for each society. The aggregate annual income of 826 societies was £15,970,329, the aggregate liabi- lities to members £17,431,545, to creditors £10,060,897, and the aggregate assets of 830 societies, £28,228,153. These figures show a considerable increase over those of the previ- ous year, when 672 societies f urnished their annual state- ment. The Trade-Union returns bore unfavourable testimony to the condition of the working classes. Out of 177 registered societies known to be in existence, 124 made returns, or 19 less than the previous year. The number of members re- turned exhibited a considerable falling off-202,984, instead of 260,222. The funds returned in like manner fell from £374,989 to £309,223. For the year 1879, 380 (of 389 forms issued) Loan Socie- ties made returns. The number of members was 33,520; the amount actually advanced and paid by depositors or shareholders in 1879, £122,160; sums in borrowers' hands on the 31st of December, 1878, £325,483, and amount circu- lated in 1878, £509,906. In the course of the year the number of valuation returns received from Friendly Societies greatly exceeded those of former years; for whereas in 1876 there were only eight such returns, in 1877 18, in 1878 40, the number for 1879 was 948. The tables of these show that only 25 were from societies not connected with the affiliated orders, the re- mainder coming almost entirely from bodies connected with the two largest of the orders, viz., the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows and the Ancient Order of Foresters. It remains to be said that of the 923 returns from societies connected with the affiliated orders only ;a were made by public valuers, the remainder being made by persons all of whom, without exception, were connected by membership with one or other of the orders. In concluding a notice of the Blue Book we append a summary of the returns:— Societies or Members. Branches. Under Friendly Societies' Act 15,379 ... 4,692,175 ...L12,148,609 Industrial and Provident Socie- ties Trades Unions 177 .•• 202,984 ... 309,223 Building Societies under Act of 1874 Loan Societies Totals If the figures are compared with those of the first summary, printed in the Chief Registrar's report for 1876, it will be found that the above shows ais increase of 1,545,707 mem- bers, and no less than £18,053,726 funds.

PARLIAMENTARY RETITRN OF ELEC- TION EXPENSES. 1. Parliamentary paper, stating the expenses of all the candidates at the Elections last year, ham just been issued. The returns record only the legitimate expenses which can- didates or agents avow, and which they deliver in obedience to statute. Everyone is well aware of the fact that the pre- sent law affords no security that the real expenditure will be disclosed by an agent, and an inquiry often brings to light large sums, all mention of which had been deliberately sup- pressed. For instance, the Commissioners who have reported so gloomily of Sandwich tell us that the expenses agent of the Conservative candidate returned the expenses of his client at £3,153, when, in point of fact, the total came to £5,600. In many constituencies, it is to be feared, the real cost of the elec- tions last April would be arrived at only by adding 30 or 40 per cent., or even more, to the returns officially made. Even as returned, the figures are very large. Let us give a few cases. The expenses of the unsuccessful candidate for the northern division of the county of Durham, Sir Geo. Elliott, the wealthy colliery owner, were returned at £12,726 14s. Bd., or £2 103. for each recorded vote. The two successful Liberal candidates-Colonel Joicey and Mr. Charles Mark Palmer-are stated to have spent each £5,548 3s. 94d. ; the total returned expenses of the division-which, it may be remarked is one where facilities for travelling to the polling stations must be ample-were £23,823 2s. 3d. In the south- ern part of the county, the contest was also an expensive one. The expenses of Mr. J. W. Pease and Mr. Lambton, the two successful joint Liberal candidates, were stated in the accounts to be £5,712 Bs. 21c1., while the defeated can- didate, Mr. Surtees, acknowledged to an expenditure of £10,664 2s. lid., or £2 12s. 6d. a vote, in his effort to win over the constituency to Conservatism. In West Kent the joint expenses of the two successful Conservative candidates -Sir Charles Mills and Lord Lewisham-were not far be- hind the figures just mentioned, they being returned at £10,646 13s. 10d. for a constituency numbering 14,300 electors. In the contest in Middlesex Lord Geo. Hamilton and Mr. Coope, the brewer, expended on an average Bs. 11d. and 9s. 4d. on each vote, and their joint expenses reached the sum of £11,506 Bs. 2d. Mr. Herbert Gladstone who fought a brave though unsuccessful battle for the Liberal cause, is returned as having spent £6,377 7s. 7d., which amounted to 14s. 4d. per vote. The most expensive of the divisional elections in our own county was that for South. East Lancashire, where the two successful candidates- Messrs. Leaks and Agnew-spent altogether £13,141 us. 9d., against £12,640 9s. 11d., the sum set down to the two who were defeated-the Hon. A. F. Egerton and Mr. Ed. , Hardcastle, the late members. Heavy as this expenditure I appears, it was a cheaper election than that of the southern I division of Northumberland, where Mr. E. Ridley, the Con- servative candidate, who was at the bottom of the poll, spent, according to the return, £6,750, or £1 17s. 3d. a vote, against only £1,223 3s. 11d., or 6s. 3d. a vote, appearing against Mr. Albert Grey, the Liberal candidate, at the head of the poll. Singularly enough, the Welsh counties appear on the list to be more expensive to fight than the English. In Montgomeryshire the unsuccessful candidate paid £6 us. 10d. per head, or in all £13,453 19s. 11; while in Car- narvonshire the contest between Mr. Watkin Williams (now Justice Williams), and Mr. Douglas Pennant, his Conser- vative opponent, cost on an average £4 3s. Bd. to the latter and 19s. 3d. to the former. Several of the Scotch elections were fought at great cost. For example, the. was the struggle between Lord Cohn Campbell and Mr. Malcolm in Argyleshire, where the first named spent £4,931 18s. 90., or £3 78. 84d. a vote, and the latter £5,201 108. Bid. For Orkney and Shetland the returns were-Mr. Laing and Mr. Badenoch-more than £3,000 each, or a 10s. Bd. and a 10s. 76. a heat respectively, an average much higher than any return for England. The historic contest of Mid-

div.p: lothian was economical in comparison with the last- mentioned. Mr. Gladstone's bill was £2,693 12s. Bd. or an average of £1 14s. lid. per vote, and Lord Dakeith's £4,068 Os. 5d., or £2 198. sid. per vote. In the borough constituencies, where the cost of conveyance does not ap- pear so great as in the counties, one would expect to find the election bills not so heavy, but the returns present some very big totals. In Birmingham the total returned ex- penses come to the large amount of £13,374, the expendi- ture of each candidate ranging from• £2,022 Ils. 6d. to . £3,654 is. Bd. At Bradford Mr. Forster and Mr. Illingworth , spent £2,686 10s. 4d. each, and Mr. Ripley £4,129 Is., but P the Metropolitan boroughs have the pre-eminence. One in- stance of these .may be stated—it is Lambeth. There Sir , James Lawrence and Mr. M'Arthur spent £10,666, and their • opponent; Mr. Morgan Howard, £7,605 10s. 9d. Generally the returns from which we have given these few quotations • are such as to show that there exists the greatest necessity , for a measure like that the Government have now intro- , dined, one of the objects of which is greatly to limit the expenses allowed as legitimate in these contests, and thus to ; impose a check on an extravagance for which a better name would perhaps be corruption.

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

A meeting of delegates of the South Yorkshire and North Derbyshire miners was held on Monday, at Barnsley. It was reported that a ballot had shown a majority in favour of demanding 5 per cent, instead of le. On Tuesday, about 800 men and boys employed at Edmunds and Swaithe Main Collieries, near Barnsley, resumed work (notwithstanding the decision of the SOuth Yorkshire Miners' Association) at the old rate of wages, pending an examination of the owners' books to ascertain if any advance is due. The South Yorkshire and North Derbyshire coal owners on Wednesday rececived the result of the ballot taken by the miners on the wages question. The miners decided by a majority against the demand for a ten rier cent advance, and agreed to accept five per cent with the right of exam- ining the owners' books. The owners have replied, de- clining to give any advance, but invite the men to resume work at the former wages, subject to a sliding scale and an examination of .the books. The strike is gradually collaps-

i ng. TAB OLDHAM COTTON THADE.—It is stated that nearly the whole of the mills where twining is carried on are work- ing. The exception 'refers to those concerns which are in such a position as regards trade that they do not wish to start. The new principle of emplzing creelers with an over-

looker is giving every satisfaction— . The employers are adopting a novel system in regard to creelero. They are paid by piece, an Indicator being placed at the end of the mule for the first time. The Oldham cotton operatives are preparing a code of rules with a view of giving relief to aged members, tkere having hitherto been no regular superannua- tion fungi.

A conference of miners' delegates was held at Wolver- hampton, on Monday. Representatives were present from the various mining districts of North and South Stafford- shire, East Worcestershire, and Cannock Chase. The prin- cipal object of the conference was the consideration of the proposed federation scheme for the districts represented, the formation of a board of management, and the consideration of a general permanent relief fund. In the course of a long discussion it was urged that the miners at the present time were very disunited, and unable properly to defend their rights when any attempt was made to unfairly reduce their wages, many of the local district unions being either broken up or very much reduced in number. Resolutions were passed generally approving of the federation scheme for the districts represented and the formation of a central fund, the detaile to be decided on at a future conference.

div.head: FIGHT BETWEEN A•MAN AND A
div.p: FIGHT BETWEEN A•MAN AND A
BULLDOG.

The little town of Stacksteads, in the Rossendale Valley, was on Saturday, writes a correspondent, the scene of a ter- rible fight between a man and a large and ferocious bulldog; and upon the circumstances becoming known in the district the greatest excitement prevailed, much indignation being felt by the inhabitants. Stacksteads is a small town about twelve miles from Manchester, the population for the most part being engaged in the cotton manufactories which abound in the neighbourhood, and in this place more than in any other in the Rossendale Valley there is a large preponder- ance of the rough element. One of the most notorious of this class is a tall and ferocious-looking individual known by the name of .."Samson," who occasionally varies the monotony of his everyday life by drinking, fighting, gam- bling, and other nefarions practices, and not unfrequently does he get through the performance of worrying live rats, to the great delight of his associates; while he occasionally tries his powerful teeth on pots, glasses, plates, &c, bones of any description being but to him as ordinary food. His last adventure took place on Saturday last, when he had a fear- ful fight, for a considerable amount of money, with a power- ful bulldog weighing about 601b5., noted for its prowess amongst the canine species. Ills owner having frequently boasted of the power: of the dog, threw down a challenge for "Samson" te fight the dog, which was no sooner done than it met with a ready response. A place of meeting was arranged, and when the day arrived on which the brutal fray was to take. place a large number of spectators had assom- bla-to witness the combat, the place in which it came off being crowded to excess by rough-looking fellows. The agreement was_ that the dog should have the same chances as if pitted against another of the canine species, whilst the man was to have his hands securely fastened in front of him. The necessary arrangements were not long in being carried out, the brutal preliminaries being entered into with great glee by the spectators. Every precaution was taken to keep the affair as secret as possible, and after everything had been cleared out of the large room in which the en- counter took place the doors were securely fastened in order to prevent the intrusion of unwelcome visitors. _Everything being ready, a bad-looking fellow; dressed in the garb of a quarry-man, gave the word "go," upon which "Samson" descended to the level of the brute, and on hands and knees awaited the attack of the dog. The latter on being unmuz- zled was hounded on by the yells of the spectators, and at once rushed at the throat of the man, and the fearful com- bat commenced. The yelling of the crowd ceased, the spec- tators of the disgusting scene looked on with bated breath. The brute made several futile attempti to seize the man's throat, and the crowd becoming impatient again and again hounded on the dog. Another struggle took place, and, although brief was .terrible, the man trying as for very life to obtain a grip of the dog's throat, whilst the dog in turn twisted itself in every conceivable form to seize the man. The latter, however, at length seized the brute with his powerful teeth, pinned it to the ground, and almost worried it. On rising to his feet he presented a horrible sight, his face and arms having been terribly Lacerated during the encounter.

Aniron bridge ncross the Tees, at Barnard Castle, was, on Wednesday, swept away by the floods, and two men were drowned. At Blackburn, on Wednesday, William Robinson, butcher, was fined ZIO and costs for having the carcase of a diseased cow in his possession which was dressed for human food. The Duke of Norfolk has commissioned Mr. G. Gilbert Scott, the architect, to prepare plans for a large church in early English style, which he is about to erect in Norwich, in fufilment of a vow. The site selected, and given by the duke, is one of the most commanding in the whole city, being that on which stood the old city gaol. At the Council meeting of the Central Chamber of Agri- culture, held on Tuesday, there was a discussion upon the Agricultural Tenants' Compensation Bills introduced by Mr. Chaplin and Sir T. Acland. The Council expressed approval of both bills, but a preference for Mr. Chaplin's, as it seeks to establish the principle that every tenant on quitting his holding should be compensated by law, by custom, or by agreement. An opinion seemed to prevail that the two bilis might with advantage be moulded into one measure. A communication from the West Suffolk Chamber was read. It contained resolutions on the subject of foreign competition, complained that agriculture and the industries of the country were suffering owing to that competition, and called upon the Council to petition Parliament to extend to the industries some measures of relief. A committee was appointed to report in respect of railway charges for carrying farm produce. At a meeting of the Farmers' Alliance a resolution was passed urging the Government to introduce at the earliest possible opportunity a comprehensive land measure to secure the tenants reasonable permanency of occupation, and a right, either by sale or arbitralion, to re- ceive on quitting payment for any addition to the letting value of their holdings due to such improvement. In the course of the discussion Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P., advised the farmers, in spite of all that had been said about revolu- tionists and communists, to formulate a land bill dealing with the whole question. A resolution was passed declaring ' that the ordinary tithe rent charge ought to be paid by the

landlord. Mr. Joseph Cowen, M.P., presided over a meeting held on Saturday night at the Westminster Palace Hotel, to con- sider the best means of uniting the working men's organisa- tions of the kingdom in a movement having for its object the promotion and settlement of the various pressing social and political questions of the day. :11r. Edwin Dunn said that as the great majority of the working classes were practically unrepresented in the House of Commons, the existing organisations should be united upon a common platform, that questions such as manhood suffrage, equal electoral districts, and payments of members should be agitated for, with reasonable prospects of success. In a con- versational discussion which followed, it was pointed out that had the proposed unity existed amongst the organisa- tions which were now almost entirely opposed to the action of the present Government, neither the Irish Coercion Bill could have passed, nor could the Transvaal War have pro- ceeded to the deplorable mint it had RONV reached.-31.r. Lloyd Jones, as an instance of that feeling, raid that recently at a meeting of 4,000 persons in Bermondsey, be saw ?1•117e about 100 voting in favour of the coercion policy. The not. present representatives of labour in Parliament r. shadowed forth any new political programme.—M Butler Johnson moved a resolution to the effect that themeele ,i ttninngr was of opinion that a central organisation was desirable,other that the co-operation of the Radical clubs a d for the demo- craticsettle organisations should be asked to agitate ment of the pressing social and politic alquestions of the day. —The resolution having been seconded, .iPnrofessit)cr: pßrenemslnety, would not support an organisation .si pi.y ...us ice Radicalism ; but let them have a definite object—"J t to Ireland," or "Justice to the Tiransveaal,"nTrarniedblieasshonualds support it.—The resolution was t .1 bn also another forming the mee c, i„inr—o a p:w, isunal coin- mittee.

A plank was laid across the rails and secured by a large stone, but the engine, belog : heavy one, cut through the obstruction without beingthrew off the line. A short time ago a threatening notice was to the company on account of the transmission of Boycottset s! a cattle, but there were none in this train. div.head: NEW AMERICAN CABINET.
div.p: THE NEW AMERICAN CABINET.

NEW YORE, Wednesday.—There is little prospect of an extra Session of Congress. The dissatisfaction with Mr. Garfield's Cabinet is subsiding before the growing impres- sion that he intends to be his own leader in financial and all other matters.

div.head: RELIGIOUS TOLERATION IN SPAIN.
div.p: RELIGIOUS TOLERATION IN SPAIN.

MADRID, Wednesday.—The Papal Nuncio has presented to the Madrid Government a protest similar to that of the Bishopsand Ultramontsnes against the admission of Liberal professors to the University, and against the religious tolera- tion granted to the judicial authorities by the recent circu- lar. The Nuncio holds both reforms to be a violation of the Concordat, and the Conservative as well as the Ultramontaue papers denounce the policy of the Cabinet in violent terms. Senor Sagasta is determined to enters his decisions, as these professors had held their places under Queen Isabella before the revolution, and Senor Canovas had admitted into the Army, the Church, and the Universities, notorious Carlists, chaplains, and active partisans of the Pretender. THE EATHQUAKE IN ISDHIA. The latest news from Naples states that one hundred and forty bodies have been dug out of the ruins of Casmiociola, and the number of deaths is now estimated at three hundred. The people are frantic with terror, and are fleeing from the coast towns to the interior, where they ramble the lulls without food and without shelter. The troops and I the officials who have arrived on the island from Naples are working with the most praisworthy zeal and courage. The bodies which have been recovered are found crushed to pieces. Detached limbs are so often dug out that the greatest care needs to be taken in the excavations, and it is extremely difficult to prosecute the painful work with the speed that is desired. From a small window near the top of a tottering gable a handkerchief was seen to flutter—a feeble call for help. Many volunteers offered instantly for the dangerous enter- prise, but Colonel Parodi restrained them all, and insisted upon his right to answer the signal. Two ladders having been procured were tied together, and the Colonel ascending them disappeared within the window. After some anxious moments of suspense he reappeared with a woman in his arms, whom he brought to the ground, with no little diffi- culty. She was unhurt, but mad, and in her terror sought to escape by flight from those who had saved her from a threatening death. The King has sent ten thousand francs for the relief of the sufferers.

div.head: TRANSVAAL WAR.
div.p: THE TRANSVAAL WAR.

A telegram from the camp at Mount Prospect says that one of Sir Evelyn Wool's first demands will be that armed resistance should at once cease. The proceedings of the Boers during the armistace do not appear to be altogether in accordance with the spirit, if they are not in contravention of the letter, of the arrangement. A "vague rumour" reached Newcastle on Wednesday that the Boers had appro- priated to their own use the waggons of provisions intended for the British garrison at Wakkersroom. No confirmation of the report has been received, but it is stated in several quarters that the Boers hays taken possession of the private property of Englishmen in tLe town of Utrecht, and acted with great harshness towards the own countrymen who are loyal to the British Crown. A telegram from Capetown says that "much apprehension prevailed among the colonists as to the effects of the armistice. The Queen's sovereignty in South Africa now depeads upon Imperial action." At Durban, the armistace has caused universal surprise. From British and Boer information the correspondent considers peace not impossible, "although the military and civilians agree in condemning peace till our prestige has been re- established."

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

Several more arrests were made in Ireland on Thursday, but they occasioned little excitement. Miss Parnell, sister of the Member for Cork, was present at a meeting held in Liverpool en Thursday night, to inaugurate a local branch of the Ladies' Irish National Land League. Miss Parnell was presented with two addresses—nne from the Ladies' League, and another from the Children's Branch. Miss Parnell stated that the onject of the Ladies' League was to undertake what she might call the relief department of the organisation. Several further arrests were made la Ireland on Monday under warrants signed by the Lord Lieutenant. They include Mr. J. NV. Nalley, one of the Dublin trayersers, who is charged with "inciting to murder ;" Mr. Kenny, the president of the Castle Island Land League; Mr. Hannighn, secretary of the Drumcollogher Land League; Mr. John MicMorrow' a National school teacher in county Leitrim; and Mr. P. Kearney, a tenant of the Permanent Under Secretary at Dublin Castle. In most of the cases the charge' of "intimidation." The returns received by the con- stabulary show that on Wednesday the total number of arrests was 28.
A STARTLING PROCLAMATION. On Wednesday evening a lengthened address appeared posted upon the dead walls of the town of Loughrea. It concludes as follows:

Fellow Countrymen,—We are confronted to-day with the most critical crisis in our national history. Never, perhaps, in the tear-dimmed history of our unhappy country did a darker cloud dim the political and social horizon of Ire- land, or a cloud within which showed a brighter or more silvery lining if we have but the manhood'and wisdom to do our duty. Victims of Irish landlordism, you need not be reminded, for the remembrance of your wrongs will be ever engraved on your recollection. A grand opportunity now presents itself of abolishing for ever this reign of fraud and injustice, and you are called in the name of your own common interests to combine like men, and crown your efforts with certain victory. Remember that the eyes of your country are upon you, and fling off now and for ever the slough of the slave and the sycophant, and be brave in the interests of your families and your fellow men. Do not be deterred from the path of duty by the suspension of the British Constitution. In your midst lift high the banner of the Land League, and stand by the men who fought under its folds and fought for your rights and liberties, for your land and your homes. Be up then, and be doing. Great issues are in your hands. Raise yourselves to the level of the emergency. No cringing to landlord' or bailiff, no cow- ing to the whispers of the agent and his minions. Let your motto be, "Our right and honour," and your watchword, "God save the people from the hands of Gladstone, Forster, Harcourt, and Co.": and remember that,
As sure as reigns the living God, As sure as shines the Run, 'Tis by the creed that Michael taught Our Nreedom must be won.
