div.head: MARKETS,
div.p: MARKETS,
111 E EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 12, 1881.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT,
HOUSE OF LORDS.-MONDAY.

THE ARMISTICE IN THE TRANSVAAL.—EarI CADOGAN asked whether the almost incredible rumour of the conclu- sion of an armistice with the Boers was correct.—The Earl of KIMBERLEY read the telegrams which half an hour earlier had been read in the House of Commons by the Prime Minister, showing that eight days' armistice had been agreed to between Sir Evelyn Wood and the Boers. TIIE ECCLESIASTICAL COURTS.—The Archbishop of CAN- TERBURY moved that an address be presented to Her Majesty, praying her to appoint a commission to inquire into the constitution and working of the Ecclesiastical Courts.—Lord ORANMORE AND BROWNE Submitted an amendment, but after some discussion the amendment was negatived and the address agreed to.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Mormey.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Mormey.

THE RULES OF THE HousE.—Mr. DILLWYN gave notice to oil' attention to the necessity for introducing fresh rules for the conduct of poblic business in the House. THE RETENTION OF CANDAHAR.—Mr. STANHOPE gave notice of his intention to propose the following resolution: "That, in the opinion of this House, the withdrawal of British troops from Afghanistan in the present critical state of affairs in that country would not be conducive to the true and permanent interests of India."—Subsequently Mr. 1 ARNOLD and Sir ALEXANDER GORDON gave notice of amend- ments traversing this resolution. THE BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.-011 the question of the rules affecting public business, Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Mr. Charles Russell, said the subject was an extremely serious one, and the Government were agreed that in some way the matter must at an early date be presented in a way that would draw forth an expression of the views of the House. In reply to Sir W. Lawson, the PREMIER said that on February 17th a telegram had been addressed to Sir George Colley in which it was written, "We do not bind your dis- cretion, but we are desirous to make an arrangement for the prevention of further effusion of blood."—Mr. CHILDERS, following the Premier, announced, amid loud cheers from the Ministerialists below the gangway, that a telegram had been received from Sir Evelyn Wood announcing the sign- ing of an armistice by himself and Joubert. The object of this armistice was to allow an opportunity for Kruger to reply to a communication received some time ago from General Colley. The armistice extends from noon on the 6th to midnight on the 14th. Both parties pledged them- selves net to make any forward movement within these days. It was also arranged that eight days' provisions should be forwarded to the beleaguered garrisons.—Mr. CHILDERS, in reply to a question', said no informati,m of the rumoured death of Sir Evelyn Wood had reached the War Office. If the statement were true he had no doubt that before the time at which he spoke an official communication would have reached him. _

..... NEW WRIT.—OR the motion of Lord RICHARD GROS- VENOR, a writ was ordered to be issued for Coventry, for an election to fill the place of Sir Henry Jackson, raised to the bench of judges. PEACH PRESERVATION (IRELAND) BILL—The House went into committee on this Bill, Sir William Harcourt having charge of the measure in the continued absence of Mr. Fors- ter. The proceedings were singularly uneventful, and were for some hours carried on in circumstances that almost liter- ally realised the conditions of an Irish Parliament. No member of the Conservative Opposition thought it worth while to be present. Only a few Liberals sat belew the gang- way, and one or two behind the Treasury Bench, on which the Home Secretary and the Solicitor-General kept watch, Mr. Parnell, who had been in the House at question time, disappeared for the greater part of the night, returning at half- past ten. Mr. Gladstone had returned a few minutes earlier, and in other quarters of the House the tide of mem- bers had flowed in again. At this time the committee were discussing an important section of the Bill which provides that any justice of the peace, constable, or peace officer, might search any person suspected of carrying arms or ammunition in contravention of the Act. This was strongly opposed by the Irish members, of whom Mr. Healey appeared to have assumed the temporary leadership. Mr. Gibaon, who had just put in an appearance on the front Opposition bench, said he was inclined to support an amend- ment providing that any person objecting to being searched might demand to be taken into custody. The Home Secre- tary, acknowledging the force of the objection urged, con- sented to withdraw this provision of the Bill, the clause now declaring that any person reasonably suspected of carrying arms or ammunition may be arrested without warrant. The Horne Secretary also agreed to an amendment by which the officer making the arrest was required "forthwith "to t Ore the suspected person before a magistrate. Progress was re- ported at a quarter to one, and the remaining orders disposed of, the House adjourned at twenty-five minutes past one. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIESDAY.

ALKALI AND NOXIOUS VAPOURS REGULATION BILL.— This bill was considered in committee.—Several amend- ments were moved by Lord MIDDLETON, but only two were adopted. One of these provides that chief inspectors ap- pointed under the measure must devote their whole time to the duties to which the Act applies; and the other requires that the reports of the inspectors as to escapes of acid gases from the works shall have append d to them the reports made by sub-inspectors to the chief inspector.—The bill was reported to the House, and their lordships adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TuEsnekv.

PERPETCAL PENSIONS.—Mr.BRADLAUGH presented 24 petitions from 0,000 persons in favour of his motion for a Select Committee to inquire into the subject of perpetual pensions. SAVINGS BANKS AT FACTORIES.—Mr. J. RUSSELL asked whether branch savings banks could be opened at large factories.—The POSTMASTER-GENERAL said the best way that he could answer the question was by giving an instance of how he had acted. Some time ago Mr. Bass offered to establish a Post-office savings bank at his brewery, and he asked permission for one of the clerks to attend twice a week. He gave permission for this to be done, and the Post-office was quite willing to give similar facilities to private firms. THE RETENTION OF CANDAHAR.—Mr. GLADSTON'E, re- plying to a question from Sir Stafford Northcote, said he was most anxious to meet the demand for an early day to discuss Mr. Stanhope's motion relative to the withdrawal of troops from South Afghanistan. He undertook that the very first opportunity at the disposal of the Government should be given to this subject. He pointed out that there were various votes to be taken in Committee of Supply which must be passed before the 21st inst. These it was not reasonable to suppose would be voted in less time than five or six days. The Ways and Means Bill, founded on these votes, must be passed before the 28th of March, and, finally, there was the Mutiny Bill that must be passed a con- siderable time before Easter. These were arrangements of an inflexible character, with respect to which the Ministry had no option. TERMS OF PEACE WITH THE BOERS.—ID reply to Lord Randolph Churchill, the PREMIER said the Government were always desirous of proceeding in harmony with the views of Parliament and the country; but it was impossible that they should first communicate to the House the pro- posed terms of peace with the Boers which were put forward at a time when actual hostilities were in progress.—ln reply to questions from Lord George Hamilton and Mr. Charles Lewis, Mr. GLADSTONE said that on the 19th of February Sir Gee4ge Colley was authorised to suspend hostile opera- tions if the terms of peace proposed by the Government. were accepted by the Boers. Without referring to documents he did not like being a party to Mr. Lewis' statement that the proposals for peace which has now resulted in the estab- lishment of an armistice, issued bathe first instance from the British Commander. THE GOVERNMENT AND THE LICENSED VICTUALLERS.— Replying to an henourable member who called attention to the publication in the Standard of what purported to be a digest of the draft of a Government measure relating to the trade of the Licensed Victuallers, the ROME SECRETARY said that there was no foundation for the statement, for two reasons—there had never been such a draft, and it had never been printed. THE PEACE PRESERVATION (IRELAND) BILL—AN Ex- TRAORDINARY SceNE.—The House again went into com- mittee on this Bill. Mr. Fotster was on the Treasury bench on his return from Ireland, but he did not disturb the Home Secretary in charge of the Bill. The proceedings were carried on for some hours in a very thin House with- out incident, beyond the illustration of one of the most useful of the new rules, which permits the Chairman in committee to call upon members to rise in their places when his decision is challenged by what is obviously a very small minority. This procedure, taken twice in succession, revealed the presence in the House of only ten Irish mem- bers. Mr. Parnell himself was not present at this time. The Irish members resented this saving of time by moving to have the House counted, which was dons several times, with the resulted showing that there were in attendance something like 200 members. On one of the numerous amendments Mr. Finigan, renewing a somewhat frequent appearance, was greeted by cries of" Oh !" from hon. members opposite. These he deprecated "beastly bellew- ings," an historic phrase which brought the Chairman to his feet with a matter-of-fact demand for its withdrawal. Mr. Finigan, whilst using O'Connell's phrase, forgot or certainly did not use the Liberator's witty term of with- drawal. He fenced with the request in a manner more familiar amongst later Irish members. The Chairman in- sisted upon complete withdrawal, and the uproar grew as Mr. Finigan hesitated. At length he withdrew the phrase. Mr. Callan and Mr. O'Donnell rose together to dispute the Chairman's ruling, being supported by shouts from the Irish members of " What words ?" The Chairman repeated that the words were ," beastly bellowings," when Mr. O'Donnell rising again, as he said, on a point of order, was met by a storm of shouting from the opposite benches. The Chairman standing up, and Mr. O'Donnell resisting his authority, he was at length named amid a scene of unprece- dented uproar, the Irish members shouting at the top of their voices. -When the House was cleared for a division Mr. Biggar, remaining seated, attempted to address the I Chairman, but, being uncovered and his own hat not being I handy, one or two were pressed into his service. When something that would fit him was put on his head, Mr. I Biggar continued to shout, "Mr. Playfair." but got no I further, his voice being partly drowned by the shouts from I the opposite side, and his efforts to interpose being checked by his compatriots, who remembered his delicate position, be ' already having been twice suspended, and feared what would happen if he persisted in his conflict with the chair. At length Mr. Biggar found an oppertunity of putting his question which was whether in the circumstances that had I, arisen it' was not necessary to send for the Speaker P The ' Chairman explained that it was not, and was next invited by Mr. Callan to state what opportunity would be supplied ' to him of impugning the Chairman's Words. Amid the

clamour, Mr. O'Donnetrduly seated and hatted, was heard to declare that he would only be moved by the constituted authority, and immediately after particularised his meaning I by stating that "A constable would be necessary to take him out." He also accused the Chairman of grossly neglecting the trust repos.d in him. All this time the House was being cleared for the division, which taken Mr. O'DonnelPs sus- pension was decreed by 127 votes against 27. The figures being announced the Speaker was sent for, and the Chairman formally reported the events of the last half hour. Mr. Parnell, rising as soon as the Speaker had taken the chair, raised a point of order on the declaration that the Chairman had not named Mr. O'Donnell, but had alluded to him as the hon. member for Dungarvan. This testimony was re- butted by Sir W. Harcourt, who observed that Mr. Parnell had not been in the House when the scene occurred. The House again divided, and the suspension was confirmed by 1411 votes against 32. As soon as the figures were announced Mr. Callan jumped up and called out, "Will I be in order in moving the adjournment of the House?" But the Speaker lfad already left the chair. Mr. Playfair returned to his place, and, as if nothing had happened, proceeded to submit "Clause 5" for discussion. After this the Howse resumed its quietude as suddenly and completely as it had broken out into uproar; and ultimately progress was reported, and the House adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. _

THE COERCION Acr.—Mr. PARNELL asked for what reason Mr. Boyton had been arrested, and was referred by the Attorney-General for Ireland to the warrant, a copy of which would be delivered to the prisoner under the provisions of the Act.--Mr. GLADSTONE moved that at three o'clock any new clauses or amendments to the Peace Preservation Bill that might then be on the paper should be put forthwith. On a division this was carried by 253 votes against 17. The Speaker then left the chair, and, Committee being resumed, further consideration of the Bill was proceeded with. At three o'clock the Committee was on the fifth amendment on the paper, and Mr. Parnell was speaking in favour of it, when the Chair- man interposed. Thereafter followed a continuous succes- sion of divisions, in which from 250 to 290 members voted with the Government, and from 30 to 35 against. At a quarter-past five the last division on amendments was taken, and the Chairman put the proposal that the Bill be reported. Mr. Parnell, attempting to address the House, was ruled out of order by the Chairman; and Mr. Callan with great violence assailed the ruling of the Chair, amid loud cries of "Order." Eventually the question was put, and by a final division the Bill was ordered to be reported by 267 votes against 31. There now remained the question, that the Chairman leave the chair; and Mr. Callan again attempted to delay the proceedings by moving to report progress. The Chairman refused to put this motion, as being out of order, and the Committee divided, with the result that the Chairman was permitted to leave the chair by 277 votes against 22. During the preliminaries of this division the Irish members, repeating a stratagem invented early in the series of amendments, lingered in the House absolutely till the last moment. When the Chairman called upon them to clear the House they disputed his authority, calling out that it was the business of the tellers to clear the House. By these and various more or less ingenious, but always noisy devices, the proceedings were prolonged till the critical hour of a quarter to six was close at hand. But the danger so clearly foreseen on both sides was just escaped, Mr. Playfair leaving the chair at twenty minutes to six. When the Speaker entered and the Chair- man reported the Bill, Mr. Parnell, remaining seated with his bat on, attempted to address the Speaker, but the right hon. gentleman proceeded with the formality of receiving the report. This done, Mr. Parnell again rose, and attempting to address the Speaker. But now Mr. Callan outwitted his own leader, having by a strategic movement taken up a position on the front Opposition bench almost under the Speaker's left ear. He now rose and raped the point of order which he had made earlier, and which was assumedly designed to ascertain whether the Chairman was justified in putting the two formal stages of the Bill under the order of urgency. The Speaker ruled that the Chairmanhad acted in accordance with the spirit of the instructions issued by the committee. But one final triumph remained for the Irish members. It was proposed to receive the re- port, but this was successfully resisted, and to-day was fixed for that stage. Mr. Forster gave notice that a motion would be made on Thursday, providing that at ten o'clock any amendment on report will be divided on forthwith. The remaining orders were run through, and the House ad- journed.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.-THIIRSDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.-THIIRSDAY.

RIVERS CONSERVANCY AND FLOODS PREVENTION BILL. —'l'liis bill was considered in committee, and, after a lengthy discussion, agreed to and reported as amended. HOUSE OF COMMONS. BRIBERY AND CORRUPTION. Mr. ONsLow gave notice that on Monday he will ask the Attorney-General whether his attention has been drawn to the evidence at Evesharn before the election judges of the conduct of a certain Mr. Nuttall, imported from the Birm- ingham League for the purposes of the late election, also to the evidence of Sir William Harcourt regarding the importa- tion into Oxford of a certain Mr. Schnadhorst, also a mem- ber of the Birmingham League; whether, should the bill for the better prevention of bribery and corrupt practices at elections unfortunately not become law this session, he will devise some means to prevent the contaminating influence of the Birmingham League—(Opposition cheers) —being in- troduced among the constituencies during contested elections, nominally for the purpose of acting as agents. (Opposition cheers.) THE SECRET TREATY WITH RUSSIA. Sir CHARLES DILEE informed Mr. Errington that the statement in a work by Charles Marvin, "that by a secret treaty of May3l, 1878. the Czar solemnly bound himself never to extend the Russian frontier in Asia Minor," was not correct. The question con- cerned Her Majesty's late Government, who gave the explan- ation which seemed to them at the time possible. He also made a statement to the House last year, on the 28th May, on that subject. He had now nothing to add to what he then stated, and, indeed, he could not add to the statement be then made with regard to confidential communications between the late Government and Russia without authority from both parties.—(Hear, hear.) THE RAILWAY Commn-rnE.—ln answer to Mr. Stanhope, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN promised to add four narnes—in9luding that of Mr. W. S. Caine—to the Railway Committee, in order to make it of a more representative character. THE PEACE NEGOCIATIONS VfITH THE BOERS.—Mr. GLADSTONE explained, in reply to Lord R. Churchill and others, that the Government had taken no steps whatever to procure an armistice after the death of Sir George Colley. The instructions sent out to that officer had already been seed to that House. With reference to the paragraph in the Queen's Speech, the right hon. gentleman said that when that paragraph was written it represented the feelings of the Government. " Much had happened in the inter- val," but the Government were .perefectly aware of their duty, and wofild sedulously guard the interests of the country. Sir Evelyn Wood had been authorised to prolong the eight days' armistice if he should find it necessary.

WITHDRAWAL or_Tooora FROM CANDAHAR.—In answer to Mr. Onslow, Lord Harrirowrow announced, amidst Minis- terial cheers, that he had received a telegram stating that the withdrawal of some of the troops fromCandahar would be made at once. Three native regiments and one European regimont would be ordered to India immediately; but any very considerable withdrawal of troops would not take place just yet. THE ARMS BILL —Mr. GLADSTONE'S motion terminating at ten o'clock all discussion on the Arms Bill upon the con- sideration of the measure as amended in committee was car- ried by an overwhelming majority-317 votes—and Mr. GLADSTONE announced that he should propose a further ap- plication of the ehlture to-day, with the view of completing the final stage of the bill this week. A number of amend- ments were then discussed.—One by Mr. CALLAN, requiring that any agricultural occupier should be entitled to a licence to carry arms if he could produce a certificate signed by two justices of the peace of the petty sessional division, was adopted by the Government.—Mr. PARNELL spoke strongly in favour of a new clause requiring persons sentenced under the Act to be treated as first-class misdemeanants ; but SirW. HARCOURT resisted it, on the ground that it would encourage people to believe they could violate the Act. The clause was not adopted.—The SPEAILER afterwardsproceeded to put the remaining proposals without debate. Several which stood in the name of Mr. O'Donnell were ruled out of order.
PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Thurs- day, at Whiston Workhouse. Mr. S. Marsh presided, mad there were also present—The Bev. T. Chambers, Rev. J. Barnacle, Messrs. J. Penketh, J. Fidler, W. Crerrard, J. Jackson, J. Harrison, J. Buckley, T. Eatock, J. Leather- barrow, W. Birchall, W. A. Meadows, W. Tyrer, J. Lowe, T. Dobell, W. Gilbody, J. Ranson, W. Swift, J. Kenwright, P. Longton, and S. H. Hartley (clerk).

THE STATE OF THE HOUSE. The MASTER reported that there were 550 inmates this week, as against 552 last week, and 542 in the corresponding week in last year. There were 156 children in the Kirkdale schools.

_ THE COST OF RELIEVING THE F.XTRIORDINARY DISTRESS. At a meeting of the special committee appointed to deal with relief and employment of able-bodied poor, held on the 4th inst., it was decided that hereafter single tickets only for food on Saturday be given; that all persons now I employed be required to produce to-morrow morning notes from late employers that they could not find them work, and that each individual produce new order for work from the !relieving officer (to give the officer an opportunity of ascertaining if their circumstances had altered) on Monday. The CLERK stated that on Saturday he communicated with most of the members of the committee, and it was resolved that no relief be given after Saturday. The frost and snow had disappeared, and the coal miners had gone to work, and the committee considered they ouglt not to give relief to able-bodied applicants. He added that it had cost the Guardians over £l,OOO to provide for this extraordinary distress.

Mr. FIRER And we have not got a return equal to £5O. A letter was read from the Local Government Board, dated 26th ult., which, after acknowledging receipt of the Guardians' letter of the 17th February, stated "it is with satisfaction that they learn from your letter and its en- closures that the Guardians of the Prescot Union are takirig active measures for dealing with the distress which unfor- tunately prevails in the Union at the present time, and especially that they recognise the importance of requiring the performance under proper supervision of work by able-bodied applicants for relief. With regard to the intended arrangements for this purpose, the Board are informed by their inspector, Mr. Cane, that on the 17th February he attended a meeting of the Guardians and conferred with them upon the subject. Mr. Cane it appears suggested some changes in the details of these arrangements, and also in the mode of relieving persons set to work, which changes the Guardians decided to adopt." Mr. JACKSON said in respect to the able-bodied applicants for relief, he was speaking to Mr. Clarke, the chairman of the Wigan Board of Guardians, and strange to say that gentleman said they had never had an able-bodied person seeking employment. The CLERK : I wish we could say the same, sir. THE MEDICAL OFFICERS.

A letter dated 25th ult. was read from the Local Govern- ment Board, stating that they saw no objection to the appoint- ment of Messrs. E. F. Hall and R. MeNicoll as medical officers for the Prescot and St. Helens districts, and approv- ing of the payment to them of salaries of £55 and £75 per annum respectively. THE ST. HELENS RELIEVING OFFICER. A letter was read from the Local Government Board ap- proving the appointment of Mr. Charles M. Stewart, to the office of relieving officer for the St. Helens No. 1 district, and the payment to him of a salary of £lOO per annum.

DEFAULTING OVERSEERS. The CLERK stated that the overseers of the following townships were in arrears with their calls to the amount stated :—Cronton £2,641, Ditton £442. Eccleston £660, Halewood £295, Huyton-with-Roby £322, Whiston £lOO, Widnes £2,231. He had a letter from the overseers of the latter township stating that they expected to pay in the sum of £7OO on Friday. The Huyton-with-Roby overseers said they would not pay their Union call until the Widnes over- seers. He, however, believed the Guardians, some 'ears ago, passed a resolution that if overseers were in at fears with general calls and they had paid the county rate they would stop that payment and pay it to the Guardians. The Huyton people had paid their county rate, but he had not drawn a cheque in favour of the treasurer.

THE ESTIMATE The estimate of probable amount of expenditure for the half year ending 29th September, 1881. was as follows : In maintenance, £3,000; out relief, £5,500; lunatics in asylums, £1,800; loan account, £250; salaries of union officers, £1,100; salaries of assistant overseers, £500; Work- house officers' rations, £200; assessment committee, £150; school attendance expenses, £100; vaccination expenses, £270; registration expenses, £220; establishment charges on Workhouse, £1,000; printing dm., £150; out-relief (extra) £1,000; paupers in schools, £1,280; school fees account, £120.-416,610.
, The estimate was approved. THE SITUATION OF LAUNDRESS.

There were three candidates for the situation of laundress viz, Mary Jones, Liverpool; E. Griffith, Glyn Cury, near Llangollin; E. Cotterill, Everton, Liverpool. The Board decided to leave the appointment in the hands of the Master.
ENSECCESSFOL APPEAL. The CLERK read the following letter from the nurse :

Gentlemen,—lhave received from Mr. Hartley a note re- qnesting my resignation, I did not expect to be so severely dealt with, and I cannot,but think I have been somewhat ,mis- understood. As to the complaint by the Master, I admit, I . was hasty, and immediately regretted it, and I was prepared to make every apology. I now very respectfully ask that you will not consider It nece4sary to adhere to your decision, and that you will think the censure conveyed in your resolution will be sufficient punishment. I am offering the matron an r apology which I am sure she will accept, and perhaps the Matron, herself, would join me In this appeal for your Indulgence on this ocoasian.—Your obedient servant, A. LEA.TITA M. • Mr. MEADOWS: It would be desirable to have the master in. The Master was then called in, and, in reply to the Chair- man, said Miss Leatham had shown anything but the spirit mentioned in the letter op to within about an hour of the Board meeting that morning. ("Oh.") A GUARDIAN: That settles it, • - • -

The MASTER: And since the last meeting of the Board we have heard of the programme she has adopted. She has told the inmates she should stop despite it, and such non- sense as that. ("Oh.") Mr. DOBELL : I think we have heard sufficient, sir. The MASTER thought, under any circumstances, even if the nurse had been ever so repentant, her stay in the house would tend to a good deal of disorder. Mr. JACKSON: Oh, we are perfectly satisfied. The CLERK: Miss Leatham was asked a fortnight ago to resign, and she had not done so. What is your next step? The CHAIRMAN: She should be discharged, of course. I made a little inquiry about her this morning, and she is not inclined, I believe, to resign. It was decided to again call upon the nurse to send in her resignation. THE NEW SCHOOLS TO BE LEFT IN ABEYANCE. Rev. T. CHAMBERS moved "That a dauceur of 150 guineas be sent to Messrs. Weeks and Ilughes ; that their plans of proposed new schools be returned to them ; and and that competitive plans of schools be advertised for to be built at a cost not exceeding £5,000." He said in adopt- ing that course he was not actuated by any feeling of dis- like to Messrs. Weeks and Hughes, but simply to extricate the Guardians from the difficulty they were placed in, and to relieve Messrs. Weeks and Hughes from an unfair posi- tion. Having referred to the time the question of schools was originated, and the obtaining of plans, he' said it ap- peared to him that some of the Guardians had played nothing but battle door and shuttlecock with the plans. He asked in the name of all that was business-like was it not time to put a stop to this puerile play. He proposed to do so, at the same time guarding most jealously that Messrs. Weeks and Hughes should lose neither in prestige nor in pocket, because the plans had proved them capable of de- signing work of the highest order. He proposed a solo- tion which he hoped would compensate them for what they had dose for the Guardians. In regard to the second clause of his resolution he would take the liberty of matting an alteration. Since his visit to the industrial schools (where everything they saw so favourably impressed them) his views of banding schools at that house had very materially changed. (Hear, hear.) The palatial building, the commodious school-room, the admirable and spacious dining room, the long-extending play grounds, the affection anti care bestowed upon the children, their healthy ap- pearance, and the military discipline they were under, all impresied him, and the thought struck him, if these children could be provided for at Kirkdale why build at Prescot at all? (Hear, hear.) He believed they could be provided for at Kirkdale, and that pauperism there was on the de- crease. He found that ample notice would be given to the Board if necessity arose for their removal. As his feelings were shared by Messrs. Dobel and Leatherbarrow he pro- posed that the building of the schools should be left in abeyance—(hear, hear)—on the ground that they were not justified in spending £5,000 or £B,OOO of the ratepayers' money considering the long continued depression of trade and agriculture, and the expense the Board had been put to in providing out-door relief in consequence of the strike. He maintained the Board would not be justified in asking the ratepayers to spend £5OOO or £B,OOO for new schools when the interest on that amount would go so far towards paying for the maintenance of the children at Kirkdale. Ha com- puted that if they had 163 children at Kirkdale at 4s. 6d. a week for food, shelter, clothing, and medicine the cost would be £2,048. If they had 163 children at Whiston they would have to pay ss. 9d., and the cost would be £2,430. On the £B,OOO which Messrs. Weeks and Hughes proposed the Board should spend in the new schools the interest or prin- ciple at 30 years would he, at the lowest, Lap, then for the three officers there, including the master and mistress, and their rations after allowing for what return would be made to the Guardians by the Local Government Board in the shape of a grant, the Guardians would have to pay £l5O which three items amounted to £2,886, take from that £2,048 the balance of £B3B showed the saving to the Union. If it was decided to leave the children there, arrangements could be made whereby a reduced scale would be given for the keeping of them. No doubt, the Guardians were under a promise to the Local Government Board to build, and build they would; but he saw no reason why they should not ask for a tem- porary release from the promise, or for an extension of time. (Hear, hear.) He proposed that the Clerk should write one of his expressive letters to the Local Government Board asking for a release or extension of time, and, if that was not successful, he would propose that a small deputatiod - . `^.• that

go groping in the dark as they had hitherto done, with the natural consequence of coming to grief. Mr. DOBELL seconded the proposition. Mr. MEADOWS rose with very great pleasure indeed to Support the proposition. Twe or three months arm he used the same arguments, showing a saving of £1,600 if the children were kept at Kirkdale. He was told that was im- possible; but as a matter of fact, if the children were kept at Kirkdale, there would be a saving of nearly £l,OOO. The children were better at Kirkdale, as there were no workhouse or paupers, and there was no doubt it would he a great bene- fit to the Union. He had had a conversation with Mr. aagor, the clerk to the Select Committee at Liverpool, and he told him they had room for a great number of children, and it would be years before they wanted space. Mr. FRYER: How is the 150 guineas to be provided? Mr. FIDLER would not create anydifficulty ; the least said about the matter the better. Mr. MLADOWS : We shall want a snecipl order from the Local Government Board to pay the money, of course. Rev. T. CHAMBRRS : Well, my motion is before the Board, and it can be passed or rejected. The CHAIRMAN did not see that the Board had power to pay the money, and he thought it would be desirable to write to the Local Government Board to ask their opinion on the matter, and at the same time give their views why they did not intend to have the schools. After some discussion as to the withdrawal by the Rev. T. Chambers of the second part of his motion, the motion was altered as follows: "That a douceur of 1.50 guineas be given to Messrs. Weeks and Hughes, that their plans of the pro- posed new schools be returned to them, and that the Clerk write to the Local Government Board asking them to release the Guardians or extend the time for building the new schools, or, failing that, that a deputation be sent to the Local Government Board." This was unanimously carried. It was then resolved that the building of the schools re- main in abeyance, and that the children be retained at Kirk- dale ; and the meeting terminated.

, LONDON CORRESPONDENCE. - The discovery of Aylward in a position of authority in the Boer camp gives fresh currency to the rumour that the Fenians have had one of their centres of operation in South Africa. It was mentioned the other day that in the estimable papers which Mr. Devoy edits there was a letter from a cor- respondent who enclosed a subscription of ten dollars. and expressed his satisfaction that "the war was being carried into South Africa." This communication occurred many , months ago, before war actually broke out with the Boers. There is no doubt that Aylward was in the Fenian coun- cils, and there is evidence that he took part in the Man- chester raid. He has been in South Africa for some years . actively employed in journalism. He was, I understand, for a long time Cape correspondent for the Daily News. It is pleasant to contrast the difference of the treatment , which ill-starred generals meet with in England with what ' falls to the lot of commanders who have failed in France. During the war with Germany there was always some general on whom the ridicule and hate of the moment were centred. Failure in battle was either to prove himself a blockhead or a traitor. Sir George Colley failed for reasons only too clearly appreciated by the public. Yet not a single angry word has disturbed the silence of his grave, and people who write or speak of him extol his bravery, and say no more. This is one of the few pleasant reflections which the battle of Majuba makes possible. The new President of the United States has done a very graceful thing. It is customary for newly-elected presidents to make a complete change in all the offices of the State from the highest to the lowest. In the ordinary course of events, Mr. Russell Lowell, minister at this court would be recalled. Mr. Lowell has, however, received a private letter from the new President, in which he invites him to remain at his post, and expresses the great satisfaction that his con- sent would give him. It will be remembered that a short time ago there were rumours current to the effect that Mr. Lowell was about to return to America. Mr. Lowell has not yet returned a definite answer to this flattering pro- posal. It can, however, scarcely fail to be in the affirma- tive, a matter which will be one of congratulation among the many people in London to whom the author of the " Biglow Papers" is personally known. The breach in the ranks of the Fourth Party is seriously widening. Mr. Gorst says it was without his consent that his name was put at the back of the famous Bill limiting the recovery of small debts. The Conservatives are very angry with the accident by which Mr. Arthur Arnold will appear in the lists against their chosen champion, Mr. Stanhope, on the Candahar resolution. This is an accident for which the Government are in no way responsible. It is due to the characteristic- readiness of Mr. Arnold to put himself forward oa all poss silrle occasions. The sudden collapse of his chivalrouy attitude on behalf of Ireland occasioned by the discovers that Salford was not entirely a constituency of Irish voters has enforced upon him a prolonged period of luietude. The Irish Coercion Bills disposed of, he naturally comes to the front, and on behalf of the Liberal party takes up the chal- lenge thrown down by the late Under-Secretary of State for India. Whilst the Ministers have had no hand in this matter, they will probably not altogether be displeased at this incide it. It has the effect of making the resolution look a little ridiculous.

It is now certain that Mr. Gladstone does not propose to legislate this session on the subject of Higher Education la Wales. The matter is one on which he has no choice. The Land Bill will answer for all the available time of the session. The Commission has not reported yet, and the answer of the Vice-President of the Council will not encourage them to make haste in preparing their report. The question seems destined to stand over indefinitely un- less indeed some ardent Welshman shoots a school inspec- tor, blows op a school house, or makes arrangements for the "Boycotting" of a few schoolmasters. A very remarktble political movement is now on foot— one that may have important results. Ido not allude to the medley of aspirations expressed at the motley assembly over which Mr. Cowen presided on Saturday night. The persons present at the Westminster Palace Hotel were ' chiefly of the busybody class, who, for lack of inclination for more profitable labour, turn their energies in the channel . . .

of political agitation. Many of them represent the real workingman much in the same way that Mr. Eccles, of "Caste," did. The long list of " associations " with high- sounding names represent chiefly from a dozen to a score ef more OT less idle men. Professor Beesly is not a politician disinclined to "go for" anything in general or particular. But even he has shrunk back from the loose and general proposals of these good people assembled to save the State. The movement to which I allude is of a more practical character. It takes the form of a definite proposal by some members of the House of Commons to the Irish party. It is to the effect that should the Land Bill not meet the views of the Irish members, and should, at the same time, in any degree affront the Radical sentiments of the advanced sec- tion of the Ministerialists, that a series of meetings should be got up throughout the great centres of population, and that pressure should be brought to bear upon the Govern- ment. It is part of the proposal that in the meantime the Irishmen should behave themselves, and should by their moderation in discussion in Committee of Supply endeavour to remove the feeling of aggravation which undoubtedly prevails throughout the provinces. The confidence of the Liberals in the success of their cause in Coventry, on Saturday, is not without some better foundation than mere guesswork. It seems that the Con- servatives have had considerable trouble with certain accounts outstanding since the last election, that their delay In dealing with them has caused some coldness and even estrangement, and that the result is disastrous. Mr. Kay Shuttleworth, too, is popular. By the way, what is the exact sum for beer whereon claims are made at Oxford? I hear talk of four figures, which neither the candidate nor the Carlton is willing to wipe off. Sir Henry Jackson has not lived to be a judge. Appointed a few days ago, he was too ill to appear before the Lord Chancellor for the purpose of taking the oaths, and he has been snatched away without taking a seat upon the bench. An illness known to have been very painful anol to have been long existent has deprived him of an honour which he coveted. He was a man of great legal learning and some forensic force; a politician who was a (staunchly Liberal partisan; a companion pleasant and genial. He dies early for a lawyer at 50. It is not difficult to perceive that this may have serious consequences. Whatever the give-and-take principles upon conflicting interests in the Cabinet can alone work may make of the Land Bill, it is certain that it will not meet the views of any extreme party, and even more certain that it will supply fresh opportunities for discussion to the Par- nellites. An agitation got up out of doors would on critical points, have a considerable influence on the House, and might lead to the strengthening of particular sections of the Cabinet, and a corresponding weakness on the part of others. Hereupon might follow resignations and a recon- struction of the Ministry in those dangerous :iircumstances described in a famous simile as "swooping horses when you are crossing a stream." It is said, but this is doubtless calumny, that there is one of the Ministers of the Cabinet who is habituated to pull strings of this kind, and that he is not unaware of what is going on. div.head: TFfE NATIONAL LIBERAL FEDERATION.
div.p: TFfE NATIONAL LIBERAL FEDERATION.

The Committee of the National Liberal Federation have issued to the Federated Associations throughout the country circulars setting forth that it was "the undoubted will of the nation, as expressed at the general election, that the violent and unjust foolish policy of the late Administration" with regard both to the Transvaal and Candahar should be "entirely reversed." The Committee of the Federation considers that the bold and consistent course pursued by Lord Hartington and his colleagues with regard to Afghani- stan deserved the warmest sympathy and support f the Federated Liberal Associations. The resolution passed by the House of Lords last Friday on the subject appeared to have been dictated merely by a desire to injure the Govern- ment established by an overwhelming vote of the constitu- encies, and its effect was to place the hereditary chamber in direct oppositioo to the will of the nation. The officers of the Federation think it desirable that in some definite man- ner the various federated associations should express their approval of the action taken by the Government, and that the vote of the House of Lords should be entirely disre- garded. At the same time, the officers think it would occur to the minds of Liberals that this attempt of the Peers to Injure the Ministry, even when the policy itself was not directly controverted gave Liberals too much reason to I expect, and therefore should warn them to prepare for con- tinued opposition when measures of importance to the best interests of the country with respect to land reform both in England and Ireland came up for practical settlement. The case with regard to the Transvaal is !Mich more pressing and painful. The officers believe that Liberals in the country and in Parliament were agreed that to insist upon the annexation of the Transvaal against the wishes of its people would be impolitic and unjust, and they urge upon the federated associations to declare at the earliest possible moment, and in the strongest terms, their opinion that the conduct of the negotiations now'commenced ought not in the slightest degree to be influenced by considerations of military prestige or of revenge for past reverses.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

littniDAY.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. George Pilkington. JUVENILE THIEVES —Hugh Quinn Peter Cullen John Burns, jun., James McDermott, John Burns, Ben., and, Thos. Burns were charged, on remand, with stealing a certain weight of scrap iron, the property of the Tharsis Sulphur and Copper Co.—Joseph Shelton, a watchman in the employ of the company, stated that on the 3rd inst. he saw the prisoners on the siding belonging to the works. Some of them were on the wagons handing down scrap iron to their companions, who placed it in bags. On going up to them, they stoned him, and he was struck on the bead several times. The stolen iron was worth Be. ed.—Abraham Ball, a driver employed at the works, said he saw McDermott on the wagon, with some scrap iron in his band. He succeeded in capturing him, bnt the other lads made their escape, leaving several bags half full of iron behind.—P.C. Montgomery gave evidence as to the apprehension of the prisoners, and said that, on being charged, they all pleaded guilty, with the exception of McDermott.—Mr. Pritchard, manager at the works, said the stealing of scrap iron by lads had become a great nuisance.—One of the prisoners remarked that he and his companions were in the habit of disposing of the iron at Simcock's marine store.—The Bench ordered that each of the lads should receive six strokes with a birch rod. STEALING A BOY'S JAVlET.—Benjamin Whalley, labourer, was charged with stealing a jacket, belonging to a lad named Joseph Hewitt, who is employed at Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co.'s chemical works.—The youth stated that on the previous Thursday ha hung his jacket against a chimney in the yard of the works, at about four o'clock in the afternoon. He saw the prisoner near the place about an hour afterwards, and the jacket, which was worth es., was missing.—A man named Joseph Edwards, of James-street, said he was in the Main-top public-house on the previous Thursday night, when the prisoner offered to sell him the coat, and he bought it.—P.C. Murray apprehended Whalley, Who pleaded guilty, and was sent to gaol one month, with hard labour. WEDNESDAY :—Befole Mr. W. L. Evans and Mr. George

Pil kington. A THOUGHTLESS FATHER.—James Roach was summoned for nart-payment of 165., arrears owing on accourt of the maintenance of his two children, who are in the Liverpool Industrial School.—The Bench made an order for the imme- diate payment and the costs (total 21s). A VIOLENT YOUNG Max.—Charles Doyle, a young man, was summoned by Mrs Thornton, beerhouse keeper, Victoria. Street, for wilfully damaging a door and window on the 3rd inst.—Complainant stated that defendant and another man were fighting behind the bar, and she ordered them out. They went, but defendant returned, kicked the door, and broke two windows with his fist.—Defendant denied the charge, and called two witnesses, who said that the window was broken by another man—The magistrates recalled Mrs. Thornton, who stated that she was prepared to swear that the defendant broke the window.—Defendant was fined Is. and costs, and 21. 6d. damages. SCHOOL BOARD PROSECITTIONS.—A number of people were summoned by the Widnes School Board for not send- ing their children to school. Mr. Danby (Clerk to the Board) prosecuted, and the cases were proved by the school attendance officers, Messrs. Davies and Woods, and each of the following had ss. including costs to pay :—Francis man, William Schumann, John McDonald, Thomas Tansey, John Hughes, Thomas Handy, Thomas Burns (two offences), Patrick Hogan, and Thomas Cleary. TWO LADS COMMITTED TO AN INDUSTRIAL SCHOOL.— Mr. Danby applied to the Bench on behalf of the School Board for an order to commit two lads, named Hugh Quinn and Thomas Stanton, to the St. George's Industrial School, Liverpool. He said Quinn was eleven years of age, and completely master over his mother, who was a widow. The Beard had paid the fees for his school attendance, but he could not be prevailed upon to go. Last Monday he was birched, by order of the magistrates, for stealing some scrap iron, and it appeared he had got connected with a gang of young thieves. It would be a great benefit to him if he could he sent to an industrial school. In the case of Stanton, his mother was very anxious to get him to attend school, but he would not do so. He was connected with the same gang as the other boy.—The magistrates committed each of the lads to the St. George's Industrial School until they are 16 years of age.

ASSAULTING A POLICE OFFICER WITH A. POKER.— Thomas Dunn, a powerful looking man, was brought up on remand charged with unlawfully wounding P.C. Strickland with a poker, and also with stealing a shirt, a cap, and two pairs of stockings, the property of Joseph Lawley, a labourer, of No. 5, Muspratt-street.—Mr. Swift, junr., St. Helens, appeared for the defence of the prisoner in ths wound- ing case, and Mr. Husband in the one of felony.—Lawley stated that on the 19th June last, he called ht. the Derby Arms Hotel, Widnes, just before closing time. He had with him a parcel containing the articles above-mentioned, in his coat pocket, and whilst he was in the bar parlour the priso- ner came and sat by him, remaining about ten minutes. On Dunn leaving the premises, be missed the parcel out of his pocket. Saspecting him, he followed the prisoner down and observed that he was carryina the missing parcel under his arm. He then went to P.C. Strickland's house, and walked with him to the prisoner's dwelling, where they saw the things. They called Dunn downstairs, and on seeing witness he remarked that the articles had been taken in a joke. He then asked witness to accept five shillings in order "to square the matter," but he told him that he could not make any such terms with him, as the case had been pat into the hands of the police. Prisoner then flew into a passion, and said if they did not leave him he would break their skulls. On seeing Dunn making for the fireplace, as if about to seize the poker, he made off as fast as he could, leaving the ofncer in the house with the man.—ln cross- examination by Mr. Husband, witness said the prisoner wag rather the worse for drink on the night of the alleged robbery. He had heard that a parcel belonging to Dunn had since been found at the Derby Arms, and he had never told him that on the night of the robbery he picked up the wrong bundle.—P.C. Strickland gave corroborative evidence, and added that on being charged with tbe felony prisoner said he intended to return the things to Lawley on the following morning. Dunn told him he would knock witness's brains out if he did not leave the premises. Prisoner escaped after a tough fight, and on apprehending him a few days ago. at Hebburn-on-Tyne, and charging him with the rob- bery, he said, "I am guilty to all that."—ln reply to Mr. Holland, witness said that whilst bringing Dunn from the north, he remarked that when he took the parcel at the Derby Arms he thought it was his own, as he had plan done containing a flannel shirt upon the seat.—Mr. Husband, for the defence, said the prisoner picked up the parcel thinking it was his own. No evidence bad been offered to prove a deliberate larceny on the part of his client—there was no animus furandi shown. In conclusion, he asked the Bench either to discharge the prisoner or deal with him under the Summary Jurisdiction Act.—The charge of, unlawfully wounding was next heard. P.C. Strickland said on going to apprehend the prisoner, and after Lawley had left the house, Dunn seized the poker. At the same moment witness felt his belt taken hold of by a woman, who was at his back, and whilst she tried to pull him down, the prisoner struck him twice on the left side of the head with the poker produced. In the struggle which followed, he and the prisoner gut into the front room. He received four additional blows with the knob end of the poker, and stzuck the prisoner with his staff. The last blow was upon his left temple, and caused partial insensibility. Before be could recover hlmaelf, Dunn made his escape by the back door. In consequence of his injuries he was off duty six days and it was a fort- night before he was able to wear his helmet. On the fol- lowing Sunday he was attended by Mr. Pattison, assistant to Dr. Cooper, and on Monday by that gentleman himself. On receiving the :prisoner into custody at Hebburn, and charging him with the assault, he replied, " lain guilty." —Dr. Cooper said he found the officer suffering from a con- tused wound on the left temple, such as would be caused by a poker, or a similar offensive weapon. There were several other injuries on the head which showed that considerable violence must have been used. Strickland was rendered unfit for duty, and complained of being weak from loss of blood.—For the defence, 'e Mr. Swift admitted there had been an assault committed. Strickland had, however, failed to say anything of one matter, viz., of how long the prisoner was laid up as the result of the blows he received from the staff. He asked that the assault might be dealt with under the Summary Jurisdiction Act —Superin- tendent Brindle said there were ten previous convictions against the prisoner, one of which was for indecent assault. —Mr. Swift remarked that since Dunn bad lived at Hebburn he had risen to a good position in a large works, and had been trying to live a better life.—The magistrates said the charge of unlawfully wounding was a very serious one, and, as it arose out of tbe case of alleged felony, they did not see their way to take either of them separately.—Prisoner was committed to the Liverpool April Selsions for trial on both charges. STEALING PIGEONS.—James Hardman and Edward Shone were charged with stealing two pigeons, the property of John Hunt, of the Vineyard Vaults, Lagsdale.—PrOSeCutOr said that about nine o'clock on the evening of the 2nd inst. he was with the prisoners in a back yard belonging to his premises, and he had occasion to leave the spot, and on doing so he closed the door of the shed and the pigeon cote. On returning in a few minutes, he found the doors of the shed and pigeon cote open, and two pigeons gone. He gave in- formation to the police, and went with P.C. Strickland to the house of Charles Thornton, *here they found the pigeons produced, which were worth 2a—Thornton, who is a dealer in pigeons, was called, and said he bought the birds produced from the prisoners for Is. 51—Shone was ordered to pay a•fine of lie., and Hardtnan to receive six strokes with the birch rod. TREET OF A TROWEL—Thomas Mack and John Mack, brothers, were convicted of having stolen a trowel, belonging to Joseph Hughes, bricklayer, Cholmondlev-street, on the 7th inst., whilst he was away at breakfast.—P.C. Ross found the lads offering the article in pledge at Mr. Syred's, and took them into custody.—Each of the prisoners was ordered to receive four strokes with the birch rod.

a measure upon the character and fate of which -An depend the future of Irish agriculture. The fd Teo, that have compelled the postponement of a se:neme of I land tenure reform,' awaited with such profound I,6l3xlety, are most unfortunete ; but we repeat em- phatically that neither Ministers nor the 'Ministerial Majority in the House of Commons ean be held ac- countable for the delay. Mr. Parnell and his Leaguers so willed it that the Government (cad the Legislature should occupy themselves with measures for the arrest of revolutionary plots and usurpation, instead of ad- dressing their attention betimes to remedies of the real grievances of Irish tenant farmers. With a Government in power less resolute, and less distinctly pledged to do Ireland justice, the flagitious excesses of the agitators who assume to represent Ireland in Parliament, and their scurrilous abase of the English people and Of English statesmen and politicians, would certainly have led to the abandonment of the intention to bring in and push forward a thorough Land Bill. But Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues, were actuated by other motives than the desire to please the Parnellites in promising such a Bill ; and they will not relinquish their purpose merely becauee these irreeoncilables scoff and vituperate. Righteous riders will seek and strive to do the right towards dis 7 contented subjects, regardless of the spirit 'and 'temper with which their efforts are received by those sought to be benefited. It 'is for the sake of the United kingdom as a whole—of the future stability, quility, and progressive prosperity of the Empire— that Irish agriculture has to be rescued out of the "slough of despond" in which it has floundered so long; not only to satisfy the present generation of tillers of the Irish soil; some of whom may have ex- pectations it is hopeless to attempt to satisfy: still leas to please a set of agitators whose manifest design I is the separation of the government of Ireland from that of the rest of the kingdom. The Irish Land Bill, which we hope it will be the good fortune and the great achievement of Mr. Grindstone's Government to. shape and pass this session, will'not see the light as loon as many of us anticipated:, but it will make its' advent yet before the spring of .1881 has given place' to summer; and when it does appear English Liberals. will be greatly deceived if it does not prove to be a measure conceived in the largest spirit of enlightenefi! policy, 'end such a scheme eyeball, when it passes into law, leave no room for any 'lrish tenant farmer to attribute to extract a decent subsistence trim his holding by his labour to the oppressive action of unjust laws. If the Government can get rid of this most urgent of outstanding. questions this year, the country will have cause to be content and thankful, although no other reform. of first-class importance should be compassed thisyear.

" Here lies a Government of light and leading, It lived some years by bluster and bleeding; It managed coastantly to pay its way, By borrowing money day by day, On beer begotten, of water it died, And when it was buried no good Liberal cried."

ROYAL COLLEGE OF Pntsrmaxs, Loloo7.c.—We notice that under the head of "Medical News," in the' Lased of the sth inst., that Surgeon A.A. Mounts, son of Dr. hi ouritz of Runcorn, was admitted a Licentiate of the College on the Ist inst.

The cost of the military occupation of the strike districts in Lancashire is estimated at over £2,000, independentl7 of the cost of the garrisons of police, which must be very heavy. These charges will have to be borne by the dis- tricts that required protection. .

FRIARS' GREEN CHAPEL, WARRINOTON.—The anniver- sary sermons in aid of the above chapel were preached on &today last, by Mr. Wm. Sanderson, of Liverpool. There were good congregations at both services, and the collections amounted to £9 14s. Pd.

Alfred Aylward, who is said to be the adviser of the Boers, was arrested in Warringten in 1868 as a Fenian at the time risings were feared in Manchester and Warrington. When the murderers of Sergeant Brett were executed several men were apprehended at Warrington.

HALTON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.-011 Mon- day evening, under the presidency of the Rev. J. Bateman Mr. A. E. Davies read a paper, written by Mr, C. Soulby, of Runcorn,entitied" The Deluge: was it partialor universal The essay has already been itt the columns of the Examiner The following gentlemen took part in the discussion which followed :—Messrs. T. Miller, "R. Hughes," S. Barrow', and G. Pennington. A vote of thanks was unanimously passed to Mr. Soulby. The large number of members present greatly regretted that gentleman's inability to be present, through illness. Euttcons MECHANICS' 'BICYCLE CLUE.—The members of this club held their annual business meeting on thie,4lh just, at the Runcorn Cocoa rooms. A communication was read from Mr. James Dobson, tendering his resigiation of the office of president, which was accepted. The election of officers resulted as follows :—Mr. J. D. Jones, president; Messrs. W. Marsh, S. Boyers, and T. Widders, vice-presi- dents; Mr. S. Worrell, secretary ; Mr. J. A. Smith, treasurer; Messrs../. A. Rushton, and A. Stanway, auditois; captain, Mr. James Littlemore; J. W. Temperley, sub-captain • Mr. and Mr. J. Crosby, bugler. It was resolved that henceforth the. club should be knownby the title of "Runcorn Wanderers' Bicycle Club." BRICK STREET AND FRIARS' GREEN SUNDAY SCHOOL BAND OP HOPE.—The last of the preeent series of enter- tainments which have been given during the winter by the members of the above Band of Elope, took place on Tues- day evening, in Brick-street schoolroom. Mr. Thomas Shaw, the president of the society, occupied the chair; andi over 200 persons wine present. A long programme of tem- perance songs, glees, recitations, and dialogues was gone through in a manner that was heartily appreciated by the audience, as was demonstrated by the frequency with which they bestowed their applause. The entertainments that have been held have been very successful, not only as regards the object of the society—a considerable number of members baying been enrolled—but also financially, a fact which must be most gratifying to the committee, who have spared no exertions to provide good programmes- Praise is also due to Mr. B. Warburton for the able way he has diseharged the duties of secretary. A MINISTER REBUKING twit ST. HELENS COLLIERS. The Congregational minister at St. Helens (the Rev. R. J. Ward), who formed one of the deputation to the masters during the late strike, preached on Sunday night on the parable of the unjust etoward (Luke 16), with special refe- rence to the words, "I cannot dig; to,beg I am ashamed." lie asked bow far was it right and how tar was it wrong to be ashamed to beg? Were they rot surrounded by those who were not half so much ashamed to beg as they ought to be? The most painful thing that struck him during the late strike was the ease, the absence of shame, should he say. with which men who had been in the habit of working hard for their daily bread took to begging. They would rather beg than werk. Seale of his hearers, he knew, would prefer acting on the lines of Dr. Abernethy, and live on 6d. a day rather than go about asking alms, width, a celebrated writer had said, was an undermining of their self-respect and the first step to pauperism. ST. HELENS AND Diersuur Assocrevros.-The quarterly meeting of the above association was held on Saturday, in Hardshaw Academy. a out of 35 members were present. This is very gratifying as far as the members are concerned, but •extremely unsatigfactory as regards the non-members over thirty of whom•took no notice whatever of the circular inviting them to the meeting and asking them to give nofice if unable to attend. After the readiag of the minutes of the. last meeting, the president (Mr. Walden), made a telling speech regarding the lension scheme. The Secretary (Mr. Enright) read the communications received from the executive, also from Liverpool, respecting the dis- trict union, and 'Bradford and Blackburn concerning half- timers. Mr. Gardner, of LiVerpool, 'was chosen to represnt ' this association at the Easter conference of the National Conference of Elementary Teachers. It was also resolved to support Mr. Bykes:as vice-president, and Mr. Vernon as a member of the N.U.E.T. After some other business matters ihad been gene into, an excellent tea was partaken of, and , the remainder of the evening was spent in an agreeable manner in social chat, songs, reading-4i, music, dt.c. A vote of thanks was given to M.A. Bournes, for the use of the room, and preparing the tea, and to Mr. Ashton, for the able manner in which ix presided at the pianoforte. A NARROW ESCAPE AT ST. EIEZENS.—On Sunday night, an accident occurred in the neighbourhood of St. Ann's which caused some consternatien, and has since re- sulted in eeme •inconvenience to one particular family in that part of the 'town. Not far frem the Bird in Hand public-house, on the opposite side of ti.,, road, there stands two small houses, fAsbably two of the oldest in St. Helena, one of which has been inhabited by the present tenant, an old man named Davies, abont seventy years. The houses stand by themselveo, and from the peculiarity of their peel- tion must suffer a great deal from the inclemency of the weather. On Sunday night about ten, o'clock Davies and his wife were awakened from their &umbers by a terrible ' crash, and itoteeded.hcit a slight effort to make them aware of their situation. Quo half of one sido of the house—that side to be seen from et. Helens—had tumbled to the ground, leaving the bedroom in which the couple were sleeping with only three sides. Help was at ha, and the man and hie wife were found accommodation for the rest ef the night; but they 'slept in an adjoining 'zoom the following evening. The house is a very old one, and the late severe weather has no doilbt 'contributed to the partial demolition of the building. Some men have beee at work clearing away the debris, and • the work of re-building will be com- menced immediately.

Sr. HELENS COUNTY ,CCECRT.—At this .court on Wednes- day, before Me. T. P. Thompson, judge, an action was hi-ought by the Widnes stilkali Company, 'to recover foom the St. Helens Chemical Company, the {ILM of £lB ss. 7d. for damages forbreach of contract in not delivering 50 tons cream caustic soda. Mr. Walton, barrister, ,Liverpool, ap- tpeared for the plaintiffs, and Mr. Seger, barrister, for the ilefendants.—Mr- Seger said there was an agreement between the parties in which there was a clause that all matters in ,s3spnte should be refsrretlt3 an arbitration, Fin A. he asked his ,honour be so refer the matter under the powers which were ,cotferred upon him by the 4th section, Ban 39 Vict. c.:50, 1875; and the Common Law Procedure Act, 1874. There was really only one serious question, and-that was the meaning of "f. o. r. St. Hslens." It was a question upon which a number of gentlemen of the trade could give their opinion from their own knowledge and the trade, and could -settle the matter, on looking.at the documents, in a very few minutes ; and it seemed to him that the application was a reasonable one. Mr. Walton-contended that the .case ought 'to proceed as the defendants ehould have made their appli- ,catian earlier. It transpired •alibsegliently that the defen- dants &eked the plaintiffs to send a man to see the soda campled and tested, but the plaintiffs replied that it was not their bus:ness to do ao. The defendants did not deliver the soda, and the plaintiffs had Logo into the market Cm a sup- ply, and now sought to recover damages for breach of con- tract. His Honour agreed that the matter should be re- ferred to arbitration, the question .of costs to be left .entirely to t&at ,gentleman.
LIVERPOOL PEACE SOCIETY. LECTURE Ai -WIDNES. - _ _

--- - On Thursday evening, Mr: J. C. Ferries of Liverpool, de- livered a lecture in the Wesleyan Methodist Schoolroom, Lacey-street, I Widnes under the auspices of the Liverpool Peace Society, on "Plain talk to Christians regarding war." Mr. Thos. Robinson presided, and amongst those present were Messrs. Martin Taylor, Holden, Davis, Benjamin Brown, and Thomas Snaps. There was a very poor atten- dance, which may perhaps be attributed in some measure to the meeting not having been advertise& The CHAIRMAN briefly introduced Mr. Farrie, and :ex- pressed regret that the attendance was so small. The Lncsrungsz first dealt with the question whether war was as unavoidable as the majority of men considered it to be. He then gave, briefly, his views of Jingoism, and satirised the so-called prestige of the English army. , A sophistry to the effect that war was very good for trade was very prevalent, and the sooner it was destroyed the better. He reviewed the principal wars of the last and the early part of the present century; and spoke in scathing terms of the contest in which Great Britain engaged with her Americaa colonies. It was supposed, at the time of the last named war, that the loss of what were now thO United States, would very prejudically affect the wealth of the country; but they all knew that since that time the development of our commercial relations with the great Republic of the West had• been something marvellous. He said be hoped that he sreske to same who followed the higher law of Christ. It seemed to him that the rules and practice of history were hopelessly at variance with what Christ taught His disciples. Even if a mau sought him or the purpose of taking his life, and if it became a quo, on of his own life to th.it of the man's, he did not think that he could justify the taking of the would-be murderer's life by the law of Christ. It was sopt»sed, and frequent asserted, that the views of ,the members and friends of. the Peres Society were the few, here l crotchets of a w, phi m lanthropists of a very modern, at d a very milk-and-water school. ..He was, however, prepare to maintain that the sin of war, as a religious obligation, was of a very ancient date The Roiiish Church, in the days of its early settlement in England, taught something approaching very closely ,to the Quaker doctrine of non-resistance. The lecturer next spoke of the horrors which frequently accompanied War, such as the destruction of houses, but he added that there were many other even viler crimes associated with it, which even good commanders acknowledged they were powerless to prevent. Let Christian men look war fairly in the face, and not examine it through the light surrounding the' re- pots of' successful generals and the special correspondents of newspapers, and then he thought they would say ' How can I do this great wickedness and sin against God 2" They could not lay blame upon the Government of the day unless they had cleared themselves of all possible complicit,i in their acts. Upon Christ's followers rested the responsibility of- delivering the world from the awfel evil of which i he was speaking. It might be very little that they could do, but let them do little, remembering that Christ's message was "Peace on earth, good will to men." It would be a grand day when the whole world beard the cry "Ye' are brethren, and ought not so to strive together." From every Christian pulpit the world was told that Christ was the Prince of Peace; but he found that the ministers of the Saviour blessed the banners of the army, and attached themselves to its flags; say, sometimes they exhorted men to resort to its dreadful deeds. The avowed followers of Christ, as a body, uttered no earnest protest against war, and so far from seeing any harm in it, they appealed to Jehovah as the God ef battles ! The Christ presented to the world was one who poured out His blessing whilst standing crops were being destroyed and the earth watered with human blood- a Christ who had not a singls reproof to utter through infants died, though the aged starved, though men and women forgot that they were created in God's image, in the hunger despair, an agony with which war surrounded them. He was a Christ who had no com- mand to give to his disciples whilst all this went on,:but who accepted their Te D8U112.4 whilst they despised his pre- cepts! How long was this armaling misrepresentation of , the Christ of Calvary to go forth to the world? Was it a Utopian fancy to suppose that this great wrong could be altered? Were they to maintain that the gospel of Christ , in its very first principles, at its very foundation, ' was an unpractical and visionary thing 2 Were they to say that it was unsuited to the wants and necessities of the world in which they lived? Rather let them say, in deeds ' as well as words, that this faith was a real thing, and that first amongst its reaties was the peace it offered to this war-worn world of ours. All creation longed and groaned for that peace. High over the storm of human passion Christ raised the light which was to guide men to the peace they needed. Let them see to it that no word or deed of theirs hid that light from the eyes of men. (Applause.) Mr, T.Suarts•restt delivered a few remarks. Votes of thanks were given to the lecturer and the chair- man, the movers and seconders being Mr. Lester, of Liver- pool; Mr. Martin Taylor, Mr. Farris, and Mr. R. H. Davis.
A re•morial was extensively signed at the close of the proceedings against the continuation of the Transvaal war.

div.p: 110 CAL NOTES,

The canal at St. Helens is not the most desirable of places for one to take his morning ablutions. The water is repul- sive to look upon, charged as it is with filth of every descrip- tion. It requires a considerable amount of courage to take a header into this collection of liquid abomination, but this is what a plucky policeman did the other morning at a quarter-past five. P.C. Fielding, hearing the screams of a woman on the canal bank, rushed off to where he beard the cries, and found a woman clinging to the coping of the wall on the opposite side of the canal. He plunged into the water, 'swam actoss,und rescued the woman who was in jeopardy. He undoubtedly saved her from the jaws of death, and Kate Donlan, who hailed from Widnes, may thank her stars that there is one plucky member of the force of St Helens who can • be brave on other "occasions than when engaged in " runnin"em in." - The kindly sympathy evinced by the other Dissenting bodies in the town,lowards the Congregationalists, who have this week been holding their annual 'county meeting in St. Helens is an evidence to our church friends that if all the elects outside the pale of the establishment are sticklers to different paths for reaching the narrow wicket gale of Paradise, they can at least recognise and appreciate each others efforts to promote the evangelisation oe the world. Congregationalism has undoubtedly come to be a strong , body in the kingdom, and its annual county gatherings have attained a degree of importance ranking with church con- gresses, and Wesleyan conferences. The meeting at St. Helens has been marked by an outspokenness and indepen-, dency of spirit that will go far to recommend the principles orCongregationalisin to a higher appreciation among the ' thinking portion of the religlous.community. The president: of the Union the Rev. WRwan Stott, of Blackburn, did not I attempt to hide the defects whidh surround and exist in the ,1 'Congregational churches of thebounty, but lifted the veil to the complete exposure of the excrescencies which have 'fastened themselves on and about our professed religious Efe ; and his address served as an excellent prelude to a paper read by the Rev. S. It. Antliff, of Preston, "On how to secure an increased attendance of the working classes at places of worship." 'The president was concerned about the inertia which existed hi church Me; and whilst he fell foul upon the occupants of the pew attending the place of worship; simply from custom, or for the sake of respectability;' or because of some given ministerial prefer- ence, he had something scathing for the ears of his fellow ministers. Some of them, he said, would make their pas- torates incumbencies, and remain in them through long•years ' •for the sake of the living, though the spiritual life of their Churches was on the wane. He contended for shorter pastorates, a giving up of narrow-minded love for old forms, and an exposition of nevrviews of the truth in keepinrwith the growing intelligence Of the people. One of Mr. Antliff's panaceas for the indifference of the working classes to at- tendence upon religious.devetions was to make the services additionally attractive. Tor some time past this line of policy has been adopted in various churches df other denominations, but It hasmot answered to the full the wish that prompted it. The teethed there is a deep-seated hollow- ness in much of env professed religious life, never seems to be grappled with by those who believe they have a mission on earth to bring all,theii4 fellows within their own particular religious fold. Though there is now much running after popular preachers the preaching of today cannot to be success ful be conductedett the:lines followed out by Latimer, Ridley Wesley, and ethers, and- subh heroes in the history of religious efforts. It scarcely ever seems to be remembered that whilst formerly the gospel and other truths had to be brought to the knowledge of the masses by pulpit orators dinning their voices into the ears of the people, the printing press has now.revelutionised the whole system of disseminat- ing the truth, and that the spread of education has-to-3-- great extent lifted the pen on a level withethopulpit. Notwithstanding that people are hedged about on every hand by literature upon religious and profane subjects to repler tion, and that they . can Alnd as much profit in eceietly reading over, by the side of their own chimney corners, the best thetights of‘the first literati and evangeliste of the day, car modern ministers will•persist in regulating their services by clock-work. On the Sunday morning services must begin at half-past ten; singing and prayer roost take up a certain time; and then comes the inevitable sermon, which must he made to last until the hour fixed for the sun to be in the meridian. 'Nomatterwhether the preacher be in "form," no matterhow indifferent his dissertation, no matter bow the congregation may be satisfied that they could be more en- tertaineet and more, profitably engaged eves by thair fire sides, or In viewing the handiwork of the Creator, by the meandering broOk, or in the epen field, the word-spinning must go on, though at the expense often of logic and COM- mon sense, until tke• regulatien hour is struck. This red- , tapeism and truckiing to old forms must give way to re- quirements born of altered circumstances, and a minister be left to czt his serm.an short, to dispense with it ,ditogOther if need be, or to substitute for it an extension of the devotional exerciser.. Conductors of religious 'establishments should remember that thise:s an age in which business is‘carrted on at a break-neck pace, that the wearied and worried have not the patience to be talked at by the 'cloak for an hotneer seat a time twice every Sunday in the e.year, that life is abort, and that there are some people who are above the 4' pride, vain glory, end hypocrisy ' 6f•obtaiting a character for " respectability " by seating themselves in the sanctuary whilst their thoughts are elsewhere. At a meeting, held on the 9th of February, it was resolved, with a view to Ire-open the bank, to issue 25,000 preference shares of LS each, upon which £2 was to be paid o-.p, and to call up £1 per share upon the.ordinary shares.
