FrICTED METHODIST FREE CHURCHES. Winsford and Sandbach circuit of the above denomination held its usual quarterly meeting at Middlewich, on Monday. There was a good attendance of preachers, stewards, and readers, and the business progressed very fairly. It is very gratifying that some parts of the•circuit have come up linasacially to the standard, and it is expected that the plans now afoot will so far supplement or spur up the others that this circuit may prove (me of the best in the Connexion. It was decided that the representatives to the next district meeting, to be held at Aberyetwith, be the Rev. W.J. Hopper and Mr. John Buckley, F.R.G.S„ and that the latter gentleman be auditor of miariion accounts. That every effort be used in and throughout the ciscnit to secure accurate retterns for the religiouseens.us to be taken throughout the Connexion on the 10th of April next. That circuit teas, with tsermon and lecture, be held—one at the Winsford and the other at the Sandbach end—in angmentation of the circuit funds. THE Styr TRADE.—The export trade during the past month has been a gond average, in spite of the *oat and toga. Stooks are much reduced and production considerably diminished by the scarcity and high price of fuel, due to the great .coal strikes. The prices now quoted are fully equal to those of former month, with avery strong tendency upward. The amount exported in February to the United States of America was 12,454 tons, as against 23,347 tone in January; to British North America 2,154 against 2.868 ; to West Indiee and South America' 1;004 against 2,21; to Africa, 1,899 against 3052; to Calcutta, 9.374 against 17,208; to Eastern Peninsula, 3,368 against 4,185; to Aus- tralia, 1,176 against 1,400; to Prussia, 16,731 against 21.066; to France and Mediterranean, 149 against 48; to British Isles, 4.353 against 2,017 Holland, 563 against 1,044; Belgium. 2.956 against 2,867; making a total from Liver- pool of 39,360 against 60,534; from Runcorn, tic., 19.069 against 6,572; grand total from Mersey of 58,429 tons, against 67,106 tons in the month of January.

WIDNES PARLIAKENTARY DEDATING SOCIETY.—At EL meeting of the members of this body on Tuesday evening, in the officers' room, at the Volunteer Hall, it was decided that there was not sufficient interest taken in the society to warrant a further continuance of the meetings.

REVIVAL SERVICES AT WIDNES.—The special revival services, held during the week in the Victoria road, Wesleyan chapel, Widnes, have been conducted by the Revs. C. Eingant, J. Teaseyrnan, and Messrs. T. Gill, T. Simister, and R. Norman.

THE CONGILEGLTIONALIST MEETINGS IN Sr. HELENS,- The delegates who attended these gatherings, which have been held during the week, from the Runcorn Bethesda Church, were Mr. Wm. Handley and Mr. John Wilson.

NurEmu, Psxstoss.—We understand that the petition in favour of Mr. Bradlaugh's motion in respect to perpetual pensions, which has been lying at the Liberal Club for signature, was on Thursday forwarded to Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P., for presentation to Parliament. The petition was 34 feet long.

HOLY TRINITY YOUNG MEN'S CURISTIAN ASSOCIATION. Before the members of this association an essay was read en Monday evening, by Mr. W. Worthington, the subject being, "Sir Henry Havelock." At the close a very interest- ing and animated debated took place upon the various points raised by the seamy let.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.—This annual event will take place in April. The retiring members are Messrs. G. 1. J. Wells, J. L. Muspratt (previously resigned, and vacancy not filled up), F. H. Gossage, Jonas Foster,.and Eustace Carey. It is stated that the candidates to be nomi- nated by the Property Owners' and Ratepayers' Association will, probably, be Messrs. T. Sadler, S. Sadler, Richard Webster, and Thomas Shuttleworth, jun.

RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.— There was a fair attendance of members and strangers on Tuesday evening. The debate on the women's rights motion of the member for Halifax (Mr. C. Nickson) was resumed by the member for Carlisle, who spoke in favour; the mem- ber for Windsor following against. The debate was con- tinued by the members for Nottingham and Burnley, and Home Secretary in favour, and the member for Birkenhead against the motion. The Premier rose to ask the member for Halifax to withdraw hia motion, considering that there was no law on the statute book atisolutely prohibiting women from taking the positions he claimed for them. Ills member for Halifax briefly replied to his opponents, snd then withdrew his motion. The member for Birkenhead gave notice to "call attention to the conduct of the Govern- meet in soliciting an armistice from the Boers, and to move a resolution thereon." The House then adjourned.

INQUEST AT WIDNII.S.—On Tussday, Mr. Barker, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Mersey Hotel, Widnes, on the body of a person named Isaac Watson, aged 55, wile, en the previous Tuesday was crushed between two railway wag. gons at the works of Messrs. T. Vickers and Sons, chemical manufacturers Deceased died on Saturday merning. the evidence showed that no blame was attached to any one, and the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

Swarm To Youieu Mute.—On Sunday evening last, the Rev John Yonge delivered his monthly sermon to young men in the Wycliffe Congregational Church, Rewey-street, Warringtoa. There was a large congregation. The rev. gentleman tog: for his text "Tie vision of Llicla's servant, er the invisible but invincible defenders of the Godly man." Mr. Yonge's remarks wore calculated to inspire confidence in those young men who were endeavouring to pursue an honest upright course in life, and to confirm them in the path of righteousness. When, through a feeling of weakness and the importunities of evil counsellors and wicked associates% they were inclined to give way in despair, they should remember that those who were with them, ready te uphold them in rightdoing, though invisible were more than those against them, and take courage.

Fins AT Win/qrs.—On Thursday, great excitement was caused in Widnes and Runcorn by the immense volumes of smoke which covered the former town, and gave the impres- sion that a conflagration of a most terrible nature was raging. Crowds aasembled across the river, wondering whatever building could be on fire which caused so much smoke as one would Suppose to be made in the entire de- struction of a city of considerable size. It was found that a quantity of mixed tar and pitch, in a large tar pot used in connection with earthenware pipes, had caught fire at Messrs. N. Mathieson and Co.'s works, It was a con- siderable thaw before the flames were got under, but the damage was inconsiderable. Tun Lamer ComaterriON or PIM:MRS.—This im. portant collection of art treasures is, as will be seen by Our advertisement columns, to be offered to the public by Messrs. Branch and Leete, at their rooms, in Liverpool, during the ensuing week. Rarely has a more, choice and valuable accumulation of paintings and articles of vertu been brought to the hammer. The array of talent which the names of the various artists. &c., indicates leaves scarcely a single artist of celebrity unrepresented. It is out of the question to enter into any detailed criticism of the works, but a few of the names of the artists represented will convey a general idea of the character of this exceptional "display. In water-colours there are specimens of G. Shef- fi-ld, J. Ward, R.A.; Feed, W. Hunt, Copley Fielding, David Cox (several important drawings); a large nuniber of the works of P. F. Poole, Orchardson, Getman, Clarkson Stanfield, F. Goodall, Calcott, Boning- ton, Pront, Landseer, De Wint, Louis Ilaghe, Fettie, Mrs. Butler (Miss Thompson), and Dore. There are also several captivating samples of Front, Hunt, Ricci, and Cox. "Old Crome " also occupies everal "niches of humour in this assembly of fame, and Frith, Linnell, Denby, Mulready, and many other painters of equal interest are profusely represented. Our greatest British artist, Millais, is included in the list, and the Ettys, Maclises, Wards, Leslies, and Nicols are plentiful enough. Going back to the earlier period of English art, Reynolds and Gainsborough may be mentioned, and one of the features of the sale will be the series of original sketches, of great interest, for Wilkie's "Village Festival." Many valuable manuscripts and autographs will be included in the sale, the importance of which can scarcely be over-estimated. WELSH CONCERT AT WIDNES.—A large audience assem- bled in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, Lacey-street, Widnes, en Tuesday, for the purpose of hearing a concert given by the choir of the Welsh Congregational Church, Liverpool. The object of the gathering was to assist in liquidating a debt of some £560 at present existing on the Welsh Congregational Chapel, Moor-lane. With a view of assisting their Widnes friends in the strenuous endeavours they are now making to reduce the debt, the choir of the Tabernacle, Liverpool, kindly offered their services gratuitously. They were accom- panied by their pastor (Dr. J. Thomas) and a large number of the members of the congregation of the Liverpool Church; and there were also present a number of Welsh friends from Ditton. Mr. Jonah Thomas, of Liverpool, pre- sided. The concert was of a miscellaneous character. Songs were given by Mr. E. Ellis Evans, Mr. W. J. Jones, Miss J. Helena Jones, Mr. R. Davies Mr. W. Jones, Mr. R. S. Jones, Miss E. Davies, Mr. H. R. liumphreys, Mr. T. Owens, and Miss Kate Roberts. Many of the songs were rendered in the tongue of the Principality. A number of anthems in Welsh and English were song by the choir. The style in which these were rendered made it evident that considerable care had been bestowed on practice, and were creditable alike to the ladies and gentlemen forming the choir and their con- ductor, Mr. Thomas Owens. The vocalists, too, were very successful, their singing being heartily applauded by the well pleased audience. Altogether, the concert was a de- cided success, and as the Liverpool friends not only gave their services free, but also defrayed the cost of their railway journey, the finances of Moor-lane Church will no doubt be substantially augmented as a result. A pleasant evening terminated with thanks being accorded to the chairman and choir. •

THE JUDGMENT IN THE BRADLAUGH CASE.

- - --- Judgment was given in the Queen's Bench yesterday, by Mr. Justice Mathew in the case of Clarke v. Bradlaugh. Plaintiff sought to recover penalties on the ground of defen. dant having sat and voted in the House of Commons with- out having subscribed the Parliamentary oaths. Defendant alleged that in a court of justice he was entitled to make a promissory declaration. He further alleged that before sit. ting and voting he did subscribe a solemn affirmation as prescribed by statute. Plaintiff demurred to the statement that defendant had made an affirmation as required, and con- tended that he was a person without religions belief, and not entitled to make and subscribe a solemn affirmation. To this defendant demurred, on the ground that he was not required by statute to profess any religious belief. Defen- dant's contention was that the Act of 18C3 contained an exemption in favour ot Quakers and other persons for the time being by law permitted to make a solemn affirmation or declaration. When the Act passed defendant was not so entitled to affirm, but the question was whether the Acts of 1869 and 1870 amended the Act of 1866, and extended the exemption of section four to the class of persons represented by the defendant; and it was urged that the Acts should be construed together. After an examina- tion of the Acts of-1869 and 1870, called "The Evidence Amendment Acts," the learned Judge said it was difficult to understand that if the Legislature intended to make a change in so important a matter they should not have ex- pressly set it forth. There was nothing!to show thai the Acts went further than was contaim2d in the Acts them- selves. The Acts were intended to rei..ove restrictions upon the admissibility of witnesses for the discovery of truth, and for no other object. Again, these Acts were less general than the Act of 1866, because they did POt apply to Scot- land, so that the Scotch members woeld not be entitled to the privilege claimed by the defendant. He had come to the conclusion that the defendant had failed to estab!ish his claim on this point, and that the demurrer to the state- ment of defence must be allowed.. The matter of reply did not appear to be relevant to defendant's contention, but, as he understood, the plaintiff suggested that the Promissory Oaths Act, 1866, must be construed as. if containing a pro- viso that no ~psrsau possessing religious belief shonld be privileged to take advantage of that enactment. On the whole, judgment would be for the plaintiff, defendant being entitled to such costs as might be attributed to the latter point, on which he succeeded. Leave was given to appcal, and action was stayed in the meantime.

THE SOUTH YORKSHIRE MINERS' CRISIS: Yesterday, the owners of Cortonwood CoLlieryzaVe iheir miners notice that the 10 per cent. advance conceded some time ago will cease in fourteen days, and their services' will not-be required after that date unless they agree to wokk at the old rate of wages. At the Oaks Collierieg the owners want miners to take in riddles at only the rate of wages. Reductions are threatened elsewhere.

div.head: ANOTHER COLLIERS' STRIKE AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: ANOTHER COLLIERS' STRIKE AT ST. HELENS.

Yesterday the men employed at the two pits belonging to Messrs. Pilkirigton struck work. ' Their statement is to the effect that when work was resumed Messrs. Pilkington promised to pay them at four o'clock every Friday, but they have just teen informed that payments will be made mai Saturday. This they contend is a breach of faith on the part of the employers, and they are determined not to sub- mit to broken conditions. THE TICHBORNE APPEAL. On the conzlusion of the arguments for the appellant, yesterday, the Lord Chancellor and the other learned lords, without calling en the counsel for the Crown, gave judg- ment dismissing the appeal, thus Kffirming the judgment of the court below. As their lordships are the final tribunal, the Claimant will undergo the remainder of his sentence of fourteen years, unless he receives the Royal pardon. ,

div.head: ANNEXATION OF THE TRANSVAAL.
div.p: THE ANNEXATION OF THE TRANSVAAL.

A meeting of the Transvaal Independent Committee wee- held at the Westminster Palace Hotel, yesterday afternoon, which was attended by several members of Parliament. Dr. Kare-Blind save a list of the names ot distinguished per. sonages in France, Germany, Austria, and Italy who had signed the protest addressed to Mr. John Brikht against the annexation of the Transvaal. It was resolved that a de. pntation on the subject should wait upon the Premier at an early dice, and it was also determined to increase all efforts in the cause.

div.head: HOME RULERS.
div.p: THE HOME RULERS.

Owing to Mr. Gladstone's announcement to declare urgency on Monday next for tbe rotes on supply, most of the members of the Irish Home Rule party, who intended going to Ireland to-day, have postponed their visits. Mr. l'arnell and those who usually vote with him will therefore be in their places on Monday, and those others who were announced to speak at various meetings in Ireland, have telegraphed their inability to do so.
ADDITIONAL TROOPS FOR THE TRANSITALL. The war office has decided to send additional drafts to Use Transvaal, and ever 300 men will embark within the next fortnight.

THE NEW ARMY -41E-G-UIATIONS—Lord HARDINGE asked if the proposed regulations for increasing the number of field officers of the line would have a retrospective effect as to officers who bad been compulsorily retired.—Earl Molnar said the regulations would have retrospective operation to the Ist of July last, but would not extend to those who had actually left the army. THE SURRENDER OF CANDATIAR.—LOni STRATENAIRN called attention to the proposed eirrender of Candabar, and strongly condemned that course of policy.—Lord ENFIELD said the Government bad performed their promises though the people of Afghanistan had broken theirs. The Govern. ment had determined to abandon Candahar. The subject dropped and their Lordships adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. THE B.EFRESENTATION OF Notrrnatarros.—Mr. GORST gave notice thaton Monday he would move that the Speaks 1 Wine his warrant for the election of a member for North. ampton in the place of Mr. Bradlaugb, who had sat and i voted in that House without having taken the oath ap- pointed by law. I THE ARMISTICE WITII THE BOERS.— Mr. GLADSTONE said nothing further had been done as regards the armistice by Her Majesty's Governmeut. General Wood had not transmitted information as to how the armistice was brought' about. Mr. Gladstone, continuing, said General Wood had transmitted a telegram, dated sth March, that the armistice was commencing on the 6th, in which hestates that General Jeubert had asked how far General Wood would meet his or President Brand's suggestion, and that he was to meet him at four that day. Mr. Gladstone's construction of the telegram was that neither the Boers nor the British initiated the armistice, but that it was President Brand's suggestion, and on that suggestion General Jonbert made the first step. With regard to peace negotiations, the names of special commissioners had been under consideration, but none had been yet named. All rumours therefore, whether of Cape or home manufacture, were premature.

IMPORTANT MINISTERIAL STATTMENT.—MT. GLADSTONE, in making a statement as regarded public business, said the Government hoped by Thursday week to give a day for dis- cussing the vote of censure proposed as regarded Candahar. The question of privilege that would be raised regarding the writ tor Northampton had raised a fresh difficulty. Votes in Supply were pressing, and a.vote of five millions for sub. vention to India in regard to the Afghan war would also require to be dealt with without delay, That subvention would take the shape of a remission of &lot of two millions, and a series of annual grants. As certain votes for the army and navy, and also the vote on account of the civil service, I were pre.sing, on Monday be would move urgency wits regard to those votes in Supply. It as desirable that the Budget statement should be made before Easter. The Land Bill would be introduced as soon as there was a reasonable prospect of the second reading being taken.—In reply to further questions, Mr. GLADSTONE said the vote of want of confidence in the Government as regarded Caudahar would take precedence of the Land Bill,—The Spitaxma said the new rules with regard to urgimcy in Supply would be laid on the table to-night.

THE ARMS BILL.—The motion for the third reading of the lush Arms Bill was made. Mr. PAYINRLL moved the rejection of the bill lie condemned the policy the Govern- ment had adopted regarding Ireland, and vindicated the action of the Land League. He maintained that the action of that body had been constitutional, and much that had been done was only in accordance with the opinions of those now high in office, who had stated that nothing was to be , got for Ireland except through terror.—Mr. NEWDEGATK supported the third reading.—Lord R. CitcrtcHat. severely criticised the Irish policy of the Government. He eon- demned the manner in which personal freedom in Ireland had been interfered with, and characterised the two measures the Government had all but passed as deplorable legislation. Sir W. Hannon/2x justified the measures the Government had submitted to Parliament, and regretted the condition of Ireland made such legislation necessary. He sarcastically replied to the observations of Lord R. Churchill, and play- fully alluded to the dissolution of the fourth party. lie criticised the observations of Mr. Parnell, and said Mr. Parnell was afraid to disavow the existence of the Fenian conspiracy either in America or Ireland, because the effect of such disavowal would be the stoppage of supplies of the Land League.— Mr. Dawson censured the repressive policy the Government had adopted towards Ireland.—Mr. T. D. SULLIVAN con- demned the Bill, and regretted the Irish members could not prevent its passirg, as the mechanical majority 91 a Government would, at the ringing of the division b swarm into the House from the smoking and reading riy and by their obedient votes carry the third reading. BYRNE opposed the second reading.--Mr. JUSTIN MCC

div.head: ;Zetters_to the editor.
div.p: ;Zetters_to the editor.

THE LAND QUESTION. &r,—The most important question of to-day is undoubt- edly the land question. A country like England, with such an immense number of various occupations, with a trade spreading itself over the whole of the known world, and with such a great love, hitherto, for the landed aristocracy, has, as yet, not felt the great importance of dealing with the land problem. The important, nay, the almost tragical im- portance with which this question is surrounded in Ireland has forced itself upon the attention of those little used to think of such subjects. At our general elections it is the usual way for the candidates to get up a few cries, some of them more or less important, but as a rule, up to the present time it has been more cry than wool. It is allowed by all those whose opinion is worth having that at last we have a Parliament worthy of the English nation, a Parliament quite prepared, and also able, to deal not only with the land ques- tion, but with that obsolete body of nincompoops and im- beciles termed the House of Lords. The people now having the franchise and their political clubs, with first-class literature in the shape of daily papers and periodicals, I saY having all this, along with the cheap literature issued in pamphlet form on every conceivable subject, cannot pos- sibly remain in ignorance any longer, but as each election time comes round must necessarily be better prepared to give, not only a free and independent, but an intelligent vote so that we must have the best men of each party, and no vote, be satiafied with Wilderspool brewers, or owners of broad acres. The people in our large tovrns are constantly having their numbers augmented to such a degree that the struggle for a bare livelihood is becoming intolerable. There is no profession or trade that is not thoroughly overdone; the artisan knows that at least a score of men are waiting for his shoe; the tradesman knows that in each branch of business there are scores ready not only for his shop, but will give an increased rent, each one thiaking or hoping he can make it pay- each profession is overstocked with applicants from parents who are anxious to get their lads settled in life. This state of things has existed for a number of years, and we have been wondering what was the cause. Employers ' have been forced to reduce wages; workmen have resisted by declaring strikes all over the country; each one seeming to be doing his best to injure the other; the country through its landlords and landlaws, forcing its redundant population into the towns. The whole of these unsatisfactory proceedings helping to place the country in e state of chaos with no order or care for the happiness of the people. America we are anxious still to supply with goods; although those goode, in the shape of locomotives and steel rails, may bring corn and cattle to injure the British farmer. We have had a report from commissioners appointed to inquire into the cause of agricultural depression, but still it is the same. With one or two exceptions, no one cares to take the bull by the horns and declare outright that we must have nationalis ition of the land. My readers may think this such a radical and extreme way of curing the disease as to cause them to turn away and pooh-pooh the whole thing. But suppose we put the matter in this way. What is the relationship existing between the people and the land? The people look to the land for the whole of the necessaries of life and, in return for labour given the land does or would yield her treasures. Thus we see tae connection is so close that our whole existence depends upon a fair and business- like method of agriculture. Nationalisation is no new scheme. I may point to the telegraphs, the post-office, and tending that way to the whole of our co-operative societies. It means the State taking to the land, and paying those who have robbed the people a certain per centage, to be agreed upon in detail. Charles Sumner said, " Nothing is settled till it is settled right." We may have one lecturer after another talking of the land laws, urging registration, and doing away with primogeniture and entail. This will merely put off the question, and not settle it right. Private property in the soil is a grievous mistake, because it is practically an ad- mission that certain favoured individuals have the right, if , they cared or dared to exercise it, of compelling the rest of the nation to starve. There are great proprietors who keep large tracts of land for nought but game purposes. The land then ought not to belong to any individual. Stuart Mill says "No man made the land, it is the original inheri- tance of the whole species." Professor Newman denounces " the crude and monstrous assumption that the land can be thel private property of anyone." I remember Earl Fitz- william telling his colliers, who were out on strike, that "he regarded his coal pits in the light of a bank upon which he and his successors might draw when and how they liked." The Duke of Newcastle put the question, "gam I not do as I like with my own ?" The answer is obvious. Private property in land and minerals is robbery. Under the feudal' system the land was assumed to be the king's, but service were required from those entrusted with its management, which they have shifted on to the shoulders of the people,' and all this time the territorial incomes of our landed mag- nates have increased enormously. In 1800 they amounted to £22,500,000, in 1850 they had swollen to £41,118,329, in 1861 they had grown to £54,678,412, to-day, including mines and minerals, they exeeed £198,000,000; while the land tax, which in 1800 was about £2,032,000 per annum, is now reduced by redemption to about one-half that amount. The enormous acreage of our landlords is some- thing startling. Take as an illustration one family, the Sutherlands. In Sutherland they have 1,176,454 acres, in Shropshire 17,495, Staffordshire 12,744, Yorkshire 1,853,1 besides the following seats :—Dunrobin Castle, Loch Inver House, House of Tongue, Tarbet House Castle Leod, all in Scotland; Stafford House, Trentham Hall in Staffordshire, Lilleshall in Shropshire, And Clifden in Bucks. One almost feels sorry for the poor family. 'The late Duchess of Sutherland burnt her tenants Out of 794,000 acres of good land. An eye witness says : " I myself :ascended a height about eleven o'clock in the evening, and counted two hundred and fifty blazing houses. The conflagration lasted six days, till the whole of the dwellings were reduced to ashes." One old woman was burnt to death. The wife of Angus Sutherland and her little ones, ill of the measles, were thrown oat of their cottage on the highway. The wife of William McKay, five days after childbirth, was, with her new born babe and other little ones, mercilessly carried out in a sheet and left on a bare hill without home or shelter. Sir, these cases might be multiplied, for it is only a question of degree between us on each side of the Irish Channel. Farmers in England must form a Land League. I read that in Mid-Kent this is already coming about. Farmers in this district are needing a league to protect them, not only against the landlords, but against themselves; the advertisements on the walls speak loudly of farms being sold up. In 1877, the number of farmers who passed through the Bankruptcy Court was 470, in 1878 the - number was 815, in 1879 it was 1,430. My advice is, let the committee of the Liberal party in Warrington at once make arrangements for lectures to be given on this question by such as Mr. Arnold, who, although lie does not go so far as I do, would at least break down some of the barriers that are now in the way. 11. W.
