-•-- - • - - - NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS. The monthly meeting of this Board was held in the Board room, at the Town Hall, Newton-le-Willows, on Monday Present—Mr. Gooch, in the chair; Messrs. Winstanley„ Emmett, Birley, Forster, Fairclough, J. E. Worsley (law clerk), R. Brierley (surveyor), and J. W. Watkins (medical officer).

THE PROVISION FOR INFECTIOUS CASES. The LAW CLERK said in accordance with the instructions be got at the last meeting he prepared a case for the opinion of the Local Government Board in the matter of Pickering, and attended the committee meeting of the Commis- sioners which was held on the 24th ultimo. Mr. Gooch, chairman of the Commissioners, read the case to the meet- ing, when it was approved, and he had sent the case forward to the Local Government Board. Its receipt had been -officially acknowledged, as follows: "I am directed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of _ . _

your letter of the 25th ultimo, and to inf;rm you that the subject to which it relates will receive their attention." In accordance also with the minute passed at the last meeting, . and a resolution passed at the committee meeting, a deputa- tion consisting of Mr. Gooch, Birley, Mr. Fairclough, Watkino, and himself attended at the Warrington Town Hall On the 24th ultimo. They were received by Alderman Burgess, who heard what the deputation had to say, but who stated that the Corporation could not reconsider the terms on which they had,proposed to receive patients; that the terms were arrived at upon a calculation of the population; that it would not be fair to the Commissioners Riad officers representing the other districts with which they had made arrangements if the terms could be varied; and that the Corporation could not vary them. Mr. WINSTANLEY said the Warrington Corporation would ' not undertake to receive their patients except they had room in the hospital at the time, but he understood the Corpora- tion had varied that because they had made arrangements for wooden hospitals to be sent down if required. Was that • se, or not ? Mr. BIRLEY : Mr. Burgess told us however many we sent they would be prepared to take them. Mr. Wrxxrentny : That is what I understood, and I think it is a very important point. Mr. BIRLEY : He met us in a very fair and liberal way, I think; and as to the cost of maintenance, he said they were loin over that to see if they could not reduce it somewhat, but they were quite prepared to take our subscription towards their hospital on the rateable population of 8,000 for 12 months. The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Burgess met them very fairly indeed. The reasons he gave for not altering the terms, he thought, were so conclusive that nothing could be said against them, and it was only lair to the other districts. The • deputation were met very fairly, he thought, on the whole question. On the question of accommodation, though they could not bind themselves to give the Commissioners accom- modation, at the same time there was no doubt the arranged snouts the Warrington Corporation had made were such that they could find plenty of accommodation, unless there was some extremely extraordinary epidemic; and steps,he had no doubt, would be taken to provide even for that, so that upon that score be thought the Commissioners were pm fectly safe. Mr. WINSTANLEY said he dared say the chairman would remember that the Board declined to enter into arrange- ments with the Sanitary Authority of Warrington, because of a clause wherein they said they would only receive patients if they had room, and the Commissioners thought they might be placed in this condition—they might go on paying the £lOO a year for several years, and when they wanted the use of the hospital would not be able to have it. The CHAIRMAN: Yes; but I think that is modified very tnneh—sufficiently modified to satisfy my mind at any rate upon the point. Mr. FAIRCLOIIGII: I think it would be far preferal le to pay them £IV for the use of the hospital than to build one our OWn.
- Mr. WINSTANLEY did not think 80. He must differ from

that. The Crum:KAN was very decidedly of opinion that if the Commissioners built a hospital and maintained it themselves the cost of outlay would be more than paying the annual rent for the use of the Warrington hospital. Mr. WINSTANLET : Have you seen the bill for Pickering's three children? The CHAIRMAN : No, I have not seen it. Mr. WINSTANLET : £27 for three, and for another case. Dr. WATKINS : For three days. That would have been avoided if you had made an arrangement before. Mr. WINSTANLET : You would be on £2 a week standing rent, and 163. a week for maintenance. The Law CLERK said after the deputation had had an interview with the Warrington authorities, he saw the chair- man of the Board of Guardians, and afterwards saw Mr. Sutton, and entered into the question with both of them, and that morning Mr. Sutton wrote him the following

Hospital.—Dear Sir,—Adverting to an Interview hereon, you in ou lbpl yas pauper v. yepa reytda letterheifffeya Publichuaor tet odtt fhhi se,FHpsGueeebtuaoerTh.dpriAayaten itpws letsv,r shuotegthegcte Commissioners fabimsi theuliti sahtsyrildsoca cases et, Guardians auwvptae rirfulodelnyv andi referred hsecesrorllt of hospital accommodation. In the rural district the arrangement with the Borough Authority treat to be inhabitants all residents I of the district contributing as inhabitants ta the rate out of which the hospital provision Is made. By section 132 the ex- penses may be recovered from a patient who is noos pauper. These expenses will be allowed by the Guardians. The Newton Relief Committee are empowered to deal with the cases. The members are large ratepayers in your district, and are not likely to deal ungenerously. No doubt they have deemed it to be unfair that no provision has been made by the Ccmmissioners, the effect being to have the inhabitants who have no claim to relief treated as paupers. The Guardians will certainly next expect you to deal, for instance, with migrating persons, lodgers, and people who are within the fair meaning of the statute paupers. Take the case of Mary Pennington, removed from Newton to the borough hospital on o l the 2nd, and dying on the sth February. The sum f 82 from is demanded from the union. Had the woman been taken rwi the rural district, the expense would have been at the rate of dlsi as n. sP es er nwt eoenk So I i Ins oymo up ot nh'es cas chargese s (a s at on, owuhui tc ht t ohve e Guar- rtB. mg aadd et huepyo nb etehne fr ur orma 1 tdhl es t br loorto, uagnhci tnhoe de demand would have have been been uau amicablyrdianswil et 1 bseptlieedar and ud to have tohuelymaegttuaersl asweahbaovvee. wTrihte Guardians o terms all round." Mr. WINSTANLEY said they could not carry out the suggestion in that letter, because, if they did, the Warring- ton people would say they would not take them as pauper

cases. The Lew CLERK : Then we should not send them as paupers, but on our right as subscribers. Mr. WINSTANLEY asked if Mr. Burgess did not tell the deputation they would not take pauper cases. The Lew CLERK said Alderman Burgess did so on one occasion, but he said on the last occasion they would not refuse anyone. The CHAIRMAN: Supposing we had an arrangement with the hospital authorities at the present time, how much of the amount that has been charged in these accounts would be saved? Dr. WATKINS : About 90 per cent. ' Mr. WINSTANLEY would not object to an arrangement with the Warrington Corporation for twelve months, but he trusted the Commissioners would go in for erecting a hos- pital for themselves, so that they would have one before twelve months passed. It was a scandalous shame to take people suffering from infectious disease, and put them into a vehicle, and drive them six or eight miles.

Dr. WATKINS: Yes, but when yo‘n have got an arrange- meet you would know of an outbreak much sooner. The CHAIRMAN: I think it would be good policy to make an arrangement for 12 months. Mr. FameLounn moved :—" That the proposed arrange- ment with :he Warrington Corporation for the reception at the Infectious Diseases Hospital, at Warringtou, of patients from the Commissioners' district, suffering from infectious disease, be accepted for one year, from the 25th day o' March, inst., upon the following terms, that is to say, the Commissioners to pay a fixed sum of £lO4 and a sum not exceeding 163. a month for the maintenance of each patient received at the hospital, and upon such further terms as to the removal of patients, the disinfecting of clothing, and other matters, as are contained in an agreement for the re- ception of patients from Lymm at present subsisting between the Corporation of Warrington and the Lymm Local Board." Mr. BIRLEY seconded the motion, which MS carried unanimously. HIGHWAYS COMMITTEE: PROPOSED CEMETERY FOR THE DISTRICT. At a meeting of the Highways, &c, Committee, held en the 21st ult., Mr. Worsley, law clerk, attended to submit his draft letter of enquiry to the Local Government Board as to whether the Commissioners or the Union were responsible for the isolation or removal to hospital of patients suffering from infections disease who had made application to the re- lieving officer for Union medical aid as in Pickering case; and the letter was approved. The medical officer's report was read, and considered in detail. Upon the necessity of increased burial ground accommodation the Committee was of opinion that the time had arrived for the Board to take steps to provide a cemetery for the district generally. The sur- veyor submitted specifications for cleansing the privies and ashpits for the ensuing three years, which were approved. Three tenders were received for the carrying out of the work, and it was resolved that the tender of Mr. Richard Hunt be accepted for a term of three years. The surveyor reported that the workmen were cindering the footpath along the side of the Railway below Park-road and the Mains archway, as ordered by the Board to the eight feet width. It was ordered with a view to prevent the flooding at Wargrave-rd. Bridge, that the Surveyor be instructed to prepare an estimate of the cost of laying larger sewer pipes along the Railway footpath, to replace the existing 12 inch pipes, laid by the Railway Co. The surveyor was ordered to make an examination of Vista-road, and estimate the cost of patting it into efficient repair, previous to its adoption by the township, The CHAIRMAN moved and Mr. BIRLEY seconded the adoption of the minutes. Mr. WINSTANLEY : Itt reference to that part of the minutes which provides for the alter2.tion of the railway bridge, going into Earlestown, I cannot help thinking that oar Surveyor ought to pay that cost for passing insufficient pipes in the first instance. The SURVEYOR: May I just say for Mr. Winstanley's in- formation, that they were laid before the Surveyor came here. Mr. WINSTANLEY : Oh, I beg your pardon. The CHAIRMAN referring to the cemetery question, said it was a matter for the Board to consider and from what he heard and saw, it was a matter of great urgency. Mr. WINSTANLEY asked that an estimate of the cost and plans of the cemetery should be placed before the Commis- sioners. Mr. BIRLEY sail the best thing was to enquire from owners of property whether they were disposed to let land for the purpose. The CHAIRMAN: Would it not be well, gentlemen, to appoint a committee to go into the question to ascertain where the best place is, and see how it can be obtained, and then make a plan. The Chairman's suggestion was approved and a committee consisting of the Chairman, Mr. Winstanley, Mr. Emmett Mr. Birley, and Mr. Pardey, was appointed. Dr. WATKINS: I don't think you will want a very large cemetery. My own opinion is that cremation must come before very long. Mr. WINSTANLET said that was a very good reason why they should wait. GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.

A meeting of the above committee was held on the 21st February. Mr. Brierly submitted drawings for rebuilding the retort ovens upon an improved plan and more economi- cal working, rendered necessary by the dilapidation of the present ovens. The drawings were approved and the cost was to be charged to the Revenue account. The minutes were passed on the proposition of Mr. BIRLEY, seconded by Mr. Fortsnrs. FINANCE COMMITTEE. At a meeting of the Finance Committee on the 21st February it was ordered that 14days' notice be given to per- sons in arrears with their private improvement rates, that unless the same were paid within that time proceedings be taken to recover the respective amounts with costs. It was ordered that it be notified to the overseers of the poor Out if the precept of £l2O for school purposes, issued on the Ist June last, be not paid within 14 days other proceedings would be taken to enforce it. Accounts amounting to BM 4s. 81 were examined and cheques signed for payment. Mr. FAIRCLOUGII moved the confirmation of the minutes, and Mr. BIRLEY seconded the motion. Mr. WINSTANLEy, adverting to the precept issued to the overseers, said they would not get the money out of the present overseers' rate. They would have to lay a separate rate, and he did not think they would like that to be done. The SURVEYOR said unless some proceedings were taken I they would have a balance on the other side of the account —in fact they had a balance on the wrong side already. The CHAIRMAN : I suppose we must make them pay. Mr. WINSTANLEy : We will make you pay. We shall have to have another rate, and you wont like that. We had better leave it over, and we will pay you out of the next rate. There is not enough money if every penny was col- lected. We have run very close as the times have been hard, and we have made the rate as low as we possibly could. Th minutes were passed, with the exception of that re- lating to the overseers. scrtoot, ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. A meeting of this Committee was held on the 21st Feb- ruary, when Mr. Ball, the school attendance officer, read his report, and gave, for the year ending December, 1880, the number on the books as 2,153, average attendance 1,578, absentees 575. On the prpposition of Mr. BIRLEY, seconded by Mr. FAIR- CLOuGH, the minutes were confirmed. TEE MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. The LAW CLERIC said he had received a communication from the Local Government Board stating that they had under cons.deration the annual report, for 1880, of the medical officer of health, and adverting to a statement therein as to the pollution of Newton Brook by the sewage of Newton and Earlestown, the writer was to request that the Board might be informed what steps the Urban Sanitary Authority proposed taking in the matter. Mr. WINSTANLEY : Would it not be be better for Mr. Brierley to write to the Local Government Board stating that the Commissioners have it under their "serious con- sieeration ? " (Laughter.) The SURVEYOR : Would it not be well to say there have been no complaints in this matter? The Surveyor was directed to reply to the Local Govern- ment Board to the effect that the Boards were considering the matter alluded to. This was all the business.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. MARCH 12,1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. MARCH 12,1881.

ANNUAL MEETING OF LANCASHIRE CONGREGATIONALISTS AT ST. HELENS. The annual meeting of the Lancashire Union of Congre- gationalists was held on Wednesday and Thursday, at St. Helens. In the morning the ministers from the various parts of Lancashire arrived, and wended their way to the Independent Chapel, Ormskirk-street, where tea and coffee was provided, and dispensed by several lady friends, who used their utmost endeavours to make the visitors com- fortable, and the various rooms connected with the schools were set apart for their convenience as lavatories, luggage room, reading and post-office rooms. At a quarter to eleven the company went to the chapel, and the Rev. John Raw- linson, Moss Side, Manchester, read a portion of the lot chapter in Corinthians, and led in prayer. The Rev. T. Willis, of Cavendish-street Chapel, the secretary, briefly in- troduced the Rev. J. MeEwan Stott, of Blackburn, who read

" SPIRITUAL INERTIA. IN CHURCH LIE: ITS CAUSE, CONSE- QUENCES, AND CURE." He said that inertia was that property in bodies through a paper on which, as they were in any given condition,whether of rester motion, they tended to remain no. Thus it was difficult, being at rest, to start them, and, again, as they had been started, to stop them. If the principle compelle.d to labour, it at the same time begot the heroism of all commencements. It kept things and persons in their several places and best i relations, and t secured the comfort, hastened the progress, and greatly augmented the success of such measures and movements as were truly wise and worthy. He had to speak, however, of spiritual inertia, and he put the thought in that way because to him the whole outward was the para- ' bleof the inward. The property which existed in matter indicated a corresponding property in souls. Spiritual inertia was a real, essential, divinely implanted instinct within the human soul, there to be appealed to and made use of for the highest and the holiest ends. The impulse was Divine, and yet it was not of itself sufficient. It was meant to be a consentaneous element with the other principles of the spiritual life, and, specially to be under the guidance of the reason and conscience. From its very nature, the prin- ciple of inertia led us in two directions. Looked at generally its impulse was just to continue as we were, but regarded more particularly, since human beings never long continued in one way, as we yielded to it, the principle was apt to make us not only fight against our destiny, but refuse our duty. It was apt to lead us to hesitate and delay where we ought to be eager and assiduous, and, again, at other times, to be too headstrong and impetuous. It therefore began to be as clear as noonday how even the same one Divine instinct, acting upon us in two relations, might nonethe less, because while it was Divine we were human, leave us on both sides in no small danger of mistake. Should further illustration be needed it was to be found with ease and in abundance. It was to be seen in the anxiety and objections which were so widely felt, a generation ago, in connection with the start- ing of their County Union, and again had notable illustra- tion in past years with regard to their new Church Aid and County Federation scheme. Growingly, however, all those fears and misgivings were being felt to be groundless. Pro- ceeding to speak more directly of the principles of spiritual inertia in Church life, he said they might ask in what direc- tionsthi it chiefly manifested itself, and with what results. All some ministers, was ministers shared it—ministers,deacons, church members, anciadherents of congregations—but looking generally over their church life it was seen to show itself in the strong disinclination, which ewy. foundNesv views of everywhere,tru truth ho wereanything dista distasteful vt oe r and were causing great concern to numbers of the older' inembers of the churches. Those wanted simply the old truths, which they desired to be presented as nearly as pos- sible in the old way. The three R's—Ruin by 'the Fall' .. Redemption by the Blood, and Regeneration by the Holy Ghost—were not the elements merely, but the very essen- tials, almost the sum total, of Evangelical preaching It was by those that NVesley gathered his churches. It was those that Whitfield preached to his assembled crowds. And it was by nothing but those that Spurgeon had taken his hold, and kept it, upon the intelligence and hearts of those thousands upon thousands to whom, alike by tongue and pen, he preached every week. It was an apostolic affirma- tion "Other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ." But the foundation was not every- thing. Christ himself said, "Behold I make all things new," and lie was always doing it. The new might thus really be the synonym of the true. Perhaps it was one of :he new views that had used to be received and remembered that it was not so much Christ for us as Christ in us which was the hope of glory. The new views must be preached. If, being ministers, they refused to preach them, it might be to retain their reputation, but it was to lose, to a great extent, their influence. New books were multiplying; new thoughts upon everything were in the air; a new spirit altogether was working within the hearts of men—a new spirit which had given purer and kindlier thoughts of God, and was impelling a larger charity towards min, a spirit which was se: against slavery, and hated war, and looked generously upon education. The new might thus be better than the old. "The good" was a new name, which the Apostle himself gave us for the time. "Prove all things, hold fast that which is good," was his summons to the Christian manhood of the first churches. Though none of their fathers ever before preached it, or seemed, at least, to make much of it, the good did assuredly vindicate itself. What in itself was pure and tended to make men geoerous and true was not devil-born but God-given. If they would mot suffer the hitherto rather disregarded truths to be brought out into prominence, if they would not have the true called by any other name than the gospel, they were contradicting the word of the Apostle, belying the spirit of the Master, making the Bible a fetish, taking away from their minister the chief reason for his full and fearless study of it, and making the man weak upon his knees. For what a struggle must it be for any man to ask God to give a fresh personal revalatiow when he knew his people to believe the revelation to be already complete. And how could the man, even if ,he did pray, in eager earnest faith, ask for taller light when lie knew that one of the first results of his getting that would be a meeting of his deacons, or an adverse resolution by his church, the curtail- ment of his salary, or, without that, the sacrifice of his man- hood if lee remained in his present charge, and the:more than whispered suspicion of his ministry if he decided upon re- moval elsewhere? So they were made ministers indeed; ' servants, serving for their place and pay. But never on such terms, could the man be to his peop?e a prophet, speak- ing to them, fully and fearlessly, the message which he had received from God. Again, if new views of divine truth were thus discounted by the working of the principle of spiritual inertia they need not be surprised to find a great I disinclination for all new modes of worship. Not long since in some of their churches there might be no hymn sung, only the Psalms of David, and still more recently there might be no chants, while even to-day- there might be no choir anthems and no congregational responses. If even an attempt were made to repeat the Lordle Prayer, there were those who set themselves to render it a failure, by their speeches against it at other times and their silence then. They were Christ's own words, but because they were so sense- lessly repeated and often irreverently gabbled over in the Church of England service, as by law established, there were bigoted Dissenters who saw in their use and repetition by the congregation, in the chapel, once upon the Sabbath-day, a most dangerous innovation, and who foresaw if such a thing was suffered the certain rupture by and bye of the sturdy oak of Nonconformity; but, if the thing was only stoutly enough resisted, the early departure of the foiled traitor into the folds of the Establishment. Soon changes were inevitable, and, as be believed, imperative, and some had been allowed to pass. The uncertainty and frequent unsatisfactoriness of their present arrangements, the wild extravagance of some, or the dreary monotony of ethers, in the conduct of their free worship; the loose hold which it seemed have in many cases upon the people, allowing them to sit during the prayers looking about them and to keep coughing, disturbing the silence which was so essential to true worship, made him feel that some change would be advisable for their own sakes. The love of the artistic was growing. Numbers of their people, especially the younger ones, occasionally strayed away to the more varied and popular services of the Established Church. Those persons were equally tired of their set persistency in the "one man system," the indifferent singing, the long nraver, and the longer sermon. Se he pleaded for a fuller liberty. Let them guard against license, but have more liberty. The Establishment even in its prime could not kill them by proscription, but now that it was nodding to its fall they might, by the use of that old, clumsy, rusty weapon, sadly hurt themseves. Another point well worthy of serious consideration was how spiritual inertia led to a great disinclination to any altered methods of church life and action. The spirit of their fathers was in the strictest manner possible to fence about the church's table, almost to the forgetting of the fact that it was the Lord's table, round which the brethren wereealled upon to gather. There must be a uniform and rigid examination of all applicants for fellowship, but their spirit must be kindly and their arrangements as flexible as possible. Let it be otherwise, and, while their creed might be correct, their spirit would be felt to be cold, and their forms by far too rigid. Inertia not only tended to prolong a state of quiescence, but also to perpetuate and intensify such movements as had already begun. Here also there was danger. The cry to-day was for some other and new thing ; and ministers were in re- quest as they were original, and were popular only in a measure as they were heretical. And there was danger of the continued growth of this. He did not retract a single word he had said in claim of a fuller liberty, but he did think it behoved some of them to regard the chameleon ministers and members who were amongst them not so much as dear brethren but as cousins simply. In methods of church life they were having various alterations made, and if inertia were alldwed to be everything they might have a complete transformation before long. In some churches there were übiquitous deacons, but in others it was the minister who was spreading out all over the church's life like an octopus. He alone saw candidates for admission, decided in cases of discipline, kept the church's books, and presided at all its meetings, and regulated its affairs and altered its services according to his own sweet will. Under thisr egime there was an open communion; and the week- night services and prayer meetings were frequently super- seded by conversaziones, concerts, literary evenings, and other popular entlrtainments. The consequence of such a course was a mischievous looseness, and in cases not a few, en absence of anything worthy the name or character of a Christian church. It was well and rightlhat such principles and actions should be resented and resisted as they were ; and were they only more faithful, and in earnest, they would protest and take action against them more strenuously than they did. Because of the frequent aberrations of different ministers and members, the unequal and irregular working

out of the obligations which that had laid upon His pro- fessed people, many of the most gracious souls among them were feeling the present condition of the Church to be but sickly. They were concerned about the speedy cure of its infirmity, its restoration to its pristine vigour and Pente- costal fire. As a cure some advocated special missions. The pressing need of the Church was the re-institution of the lapsed order of Evangelists. Let them not be so much afraid of novelty, for it was their dull, spiritless, over- weighted organisation which was lying like a dead weight upon their churches. Let them break away from their routine and monotony. As the loosening of at least one cord that bound them the suggestion which was made in some quarters was that they should have shorter pastorates. It was only the few men who bad exceptional gifts that could stay for a lifetime in the same sphere, and yet exercise a really effective ministry. More and more, in all the professions, and even in Parliament, we were coming down to mediocre men. This was the result of our generally diffused education and the common life we were living, through the continual massing together of the people in the larger towns. Let ministers, therefore, change more frequently, so that the fresh beginning, with its fervour and I force he thenew place, might court the coming of that breath from Heaven, which alone could give them the full vigour of the life spiritual and eternal. But neither in that was their effective deliverance, in his judgment. He feared they were too restless, and their average pastorates too short. The conclusion which cursory observation gave, and which he was persuaded closer examination would 'only confirm, was that it was those ministers and congrega- tions who were the most changeable who had the poorest tale to give of true, faithful, and real spiritual accomplish- ment, seen in consolidated, peaceful, vigorous churches, beautiful alike to angels and men, for their prevailing mem- bership of strong, harmoniously developed, nobly Christian men, They might need something, but it was no new thing. It was rather larger measures of what they had already. They might need some new and improved presen- tation of it, but they must have the old gospel. Instead, however, of insisting on that, was there not a danger that their younger ministers were exercising theenselves too much upon things too high for them, and exercising their people by the frequent discussion of questions for which they did not care, and in which, if they could answer them, there were but little help ? The peril was that thus the would-be saints were prevented and the sceptics multiplied. Numbers of people only knew of those difficulties from the pulpit, and others only realised bow much there was in them as they Frew some novices trying uselessly to battle with and lay them. The study was the place for such wrest- lings. In the pulpit the business of the minister was to con- firm the faith of men, and to shake it. What they needed most in their pulpits was a return to the preaching, with the simplicity of assured conviction, and the earneaness of a personal faith, cf the doctrine of the Apostles, the doctrine by which they gathered and founded their churches, and nourished the members of them to the consistency of a Christian manhood, and nerved them even to the heroism of a martyr death. The need of the church was not a revolu- tion but a revival. And they did not get a revival by the occasional, spasmodic excitement of promiscuous crowds. The life must be there also if there was to be a revival. The revival in which he alone believed, and from which only be hoped for permanent result, was a revival of the church, and for this the church must be brought down upon its knees. Only let them have Christ in the midst of them in permanent, regenerating, sanctifying influences of His spirit, and they, servants of His, should be even as He, their Master, was ; in the church, most brotherly' in the world, a ministry of all that was most tender and beneficent; and before God, their Father, each one of them, true members of that One Church "which is Christ's body, the fulness of Him that filleth all in all." (Loud applause.) The Rev. JOHN HODGSON, of Oldham, made a few re- marks on the paper, and said that when a person was lamenting the lack of spiritual feeling he was introducing amongst them a spirit which was lamenting the spirit of the Lord. It was far better for them to cease from such judg- ment, but leave it to the Master. He found there was much in his own limited sphere to be grateful for. The chairman thought it was detrimental to remain too long at a certain place. He had been all his life at Oldham, and his friend there very much longer still, but he did not feel pained at what had been said. He thoroughly believed in the supre- macy of the Lord Jesus Christ. who placed his servants I where they were; and he believed in the loyalty of the Christian brethren of their churches, and if they did not esteem him they loved the Saviour for whom he worked. If they thought it would conduce to the furtherance of the Saviour's work for him to go, he believed they had the candour to say so. The churches had largely multiplied, the congregations had greatly increased, there was more liberality and activity manifested, and it would be very strange if they were not exceedingly grateful for these manifestations of Divine power and faithfulness. But he thought they must acknowledge they had not increased in proportion to the population; and, if their people had been marked by zeal and liberality, he thought they must also " acknowledge that it had not been commensurate with their abilities. There was a want of high-toned spiritual life. Where was there that earnest piety which taught men to seek habitually the glory of God? They saw men go to their houses of prayer and worship, but how many of them seemed as if they could very readily sink down into the habits of the world? What was the cause of it? He thought it was in no small degree owing to ministers. They might be men of faith, but was it that faith that entered grandly into God's plan of redemption? Their congrega- tions were requiring a certain kind of behaviour and a certain kind of work from them, but against that there was the question, "Are we to shrink from what our Master would like ?" The Rev. J. YONGH (Warrington) said be really did not feel, the spirit of prophecy upon him that morning. He had spoken so recently on that subject, and that address had ap- peared in a magazine, that he felt it would be an intrusion to speak again the same matter. There were a great many brethren who had feelings to which they wished to give expression upon that subject—a subject the importance of which was very great, and had been most ably handled, and beautifully, by their Chairman. He did not know at the outset where he was going to lead them—(laughter)—but he did hope that many of the practical suggestions which had been, thrown out, especially that with regard to not being afraid of speaking out, the truth would be laid hold of. It was their bounden duty to give the testimony whether men would hear or forbear; and he hoped also there would be greater willingness on the part of the deacons and mem- bers to allow a wider attitude in their church worship. He did not think he had a deacon present to bear him make a confession ; but he confessed he had been trying heed for the last twelve months to introduce the practice of repeating the Lord's Prayer, and he had failed. (Laughter.) There seemed tlehe a Conservative element in that Radical congre- gation at Wycliffe; but he thought it would be an improve- ment if they could once on the Lord's Day repeat a very beautiful prayer. It came from the Master himself, and it invariably happened at such meetings as the present dea- cons' voices, as well as the minister's, were beard to repeat it. He did not know that he felt at liberty, or able. to add anything now to the discussion on that subject. He hoped the members would take to heart that admirable circular- letter which had been issued by the Executive Committee of the Union. It reflected credit on the man who had drawn it up, as he had caught the spirit of their brethren. He had collected the various reports from the different parts of the Union, and he hoped that letter would be laid before the church meeting all throught the county, and that the calling attention of that subject might produce very great and blessed results in their church life everywhere. In nearly all the conferences held recently that subject, it had been said, had not too soon been called attention to. The Rev. R. M. Davrcs, of Liverpool, said the Congrega- tionalistelwere in the habit of condemning themselves too much; but they ought to condemn judiciously. During the delivery of the chairman's address he felt himself agreeing with him in some things, and in the next sentence found himself at the opposite pole—(laughter)—and he thought many of them were in the same position. The introduction of the Lord's prayer in their service had a tendency to crystallise, and would become a form in time. He thought they might, perhaps, have the liberty to use such prayer— and he conceived that even the Liturgy now and again would be an advantage to the Church. If they thonght it was judicious to use it, then they should have the liberty to do so. He had never known any difficulty arising ftom the deacons and members of the congregation with whom he had been associated in connection with the free teaching of the ministry. But that must be prophetical and must be posi- tive. (Applause.) The Rev. E. Hassare, of Wavertree, and the Rev. R. CRAIG, of Manchester, briefly addressed the meeting on the subject a the paper. It having been announced that lay brethren might take part in the discussion, Mr. JEssra BRYAN, of Manchester, said the chairman, in his paper, recognised deacons as obstructions, and he said something to the effect that if the pulpit had never troubled itself with questions about which they had no very settled convictions, a good many of the doubts in the minds of the people at present would net exist; and further, be said that it was the mission of the minister to confirm men in the faith. But if a man were to be taught what was new his faith was not confirmed, but shaken. (Laughter.) No doubt there was full deliverance from those doubts by the new teaching if they could only see it. (Laughter.) Before a minister talked about doubts he must see the point clear himself; in the words of Robertson, "Every thinker must consume his own smoke." Having settled it for himself, then was the time for him to speak to others. As to the Liturgy, that might become a matter of form, though the reading of the Bible itself was open to the same objection, and was one of the worst read books on the earth ; and to allow it to have its fullest effect it must be read with the very soul, and with energy. When the reading of the Bible was per- formed in a perfunctory manner it was of no effect, though the very words were bristling with life and energy, and if a man's soul did not get on fire, it was because he was making a mistake. (Applause.) The Rev. E. M. DAYIES moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman for his address, seconded by the Rev. E. B. DAWSON', and it was carried unanimously. THE DINNER. The assembly then broke up, and the company wended their way to the assembly room of the Town Hall, where a substantial dinner was provided by the Executive Committee. Major Pilkineton presided, and he was supported on his rieert and left by the Revs. McEwan Stott (chairman of the union), T. Willis, R. M. Davis, E. B. Dawson, LL.D. (of Messrs. It. Pilkington, J.P., William Armitage, J.Lancaster), aosf te r) m ahchester, dm.; and the vice-chairmen were—Rev. J. P. Ritchie, Messrs. R. Pilkington, Dr. Gaskell, James C. Sharpies, Henry Martin, F. France, William Srsiarmitshh,(Sutton glass works), H. and R. Lacey. Among those present were the rev, gentlemen of the other Nonconformist

nemtinations in the town, and after dinner the following let Let , signed by them, was read : •• St. Helens, Lancashire, 9th March, 1881.—To the Ministers and Delegates of the Lancashire Congregational Union.—Dear Brethren —As Nonconformist ministers of St Helens, we give to you—on behalf of our churches, as well as ourselves—a cordial and hearty greeting on this the first occasion of your association meeting in this town. We would have asked for permissbm to wait upon you in your sessional gathering, that we might personally present our good wishes to you. repre- senting as you do a large and important branch of the churches of our country; but knowing the limited time at your disposal, and tearing in any way to interfere with your preliminary arrangements, or to create a precedent which might, perhaps, only with ,iffficulty be followed in similar gatherings of other churches, we venture thus to approach you by letter, assuring you of our sincere wishes for the complete success of your present gathering, and for the spiritual prosperity of all the Congregational Churches throughout this large and important county. We do not forget that, amidst all our differences in church order, and polity, and doctrine, we are yet essentially one in all the great vital questions of our common faith. In common devotion to the • one Lord,' in deperrience upon the grace of the same ' Holy Ghost,' in recognition of the supreme authority of • Holy Scripture ; ' as also it a common and holy hatred to all anti-Protestant teaching and ritual, and to all that would interfere with the free life of our churches, we are not far from one another. And in presence of the common foe we hail anything which will visibly indicate the real unity that subsists between us, and which will tend to lessen any distance, however small, that ntay yet separate us in our church life. Ton will rejoice with us in grateful recognition of that kindly feeling which certainly exists among the various Nonconformist ministers and churches of this town; and we again wish toyoa, in all your churches and organisations, good speed in the name of the Lord. 'Peace be within your walls, and prosperity within your . Because of the house of the Lord our God we will seek your good.'—We are, dear brethren, yours in the bonds of Christian love, James Brown, Presbyterian; Thomas Wilshaw, Primitive Methodist; Henry J. Weather- head. United Methodist Free Church; William Charles Taylor, Baptist; John A. B. Harry, Wesleyan." (Applause.)

_ The CHAIRMAN (Mr. W. W. Pilkiugton) said that at those gatherings they never forgot Her Gracious Majesty the Queen, and almost in the words of an illustrious personage lie could say "Good Queen. live for ever." She had reigned over them well and would live for ever in a higher and _ . . . .

better wcrld than that. He would ask them to driiik to her health. This having been done, The Rev. .1. McEwAN STOTT proposed "Our Brethren's Good," and spoke of the sympathy that existed between the various religious denominations. He said they ought to sympathise with one another's difficulties and rejoice with one another's success, and .they should fight against ignorance, infidelity, superstition, drunkenness and carry on the conflict in the name of the one Crnmon Cord.

The Rev. J. A. B. HARRY responded, and said they had done credit to the Nonconformists of that town that after- noon. There was in it a true Nonconformist ring, recog- nising all as Christian brethren. He hardly knew what to make of that word "Nonconformist." What were Noncon- formists? A minister was told by a certain high-church clergyman that he was a Nonconformist. He replied "No, tam not a Nonconformist; you are a Nonconformist." How so? "Because you don't conform to me." He hoped the time would come speedily when that word would be used far less frequently than it was to-day; when it would be dropped into comparative disuse, to be known as a lingual fossil re- main. He saw before him that morning representatives of old Puritanism. He thought he heard some one say that deacons were Puritans of the Puritans; bound up by harsh- ness and rigidity. In that sense he did not think they re- presented the old Puritans, for he saw before him an assembly of happy f ‘ces, and he was going to say portly forms,—(laughter)—and there was as well something of a very Cavalier look about them. He believed they had more work to do in connection with their cause; there was a special work belonging to each sacred church. They (the Wesleyans) were taking many a leaf out of the book of In- dependency, and the Independents were taking a few leaves out of the books of other churches; and though they held different colours they all dipped them in the presence of the one Common Standard. The Rev. J. Buowx (Presbyterian) said that as the coming of the Bishop of Liverpool had given an impulse to the Episcopal Church, so the holding of the Lancashire Con- gregational Union's meeting would give an impetus to not only their own particular sect, but to the whole of Noncon- formists in the town, and he wished them a God speed. Mr. JESSIE BRYAN, of Manchester, asked them to drink success to the town of St. Helens, and lit hoped that trade would revive, as he believed it would, as that had a great deal to do with the sustenance of that organization with which they were connected.

The toast was given, and Mr. R. PILEINGTON said they had heard a great deal about spiritual life in another place, and there was a great deal to lament about, and a little about which, perhaps, they ought to rejoice. They who had been long in busi- ness knew that there 'tad been a depression in trade, as there was: sometimes a depression in spiritual matters. But they could not expect always to be singing hymns and enjoy- ing themselves in spiritual delights. The chief part in re- ligion was working hard and working well, and there were times when they had their successes. There was a time to sow and a time to reap, and the reaping might not have been so good as they would have liked it, but they had to look to the future for the results. It was a great honour that was being conferred upon St. Helens that day- Never in his life had the annual meeting been held there, and it was an epoch in their history to have so many ministers of Christ assembled there, and one which they would not easily forget, art/ the townwould be' very much better for what they had done there that day. (Applause.) PUBLIC MEETING. -- - ^

In the evening a public meeting was held in the Congre- gational Chapel, presided over by Mr. Hy. Lee, M.P. There were also on the platform, besides several ministers, Mr. W. W. Pilkington and Mr. R. Pilkington. The Rev. R. M. DAYIF.C, one of the secretaries of the Union, read the seventy-fourth annual report of the Union. It stated that the previous report was rather discouraging in tone, for although in financial results there was the increase n upon former contributions, they did not meet he exhiatexistingclaims. The statement of the treasurer showed that t e col lections and subscriptions in the past year had reached an amount enequalled hitherto. The year began, not Church Aid only with a deficit, but with a balance owing to th Society of £320. This had been met, and, deeply impressed by the. fact of their obligations to promote home missionary work, the committee had only recommended such grants as were needful for efficient working in the county, but had promised a contribution to the general fund of at least £l7O. It must be remembered, however, that this was not an in- crease of, or a new, expenditure, but a less amount actualjy than had been formerly contributed. The statistical sheets of the reports of the stations for the past year showed pro- gress in moot of the missions and churches. Further assis- tance was not required in two cases, and in two others pros- perity was indicated by less assistance being sought. Im- proved arraneomnts and enlarged accommodation had been " executed at five stations, and at another vigourons efforts had been called forth by the erection of i a manse, t being impossible to rent a house for the ministers. School chapels ba been opened at three stations, and handsome and com- modious houses of prayer had been erected at three ether stations. New structures for religious worship and instruction had been opened in four localities, and the hope was cherished that the Lancashire Chapel Building Fund would be so augmented as to afford people the encouragement they required. One devoted and earnest agent had died since the issuing of the last report, and two ministers had resigned, in order to enter upon new spheres. Three churches before vacant had wel- comed pastors, and one new church had been formed under auspicious and hopefnl circumstances. The commtee had sought to work two stations together, and had succeeded so well in the Fylde district that fresh arrangements had been made to do likewise in two other stations. Much labour had been got through adring the year, and the strength pat forth had not been "spent for naught." Congregations numbering in the aggregate 14,516 had heard the Gospel preached on the Lord's day, 349 persons had been received into Church fellowship, and 211 names had been erased from the Church records through death, removals, &c. The Sun- day schools were, on the whole, in a healthy state, the num- ber of teachers and scholarsbeing favourable when compared with former lists. The diffusion of pure literature, promo- tion of temperance, &c., had been carried on with success. The total amount of money raised at the ta-airso iozsmstoatilosnss, during the year was .£14,002 55., and oh I supplemented by grants voted at former meetings, had been paid to stated and occasional ministers; and £2,445 to the reduction of debts and improvement of premises. For the support of schools £1,480 had been given, and the balance of the amount had gone to defray incidental expenses and to assist benevolent objects. The report, in conclusion, re- ferred to the death of Mr. William Crosfield, J.P., of Liver- pool, saying that the Union for the past forty years had had no more attached friend. His regular attendance at the annual and district meetings made not only his name but his person familiar to them all. It could even be per- ceived by the casual observer that in the deceased gentleman there was a good man "full of faith and of the Holy Ghost." His utterances always had been kind, his aspirations gener- ous, and accordant with these were his actions. The CHAIRMAN, who was received with applause, moved the adoption of the report, which he said presented two aspects, one of which was that they rejoiced at the work done, though they mourned at the loss they had sustained, hut that must always be the case in every human assembly. They were passing to and fro, but many young men were rising up around them, and those who had attained to years would soan have to pass away from their midst; but this should not give them the slightest uneasiness or cause them to despair of the future. It was better, he thought, that some of them should drop out of the way and make room for those who came afterwards, and he hoped many young men would occupy the position of usefulness, and with more power and more energy fulfil the great object they had in view in that union. They had passed and were passing through a time of trial, and since their union was federated with their Church Aid Society they had had to pass through a period of trial greater than any they met for many years. This time of trial served another purpose ; it not only brought out efforts which probably otherwise would not have been brought forward, but it was a test of their Christian character. (Applause.) They had every confidence in the great principles they were endeavouring to advocate. In this country, as in all countries, the greatest amount of good could only be effected amongst the masses upon a religious basis. (Applause.) In many quarters there was a sceptical feeling, he was afraid, promoted by young men; but that, he thought, would pass away. On occasions like the present it was well for them to look fairly at the great results from that association. Religion, when looked upon as a matter of form, was a very injurious thing, but when ; took posses- sion of the heart it inspired a man with new 'motives, and moved him to act from a sincere 1014' to his fellows, and from a sincere desire to fulfil his duty to God. They must

try in every possible way to show that they were animated by deep, earnest feelings, which would find their expression in acts of liberality, and also in acts of devotion to the ser- vice of God. That union should be an incentive to labour in spreading abroad the principles of the Word of God. Those of them who could look back in the past could feel how much advantage had accrued to them, because they had been led in the paths of righteousness and overcome difficulties to which they had been exposed, and he believed that every young man who conscientiously tried to work for God received not only the reward to his own person, but received a reward in the blessing in relation to all his per- sonal substance. He had never known it otherwise. When a young man commenced life, and tried to fulfil his duties and laboured bard, he had never known him to fail. As to chapel debts, he thought it was an injury to keep on build- ing chapels when there was no prospect of a speedy clearing off of the debt. The ready money system in this country would prove to be a wonderful advantage. They ought to conduct their church business as carefully as they did their own business in their counting houses, and not only in respect to cash matters, but also in respect to the other matters of church management, such as properly reading the minutes, and drawing up a balance sheet regularly; in fact a church should be a model of the best way in which a class of persons could be conducted. (Applause.) He was afraid they had not always thought of that. A church should be an example both in regard to spirituul and temporal transactions. He could not separate his business life from his church life, and he felt he was bound to carry out in his church work all the principles he recognised in his business, and the principle of "What thy hand finds to de, do it with all thy might," should be acted upon in all their transactions. (Applause.) Mr. W. W. PILKINGTON briefly seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. The Rev. Giles Scow, of Knowle Green, then read a paper on "A country pastor's work and experience." The scene of his labour was Knowle Green, a plek.santly situated country village, 9 miles from Preston, 9 from Blackburn, 9 from Clitheroe, and 9 from the great Stonyhurst college. (Laugh- ter.) Tbe population was about 600 for two miles round, and the only place of worship in the place was his own, so that he was bishop of the diocese. (Laughter.) Congrega- tionalism first found its local habitation in that village through the hands of a godly, devoted man William Hay- hurst, who came from Blackburn. Be had been an active, I useful, and energetic member under the pastoral care of the late Dr. Fletcher. The morals of the people of Knowle Green were at that time very low; drunkenness, prize-fight- ing, and football matches being played on Sunday; the people were in spiritual darkness without God and hope in the world. Ultimately a chapel was built which cost £lOO and accommodated 200 people; and the people digged for the foundation and carted atone and bricks. The cause grew and flourished, and Mr. Hayhurst was called to become its pastor. For 29 years that God-fearing man toiled and laboured on, then entered into rest, leaving behind him a name which was universally deplored. After that, pastors ' were supplied from Clitheroe. He was one of the number and received a unanimous call to be pastor. He accepted the call and commenced his labours in 1359 having pre- viously been engaged with others in preaching at times at Tosside, Martin Top, Wiswell, and Wyming Houses. and they took their provisions with them and drank in the brook by the way. (Applause.) It was a good school for training. (Laughter.) Many wise, practical lessons proved eminently useful t 3 him. After labouring at Knowle Green four years he was brought face to face with anew difficulty, employment being scarce, but they managed to tide over the difficulty and they opened a small tibernacle at Longridge,a short distance off. For four years he went every Thursday, receiving for his labours £1 a quarter, which was a decided advance on that given by the trustees at Waterfold— (laughter)—who gave £1 for four yearsand a vote of thanks. (Loud laughter.) Ultimately they at Knowle Green secured a place which should have been a public-house for £3OO able to accommodate 300 people, and it was now generally admitted to be the neatest and the prettiest chapel for 50 miles round. (Cheers.) They opened their new sanc- tuary in 1861, at a cost of £5OO, and it was declared on the day of opening to be free of cost. Among the numerous contributors were Lord Derby, the Marquis of Hartington, and Mr. F. W. Grafton, M.P. (Cheers.) They had now a sick society worth £9OO, and during the 23 years he had been the pastor a great work had been accomplished. (Applause) ATTENDANCE OF WORKING CLASSES AT SUNDAY SERVICE.

The Rev. SAMUEL R. ANTCLIFF, of Preston, read a paper on "How to secure an increased attendance of the working classes at public worship." He said that in eight large towns in this county, it appeared from statistics all denomi- nations together did not provide sitting for more than 32 per cent, of the population, and those towns were Manchester, Salford, Liverpool, Bolton, Rochdale, Oldham, Warrington, , and St. Helens. To the argument advanced by some "that ' they worshipped God in nature's temple under the vaulted roof of Heaven with the birds as choristers," he asked how many of those walked into the country for the purpose of worshipping God. There were disrespectful sentiments ex- pressed to the ministry, not uncommonly by the working classes. But to prepare and deliver three discourses and an extra address or two in the week, and to lead the devotions of others when the stated time arrived, though his own brain be weary or his heart sad, was work enough for an ordinary man, and if done fairly well ought to be received with that same generous sympathy of which the minister was expected to give so much; but when they considered the amount of correspondence, the calls, and the presiding over all sorts of classes, baptise the children, marry the young people, and bury the dead, it was highly ridiculous and scornworthy to speak of ministers in general as a selfish body of men. To secure an increased attendance they must remove hindrances in the shape of the attractions of the public-house, and ex- cessive charges for pew rents. He would have the poor man feel as welcome to his Father's house as his richer brother. He should neither be driven to the free sittings unless all were free; nor be bidden to take the lowest room in an uncomfortably situated pew. If there be seat rents let the working man pay as much as he could afford honestly and fairly, and let the middle class and wealthier members of the congregation see to it that the deficiency be made up by their gifts. He would have all pews cushioned and carpeted alike, and the first corner should he first served. Having done this, they should go amongst the people and compel them to come in," and this should be done by all the members and not only the minister. The services should be made as attractive as it was possible to make them with- ' out interfering with their great and primary purpose. The Rev. ROBERT CRAIG, of Manchester, read a Paper on" Christian union approved and maintained by inde- pendents." The Rev. T. CAINE moved, and the Rev. R. J. IVA" seconded, a vote of thanks to the Chairman, Mr. Ward re- marking that the visit was an era in the history of St. Helens, and would not soon be forgotten. BUSR,TESS MEETING. The annual business meeting was held on Thursday morning, Mr. William Armitage, the treasurer, presiding. The TREASURER said the contributions to the Union had been as follow: Blackburn District, £3lB, as against £283 the year previous; Liverpool District, £1,102. against £1,016: Manchester District, £1,603, against £1,870 ; Pres- ton. £203, against £177. They, began the year with a debt of £360 16s. 11d.; they had paid to the London Board £320. Lancashire had given £420 towards the Church Aid Society during the year. The receipts had been £3,332, and the expenditure £3,539, leaving £207 on the wrong side, but that showed they were in a much better position than they were before. £13,000 they had invested in various ways. Mr. ROBERT MANSERGH moved the adoption of the state- ment, and Mr. ALFRED BARNES, J.P., seconded the motion, remarking that they should not forget their poorer churches that were struggling hard. Though the London Missionary Society had its claim upon them, they should not forget their own country. On the motion of Mr. MORTON SEABEES, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Armitage, the treasurer. ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN. The Rev. John Hutchison, M.A., Ashton-under-LYne, was elected chairman of the Union, on the motion of the Rev. M`Ewsw, of St. Helens, seconded by Rev. T. WILLIS, of Manchester.

NEXT ANNUAL MEETING. A letter of invitation from the Rev. H. Davies, of Burn- ley, was read, desiring that the nest annual meeting should he held at Burnley. The Rev. T. WILLIS moved that the invitation be ac- cepted. This was seconded by the Rev. Mr. BOLTC,N, of Burnley, and carried. The secretaries, the Revs. R. M. Davis and T. Willis wero re-elected.

THE REGISTRARS PRESENCE AT MARRIAGES. The Rev. J. WAYMAN, of Blackpool, moved "that the annual meeting of the Congregational Union of Lancashire desires to express its conviction that the official presence of the registrar at Nonconformist marriages is contrary to the spirit of religious liberty, a frequent source of much annoy- ance, inconvenience end expense to persons getting married, and in every sense a grievance which ought to be removed ; it also wishes to record its opinion that measures such as Mr. Briggs was about to bring into Parliament, and framed upon the Scotch Act of 1878, is calculated to meet the wishes of Nonconformists generally and to give that relief they seek. This meeting further pledges itself to support Mr. Briggs in every possible way." (Applause.) That was a pretty strong resolution. He said nothing against the registrar himself, but the inconvenience and expense of the present arrangement drove two out of three to the Church of England to get married; and they ought to eater their protest against state control which forced the registrar to witness whether A B would have C D in a proper and legal form. (Laughter.) The Rev. H. CAMPBELL 'seconded the motion, and it wag carried unanimously.

THE TRANSVAAL WAR The Rev. W. H. Dun Err, of Manchester " that ter, moved this meeting has heard with the greatest satisfaction of the armistice coricluded with the Boer's, and earnestly hope.? that no consideration of national and military prestige will be suffered to prevent such honourable conce.ssions as may bring to a close a war which it regards as unnecessary and unjust." (Applause.) The Rev. JAMES CLOUGH of Manchester, seconded the motion, which Was carried Unanimously; and the meeting then adjourned to the Town Hall to

°At. Inst

and then put it on the train. On arriving at St. Helene he attempted to ride the horse which threw him three times. He asked that prisoner might be detained until he had received a telegram from the superintendent of pollee at Mold.—Prisoner denied being drunk, but said the horse threw him. His character could be learnt by writing to nergeani Lawless of Rainford.—The application of Mr. Johnstone was granted and the prisoner fined 75. 6d. and costs for being drunk. A groLENT INvem.—Patrick Mitchell was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Sutton, on the 12th February, and also with assaulting P.S. Banks. Prisoner pleaded guilty. P.S. Banks said the prisoner with about 20 others, was making a disturbance at Wonky Brow. Witness told them to be quiet and go home like good fellows. They refused to do so and shouted "Lets Boycott him; lets skull drag him; no sureeder boys." Several of the men assaulted witness, and prisoner threw a piece of slag, which broke his helmet and hurt him. Prisoner who appeared very ill, said he had only been out of the workhouse hospital a month, and had not been able to eat anything in the cells. He was continually spitting blood, and looked "a likely man to Boycott anybody."—He was fined £5 and costs, the same as ' the ether prisoners, who had been previously dealt with. MONDAY.—Before Messrs7V, L. Evans and Willis. TRAVELLING ON THE RAILWAY WITHOUT A TICKET.— Thomas Kilshaw was charged with travelling on the rail- way with intent to avoid payment. —George Snow, foreman porter, said prisoner arrived at the St. Helens station by the 11-15 p.m. train, on Saturday, from Liverpool. He had no ticket, and refused to pay his fare. Witness told him to stand on one side until the other passengers• had left the station, but he got out and ran away.—P.C.lreland said the prisoner had uid. in his possession when apprehended.— He was fined Sc. and cost, or seven days' imprisonment. MIDNIGHT DISTURBERS.—Cormick Powell was charged with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting a police con- stable whilst in the execution of his duty; also with assault- ing James Hart, on Saturday night.—Mary Powell was charged with assaulting the police.—P.t. Macfarlane said that about twelve o'clock midnight a row was going on in a public house in Sandfield Crescent; and he was told that the female prisoner had stabbed a man. He went there, and found that the man had only a slight scratch on the thumb. The landldrd said he wished the prisoners to be potent. He took the female prisoner into custody, but he allowed her to go into her own house for the purpose of fetching somel clethes. She went upstairs, and as he was passing the bot- tom of the stairs, the female prisoner threw the contents of a chamber utensil upon him, and afterwards broke the vessel upon his head. He took the female prisoner into custody, the male prisoner following and swearing at them. The female prisoner lay down in the street, and the male prisoner came up to P.C. Sanguine and struck him several times in the face. At this time Mr. Hart, borough engineer, came ) upon the scene, and got hold of the male prisoner. The female prisoner struck witness twice in the face at the police station.—P.C. Sanguine gave corroborative e idence.— James Hart said he was passing the end of Saudfield Crescent when he heard a woman crying out "murder." He ran to where he thought the disturbance was, and he found two con- stables trying to take the female prisoner into custody. The male prisoner came rushing up to the officer Sanguine, whom he hit en the back, the force of the blow nearly knock- ing down the officer. The male prisoner attempted to deliver another blow, but was stopped by witness, who, at the request of the officer, kept firm his hold of the prisoner; and afterwards accompanied the officers to the Town Hall with the prisoners.—Saperintendent Johnston said he did not think their worships could have two worse prisoners before them. The female prisoner had been up 34 times for drunken- ness, breathes of the peace, and prostitution; and the male prisoner had been 18 times before the magistrates.—Mr. Evans': What is heti—Superintendent Johnstone: He is a labourer, and she is a prostitute' they are married.—Male prisoner: If I had means I would make you prove that word; I would that' I would make yen prove your words.—Superintendent Johnstone: Well,they may not be married, but they live together. I don't know whether they are married or nob—Mr. Evans: You appear to be about as bad characters as exist, and we shall give you the utmost penalty in our power. Six months' imprisonment with hard labour for the woman, and Cormick Powell will have six months' bard labour for the assault upon the police, and two months for the assault upon Mr. Hart.—The male prisoner: It a good job you can't say any more. MESSRS. PILKINGTONS AND THEIR APPRENTICES .—mar.) Swift, on behalf of Messrs. Pilkington Bros., brought a claim against Edward Charles D. Lee, of £1 45., for absent- ing himself from work; and an order was also &eked folyto compel defendant to attend to his werk.—Mr. Swift said de- fendant was bound to servo Messrs. Pilkington Bros. as an apprentice sheet glass maker for six Tears and nine months, from April 15th, 1876, so that on the 15th April next, he would have completed five years. His wages at.present were ngFaorcesrotmaieu tiammeoptianett of he whaodrkbeeken eforeumldweearrnb mitosr"e btuhtanbythdaoti. and pretended that his absence had been caused by sickness. All that was untrue, he could prove conclusively; and when he was asked to bring a medical certificate he did nothing of the sort, but on one occasion produced a medicine bottle. He would call the landlady with whom he lived'who would say that he got the medicine bottle but did not use any 'quantity of the medicine. In the month of Webruary he owed his landlady some money, stud she went with him to the works and an order was got from one of the cashiers that 10s. should be advanced to enable him be pay his land- lady what was owing. The landlady had not time' to wait, the cashier not being in, but told the defendant to get the money, which he did, and she had not -seen the defendant or the money since.—John Edmondson, general works manager, at the Crown and Sheet Glass Works, and one or two of the men proved that the defendant had been absent from work. —Charlotte Grime said the defendant bad heed with her a short time, and although he kad obtained a bottle of medi- cine he bad only once tasted it, and he was not ill,'hut was in the habit of staying out late at night, playing the flute and cencertina.—The money was ordered to be .paid by weekly instalments, and an order was madefor his-return to work. STEALING. A WINDOW BLIND AND CLOGS. Julia Nokeley, a widow, who said she had "three orphans," was charged with stealing a window blind, value 4d.,,the pro- perty of David Kenny, licensed victualler, Liverpool-road, on Saturday night.—'Prisoner was found on the !adding of the staircase by the landlady, who asked 'her what she was doing there. She said "I am in the wrong place," and to a man at the bottom she said "We are wrong here, Jim." She afterwards saw that a window blind was missing and told her husband, who immediately afterwards found' the prisoner in the backyard, where, on seeing him she dropped the window blind.—She was then charged with stealing a pair of clogs, value 45., the property of Edward ,Itimmer, clogger, Bridge-street—The woman said she had been "teetotal these long three years, but 'broke on faturday night," and hoped the Bench would be lenient with her.— On the first charge she was committed for 7 days, and'l4 days on the other.—Prisoner: Thank your worship; long life to you. DISCORD IN TILE WORESHOP.—John Fairhurst, a striker at the smithy of Messrs. Pilkingtons' Bottom Works, eum- mooed Samuel Winstanley, the foreman smith, for assault- ing him on tile morning of the let March; and Winstarnley, for whom Mr. Swift appeared, summoned Fairhurst for assaulting him on the same date.—Fairhurst made a long statement from which it appeared that shortly before break- fast on Tuesday he was called by the foreman to finish painting a cart which the foreman had set him to do the previous day. Fairhurst alleged that the foreman imputed all sorts of bad conduct to him, and struck him in the face, saying that he and Eaves were a good pair to be "chucked" into the "cut." He (complainant) protested against such' -remarks, and said that the leaving of the cart in an Un- finished state was merely a mistake. Ultimately the fore- man got him across an anvil, and commenced to abuse him in such a fashion that he was obliged to defend himself, and he did strike him ihtiie face.—Frederick Travis, an appren- tice, and William Eaves, a striker, said that Winstanley, the foreman, struck the first blow; and the first witness, in answer to Mr. Swift, said that Fairhurst used bad language to Winstanley.—Whistanley was then put into the witness box and he said that Fairhurst, on being told to finish the Cart, became very violent, and a quarrel and struggle en- sued—.A witness was called, who said that both the men were striking each other "at once" when he saw them.— Both cases were dismissed.

div.head: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL.

HEALTH COMMITTEE. A meeting of the Health Committee was held on Wednes- day, at the Town Hall, Cioaacillor Twyford presiding. There were also present the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Councillors Foster, Brook, Wilcock, Belsher, Walker, and Messrs. J. H. Craik (deputy town clerk), McNicoll (medical officer), and Hart (surveyor.) CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACT. The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK stated that in accordance with a resolution passed at the last meeting in reference to the above Act, he wrote to the local authorities mentioned, and with the exception of Lancaster all the authorities of the places named agree with the St. Helens Authority to require a second license when animals were removed out of their districts into the St. Helens district.

iNSANITARY STREETS. The SURVEYOR ealleti attention to the insanitary condition of Wood, Vernon, and Barber-streets, which were neither paved, flagged, nor sewered. On the motion of tile MAYOR, the matter was referred to the Paving Committee.

TILE GLOBE ALKALI WORKS AND THE INSPECTORS. The SURVEYOR reported that a wall belonging to the Globe alkali works had fallen into the brook, causing an obstruc- tion and preventing access to the drains. He wrote to the Company calling their attention to the matter, but they denied the right of the Authority to interfere. He subse- quently received a letter from the solicitor to the Company, Mr. H. L. Riley, withdrawing the terms given the inspectors to enter the Company's premises. The DEPUTY CLERK, in answer to the chairman, stated the Act of Parliament set forth that the local authority had power to enter premises for a certain purpose, and that if the Company refused them admission a justice of the peace had power to issue a warrant empowering them to make such entry. The SURVEYOR said the officers would require to go ori to the premises for the purpose mentioned in the Act. It was directed that if the owners refusal the inspectors admission, an order be applied for to empower the inspectors logo upon the premises. • -

mortality per 1,000 inhabitants during the first week was 1762, secend week 15.86, third 22.03, and fourth 2203. Samples of that portion of the brook called Eccleston Brook had been taken by *lnspector Williams from the usual places between Spray Bridge and Messrs. Lyon's bottle works, and submitted to him. All were found to be free of acid, but one sample from the Bridgewater works drain, taken in Messrs. Daglish's works, contained a trace of acid, about ten grains to the gallon. Samples of the brook where it had become Hardshaw Brook had been taken by Inspec- tor Houghton from usual places between Messrs. Lyon's bottle works and Langtree-street. These did net contain any acid. Water taken from drain belonging to St. Helms chemical works had acid in it to the extent of 450 grains to the gallon. Samples taken at the same hour at the new ventilator near the brook in Warrington New Road had weak acid in them, one to the extent of 15 grains to the gallon, and one 35 grains to the gallon. Raintord brook had bees [free of acid. The swollen state of the brook, from rains, had tprevented the inspector from taking any drainage flowing I from the Globe Alkali Works. The inspector reported that a wall had fallen into the brook, and prevented access to the drains of the two chemical works in the neighbourhood of Ireland Brow bridge. The health of the town continued to be satisfactory, the dee* rate being below the average. During the last two weeks there had been many deaths from consumption and other chest affection% and in the month 11 children had died from infectious diseases. Dr. Beard, the inspector of vaccination, was here lately and warned the medical officer that small pox was in the district, and that the hospital for infectious diseases should beready to receive any cases that might be imported. Inspector Houghton bad called his attention to the state of two houses in Watson-at., tenanted by James Roughley and Wm. Taben. In the pre- sent state they were not habitable, and he preposed calling OR the owners to ask them to repair the property.

THB BATHS CgrESTION. Mr. BROOK moved the following resolution: "That witk a view of additional provision of public baths for *. Helens the following members, namely, Alderman Mcßryile, Cou&• cillors Twyford, Massey, Belsher, Brook, and Wilcock, be appointed to consider this question, and report thereon to this committee. Councillot WILCOCK seconded the motion, which was carried. This was all the business. WATER COMMITTEE.

A meeting of this Committee was held on Wednesday. Present:—Alderman Gamble, in the chair; Alderman J. Cook, Councillors T. Cook, J. t. Gamble, Foster, and Bishop; Messrs. Craik (deputy town clerk), and askin (water engineer).
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 12, 1881.

div.head: YIELD OF THE WELLS.
div.p: YIELD OF THE WELLS.

Mr. GASZIN reported that the total delivery of water during the month, at Eccleston Hill, was 9,218,502 gallons; daily average, 329,232 gallons; last month's daily average, 372,365 gallons. Whiston : Total delivery, lobs; the daily average, 550,103 gallons; last month's daily average, 668,814 gallons. The minimum column of water in the well was 18 feet 10 inches. At Sutton-road the total delivery was 20,077,862 gallons.; the daily average, 717,066 gallons; last month's daily average, 720,017 gallons. Mr. GAMIN also reported that dry rot had made its ap- pearance in several of the firemen's cottages. Owing to the late severe winter the banks of the Eccleston water courses had been injured more than 'usual, the sides of the courses in many places having fallen in. He had commenced to repair them. He also called attention to an account ren- dered by Mr. Cook for alleged damages to clover roots whilst cleansing covered water courses in his field. The cleansing of this coarse had been left until the standing crops had been removed, and in all cases where the courses had been covered with any crops they had avoided walking over them, in order to prevent any unnecessary damage, although he presumed the Corporation had a right of way over and along the courses at all times. _
It was resolved that the Water Engineer examine each of the cottages and have the lobbies of the cottages tiled where dry rot exists; and Mr. Cook's claim was referred to the Town Clerk.
THE WATER INSPECTORS. It was decided that the water inspectors should be sup- plied with caps au,libadges.

- MEETING OF MINERS AT BT. HELENS LiST NIGHT. —A meeting of Messrs. Pilkington's colliers was held on Thursday night at the George Inn, George-street, It ap- peared from ths statement ef the men that Messrs. Puking- tort bad, on the men going in, agreed to pay weekly, on Friday nights. The masters have, however, intimated that they intend paying on Saturdays at half-past one. This the Men object to strongly, and they resolved to stop work on Monday if the masters do net abide by their former deci- sion to pay ou Friday night, all the other firms having so far done so since the men went in. They also resolved to work five full days a week, and expressed their strong determina- tion to play on Saturdays.
