RUNCORN -- BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. The monthly meeting took place on Monday, Mr. George '.l....Marshall presiding, and there were also present Messrs. :(orman, Dobson, Lyon, Steele, Williams, Handley, Frith, Meadowcroft, McDsugall,Hazlehurst, P. Speakman, Linaker (law clerk), Urookes secretary), Monritz (medical officer). and Barker (surveyor.) MEDICAL OFFICER'S RETORT. _ - .

_ This document, which was presented by Dr. Mouritz, stated that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn I during the month were 26, representing a death rate of 22 per 1,000 per annum. Of these six were due to pulmonary , affections, five to diseases of the nervous system, four to abdominal complaints, three to senile decay, three to whoop jag cough, and two to cardiac diseases. Debility, dentition, and premature birth accounted for one each. Fourteen deaths occurred among children three years old and under, and of these 13 were under one year. Two inquests were held dming the month, making the total deaths 20. The births numered 45, averagiug 33 per 1,000.

HIGHWAY AND SANITAEY COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee stated that a report had been presented with reference to the footway in street, and and a resolution passed appointing a sub -committee to consider and report upon the condition of the sewer and the construction of the street. The sub-committee's repott , en street cleansing was to the effect that it was desirable the work should be done by contract. The sub-committee bad been instructed to prepare the conditions of the same. The surveyor had been requested to have all the houses numoered. The committee appointed to examine and re- t' port upon the accommodation required in the offices, stated that they did not think it desirable to increase the accom- -11- imitation in the present offices.—ltecommended, that a sub- committee consisting of Messrs. Norman, Frith, Handley, • and P. Speakman be appointed to consider the properties of ad the Board, and report to a future meeting. The report of the sub-committee as to the construction of Ashridge-street 'had been adopted. It recommended that the street be made throughout with new kerbs and flags, the present kerbs and flags to be used by the owners or purchased by the Commis- , 44_sicner+ at a valuation. The document stated that the eopresent sewer was quite sufficient for the requirements of the ~,property, and in good working order. The plan of altera- tions to a building near Waterloo bridge, for Messrs. P. Stubbs and Co., and permission to erect a platform and gateway from the building on to the station road had been

approved. Mr. STEELE proposed, and Mr. Nonmax seconded, the motion for passing the minutes. Mr. DOBSON asked certain questions involving explana- tions of the minutes, and also proposed that the names of Dr. McDougall and Dr. Steele be added to the sub-committee to consider the properties of the Board. The mover and seconder of the original motion agreed to accept this addi- tion, so that the amendment, though seconded by Mr. Lyon, was not put. Mr. lYleadowcroft and Dr. McDougall asked several ques- tions as to the sewer in Ashridge-steet, which were replied .to by Mr. Frith, after which the minutes were passed. DISCUSSION ON THE HOSPITAL QUESTION. T e minutes of the Canal Boats and Hospital Committee contained the following :—Recommended, that no patient be admitted into the hospital except by consent of the Chair- man of the Board.—Resolved, that application be made to U. Whitehouse for £2 10s. for professional attendance on him at the hospital.—That the Law Clerk be instructed to write to the Marquis of Cholmondley with reference to the , acquisition of land on the Weston-road, and that unless a satisfactory r:.p:y be received before a fixed time, a meeting of the freehelde-s be called.—That the surveyor prepare plans of a hospital to contain eight beds suitable for erection on the Weston-road site. Mr. P. SPEARMAN moved that the minutes be approved, " and Mr. Fntra seconded the proposition. Mr. HAZLEHURST asked for an explanation about the re- commendation as to the chairman and the hospital. Mr. HANDLEY said the fact of such a recommendation coming before the Board was clearly owing to the very lix system which had been in operation Is •a the admission of patients to the hospital. There had scarcely been a single , case admitted but some dispute had followed. The corn- ,- mittee had considered it only right that, as a sort of ad interim arrangement before the preparation of definite bye- laws, the plan should be entered into, so as to introduce something like order in the future. As to the application to C.-. Whitehouse for payment of 505., he might say that ther were doubts in that case as to whether he had been ad,r,itted to the hoTital in a proper way, and the committee con ,idered it was only right they should protect the Board against any misuse of the building. They found that even the very steps which the Act imperatively laid down had not eon taken. Mr: HAZLEIMRST asked what would be done in case the chairman of the committee was away from home, and a casual case, such as an accident, had to be admitted. The 'CHAIRMAN Accidents do not go to the hospital,

air. Mr. HAZLEILVELST said that be was only wondering d- whether such a duty ought to be delegated to the chairman -; 14 the Board, or be left to the medical men. A,. NORMAN remarked that Mr. Hazlehurst was quite correct as to such duties being left to the officials of the authority in other towns but it appeared that the law by , which the Commissioners in Runcorn were governed in such . matters was very vague. Each case that had been admitted so flr had gone into the building on wrong conditions. The CHAIRMAN observed that the Board had no bye-laws relating to such a matter, acd it was decided that, as when- ever applications were made for admission to the hospital the Medical Officer appeared to be in a dilemma as to whether to admit or not, the decision should be left to him (the speaker); so as to avoid confusion. The arrangement was, however, only a temporary one until the proper bye- -13w5 were prepared. Mr. DOBSON (t 0 the Chairman): If the medical officer finds himself in a dilemma as to sending cases to the hospi- tal. upon w•lose authority do you act? (Laughter.) • The Chairman: I have not asked for this power to be given to me. Mr. DOBSON (again): Who has invested you with power to use your own discretion when a case presents itself? (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN : Perhaps you will ask the committee? Mr. amaze : Well, perhaps the committee will give me information as to where they derived their authority to give .1 you the authority. (Laughter.) 4 Mr. LYON quite sympathised with the remarks of Mr. Hazlehurst, because it seemed to him that, if the resolution • was passed, it would throw upon the chairman a responsi- bility which he did, not think the Board ought to put upon the gentleman who presided over them. It was more the duty of a medical man, or some officer of the Board, to de- cide whether a case was a proper one for admission to the hosnital or not. If he were chairman, he should shrink from accepting a responsibility of the kind. - Mr. P. SPEAKMAN thought that when they were so near the completion of the new hospital the matter might be left over. (Loud laughter.) Mr. HAZLEBURST said he would second a proposition of this kind. Pr. MCDOrGALL thought it was scarcely fair to hand the responsibility of sending these cases into the hospital into the hands of the chairman, when he was the cause of the case of Whitehouse being sent into the building. Mr. Mar- shall alleged that he found the Medical Officer in a dilemma on the question, and it appeared that he came to the rescue. (A laugh.) He had reason to believe that in respect to every case which had been admitted into the hospital, whether taken in ky the instruction of officers of the Board or not, it had been sent there through the cor.cession of several of the Commissioners, but when it was discovered that bills had to be paid no one was found to admit any responsibility. Some rule should be provided as to the cost of admission in any case considered suitable by a medical man for treatment in the building. If Whitehouse volun- tarily consented to pay the money asked of him, well and good, but if no contract had been entered into voluntarily, he failed to see how the commis- sioners could establish any case in court, supposing it were ultimately considered necessary to go there. The recom- mendation about the Chairman ought to be referred back, and 3 decision come to that firstly, whenever a case was re- , commended for adgiission to the hospital, a medical certiti- cats should be produced, showing that the patient was suffering from a certain infectious disease; secondly, that the terms upon which the admission was ranted should be named upon the document; and thirdly, that an a/range. • anent be made that all cases admitted be subject to an arrangement between the medical man attending patient or his friends. He should be extremely andliol the see a resolution placing such power in the hands of the Chairman placed upon the books. Mr. HAZLEIDIRST was of opinion that it was not advisable •to leave such a power as that referred to in the hands of the Chairman. Mr. HANDLEY considered that the discussion had pro- ceeded, thus far, on rather a false assumption, viz., that the medical officer was either incompetent to perform his -duties—[Dr. McDoroarA.: No, no.]—and that the chair- man was to exercise rule over that officer. This was not at all the intention of the committee, who only came to the decision at which they arrived after discussion at several meetings. They decided that it was necessary to have some rather stringent rule for the admission of patients, and think- ing that if the chairman were associated with the medical officer and the sanitary inspector in the granting of orders, there would be a greater guarantee for the proper order of of proceeding being observed, they passed the resolution. If they went to the Act of Parliament for direction, they could only proceed on certain lines, which had not been acted on in any one case. They had to do with this hospital busi- Wes six or seven years, and the committee were of opinion that it was time they got a little further. Application had to be made to the magistrates in order to enable the autho- rity to recover, for that Board was in no sense a relief authority. If the committee admitted anyone to the hospi- tal, whether it was proper or not that they should be granted such a privilege, the ratepayers' were simply paying twice over. As guardians of the public purse, the commissioners ought to be very jealous of bringing about such a result. ILMr. Nortmats : Hear, hear.] The proposal of the committee was net intended to clash in any way with the duties of the medical officer. There was a rule that, pending any bye- laws being drawn up, the medical officer should, at the next meeting after the admission of a patient, produce his book, stating the reasons why he had been granted the privileges of the institution, and other particulars. With the exception of one particular case—and in this there were very grave doubts whether the entries in the book had not been made after at- tention had been drawn to the matter—this had not been alone. Considering the fact that the committee were all of

one mind in the matter, he thought it would be preferable that they should discuss the question thoroughly at that meeting; and if such a course was adopted, there could be no objection taken to the expunging of the minute. There would be no good in wasting any more time by referring the subject back. By permission of the chairman, Dr. MCDOUGALL again rose and said there was no Act of Parliament to prevent a medical Ul`t3 attending his own patient in the hospital, if he thought proper to do so. If it were considered desirable in any particular case, such an arrangement might be entered into between a medical man and the relatives of any particu- lar patient. It ought not to go forth to the public that they were bound to one medical man in the case of any patient admitted, for they were not. Mr. HAZLEHURST enquired if Dr. McDougall could give tho commissioners anyinformation as to the rules which prevailed in hospitals in Liverpool and Manchester. Dr. MCDOUGALL: There is no doubt that all hospitals pro- vided by urban districts like ours, provide solely for pay- ing cases. Mr. HAZLEHURST was of opinion that it would be well for the Board, or the committee, to obtain the rules of several other hospitals, which might prove a guide to them. Mr. HANDLEY said that the Bye-laws Committee had not overlooked the suggestion now offered by Mr. Hazlehurst. They were now engaged upon the building bye-laws, and the hospital bye-laws had only been put off for a few weeks. Mr. HAZLEHURST moved that the minute having reference to the chairman of the Board and the hospital be referred hick to the committee, and that a number of the rules of other such institutions be obtained. Mr. DOBSON seconded the amendment. Dr. McDouGam, asked Mr. Hazlehurst how the matter , stood now. Mr. MARSHALL wished to be allowed to conduct the busi- ness pf the meeting, as he was chairman. He did not take exception to the proceeding of any gentleman who wished to air his professional knowledge, or otherwise, impugning his judgment; but when any gentleman on that Board im- pugned his truthfulness, be could not afford to be silent any longer. He begged to say that he never consented to the admission of Whitehouse inte the hospital, and he told the doctor that he would have to be responsible. [Dr. McDougall here interrupted the Chairman.] He must re- mind Dr. McDougall that he was speaking, and he could not permit him to interrupt. After the statement he had made, he thought it was only due to him that Dr. McDougall should withdraw the remark to which he bad given utter- ance, as it was a reflection on his (the speaker's) truthful- ness. If the last-named gentleman was desirous of lecturing the Board on the subject, he ought at least to stick to the truth in what he said. Dr. MCDOUGALL. who spoke very indistinctly, was under- stood to say that he would only withdraw what he had said on condition that the Chairman withdrew his remarks con- cerning himself. The amendment was then put and carried unanimously, after which the minutes were passed. GENERAL PURPOSES. The minutes of this committee were passed, on the motion of Dr. MCDOUGALL, seconded by Mr. NORMAN. The minutes stated that the market inspector had been instructed to allow r • person in the Market Hall during closed hours except -.oder his personal control. Proceeding,s were ordered to be taken against Mr. Jacob Hedley for the recovery of his slaughter-house rent, which, it was stated, he had re- fused to pay.

A SCENE. 1 The Finance Committee's minutes stated that the receipts for February had been £4Ol 19s. 3d., of which £23 19s. 3d. ! was for market rents and tolls, £285 14s. id. private provements, and £22 14s. 6d. on account of the Fire Brigade. ' Accounts amounting to £479 4s. Ild, had been passed for payment. Mr. LYON moved, and Mr. FRITH seconded, the confirma- tion of the minutes. In answer to Dr. McDougall, the SECRETARY (Mr. Brookes) stated that the irrecoverable arrears up to the 25th inst. would be about £lOO. The motion was passed. Mr. LYON then suggested that the Board should adjourn, and meet, as usual, on some day before the end Of the month in order to pass the accounts for the year. Some of the members thought it was not necessary to have a special meeting for the purpose. Dr. MCDOUGALL : I think it is scarcely fair to the Board and the public to depart from what has been the custom of the Board from the date of its establishment— ' The CHAIRMAN (interrupting) : Are you going to make a proposition, Doctor? Dr. McDoccatr, (testily): Yes; and, if you like, I will move that you leave the chair. I The CHAIRMAN (excitedly and sotto voee): Yes, you have impudence enough. Dr. McDounALL (assuming a very dramatic pose, and stretching forth his right hand) : What is that, sir? What do you say? The CHAIRMAN : Goon, sir; never mind what I said. Dr. McDounau. : I can assure you I shall move a very strong resolution if you don't withdraw your impertinent remarks. The CratustAN : I shall not until you withdraw yours. Dr. McDonoara, : It is quite immaterial to me what you say about myself • but in your position as Chairman we ex- pect you to uphold the dignity and honour of the Board. But instead of that, you have disgraced and degraded it by using language which your position does not admit of. You ought not to forget your position as Chairman of the Board; and to-day you have added another link to the discredit and dinhonour which your conduct has brought upon its members. The CHAIRMAN (rising) : Will you move a resolution; or I shall vacate the chair? After some further discussion as to the advisability of adjournment, in which Mr. Norman, Mr. Handley, and Mr. P. Speakman joined, it was resolved on the motion of Dr. McDougall, seconded by Mr. I yon, that the meeting should stand adjourned until the 24th inst. The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guar- dians was held on Tuesday, at Dutton Workhouse. Present —The Rev. Canon Barclay. (in the chair), Mr. J. Brundrit (ex-officio), the Rev. Canon Dodd, the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. J. Ashton, J. Weir, J. Darbvshire, 11. Lowe, J. M'lntvre, J. Harrison, W. Pickering, J. Midwood, R. Ashton, H.Neild, J. challinor, T. Norman, P, Briscoe, G. R. Hazleiturst, J. Lowe, W. Wilkinson, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). The minures of the last meeting having been read, Mr. Loww said : I think the proceedings of last Board day require a little explanation. The Careanntsw : I don't see your name as being present last Board day, and you cannot object to the truth of the record. That is all that is before the meeting now. Mr. LOWE : Well, I wish to give an explanation. Rev. J. W. N. TANNER : As Mr. Lowe is going to intro- duce the subject I beg to say it has been fully discussed and disposed of, and therefore cannot be re-opened. Mr. LOWE : I beg to propose this, that our Clerk write to the Local Government Board— The CHAIRMAN: The question before the Board is the correctness of these minutes. Mr. Lowe resumed his seat, and the minutes were con- firmed. Mr. LowE: Now, am I in order in proposing— rho CHAIRMAN: Have you given notice of any motion ? I think we ought to take the agenda first. Mr. LOWE thought after the language used at the last Board meeting no gentleman Ought to object to an explana- tion. The CrrattnuAw : All I say is, there is no notice of your motion, and there is a long agenda to go through. Rev. J. W. N. TANNER: I rise to order. It has been fully discussed and disposed of. Mr. Lowe: I can prove what the gentlemen said in their speeches— The CHAIRMAN: We have nothing to do with that. If you were not here, how can you tell what passed? Mr. LOWE : I can, by the reports. The CHAIRMAN : We have nothing to do with the news- papers.

div.head: COUNTY' RATE.
div.p: THE COUNTY' RATE.

Mr. MCINTYRE, in accordance with notice of motion, pro- posed that a committee be appointed to enquire into the expenditure of the county rate. He had had before him that day, as a member of the Finance Committee, a state- ment as to the call that would be made upon the Union. It amounted to aid. in the pound, and he believed he would be correct in saying that 3d. out of the 611. it was estimated would be required for the county rate. He merely stated that to show how the call upon the various unions in the , county, and this union especially, in this case was growing. They were there as the representatives of the ratepayers who had to contribute the money, and it seemed to him that the time had come when a little investigation into these matters might he very useful in the interests of the ratepayers. (Hear, hear.) He believed the county rate was still levied upon the basis charged during the year 1873. Since that period the rateable value of many of the townships had inaterially increased, and as a matter of course, those which had increased the most were paying under their just propor- tion of the common charges of the county rate. It would appear that their own Union had increased in rateable value since 1873 about 16 per cent., Altrincham had increased 25 per cent., Northvrich 27, Nantwich 2., Congleton between 17 and 18, Macclesfield, 11, and Stockport he thought had in- creased about 74 per cent. From this the Board would see very plainly that the basis required revision, and it was an evidence that the various Unions whose rateable value had increased very much were not at the present time paving their just proportion. There were various anomalies which he would rather net go into at the present time, but he thought there were sufficient grounds to justify him in ask- ing the Board to appoint a committee to investigate these little matters. He believed, for instance, that the auditing of the accounts of the county cost over £5OO, and that the police of the county cost £27,000. He thought the time had come when these matters ought to be taken up in the interests of the ratepayers, and investigated to see where the money went. The Board would see that nearly one half, or 3d. cut of the 61d., as estimated, was required for the county. That seemed to him to be a large sum of money to be drawn from the rate- payers without their representatives having the power to make any investigation. He, therefore, begged to move that a committee be appointed to look into these matters and report to the Board. Mr. WEIR seconded the motion, which was carried. The following committee was then appointed: The Chairman, Vice-Chairman, Messrs. Derbyshire, Norman, Weir, Neild, R. Ashton, Hazlehurst, and Mclntye.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY MARCH 12, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY MARCH 12, 1881.

The Clerk was directed to apply to the county authorities in the name of the Guardians, for suck information as he found might be required by the committee. TFIE Luxcit Qngsvoil. On Mr. CIIILLONER'S motion in respect to the provision of lunch for the members coming up for discussion, The DEPUTY CLERK said: We have written to the Local Government Board for the information you ask, but we have no reply. It is a question whether you will move it to-day, or wait until We get a reply. Mr. IlitztEutrasr thought it would be better to await a reply, because the Local Government Board might sanction what they wanted. Of course, Mr. Linaker might see that Mr. Jones had dinner ready for those who came before

twelve o'clock next time. Mr. CHALLONER hoped the Guardians woull not think he was afraid of bringing the matter forward. (Laughter.) If they did, they were sadly mistaken. He courted neither favour nor affection from anyore. As Mr. Hazlehurt said, it perhaps might be as well to wait until the information came. The CLERK said he wrote asking for the information to be sent in time for that mseting, bat he had not heard

anything. Mr. LOWE: I think it might be pressed, Mr. Clerk; they seem very anxious. The CLERK read the letter he had sent to the Local Go- vernment Board, in which he asked if the Board would sanction an expenditure of £lO per annum to provide lunch for the guardians who came about ten a.m. and left at four in the afternoon, and stating that the workhouse was in the country, and that there was no place near at which the guardians could obtain refreshments. Mr. CHALLONER thought it a very favourable letter, and that the clerk had given all the information he could have wished to give the Local Government Board. He quite confirmed what the clerk had written, but thought it would be wise to postpone his motion until the Board gave a reply to the letter. Mr. HAZLEHORST: Would you propose Mr. Challoner that it letter be written reminding then. Mr. LOWE : Gentlemen generally dine after six o'clock, I don't see why you want a dinner. The CHAIRMAN: This is lunch, Mr. Lowe. It was decided that the clerk write to the Local Govern- ment Board asking for a reply to the letter.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. The CLERK reported that during the year ended the 31st December last, the committee held fourteen meetings and investigated 397 cases. The school attendance officers had, under the direction of the committee, served warnings for regular or non- attendance of children at school upon 147 parents ii respect Of 227 children. The officers had, how- ever, exercised their discretion in the service of preliminary not:ces in the form of a circular letter referred to in last report, and had found results to be very satisfactory, as in many cases the requirements of the Education Acts had been complied with, and thus avoided the necessity of bring- ing such cases before the committee or serving the legal warning required. The committee had authorised proceed- ings against 19 parents in respect of 22 children, and suc- ceeded in obtaining school attendance orders in respect of 19 instance where The township of Weston was the only where bye-laws had been adopted, and proceedings had been taken 'under them against 9 parents. The pro- ceedings for violation of school attendance orders were successful *against 15 parents affecting 30 children, and committal orders in:default of payment of fines were necessary against 5 parents; and in 2 cases the order was carried out, and the parents sent to prison. The recommendation contained in the last report for the adoption of bye-laws was adopted, but as the attention of the Legisla- tionhad bean directed to the subject the necessary steps were deferred. On the 26th August last, the Elementary Education Act, 1880, came into operation requiring bye-laws t. be made before the 31st December in every school dis- t: ict where they had not previously been adopted, and on the sth October, 1880, the committee settled the bye-laws for townships in their district, and the same were approved be' Iler Majesty in Council on the 16th December last, and had since been duly published in the district. The highest average attendance and the nnmber of children on the books when the said average was made during any week in each of the last 3 years ending 31st December was-1078 highest average 2.216, number on the books 2,851; 1879 2,358, 2.978; 1880 2,385. 3,001. The attendance of the children at school in comparison with the number on the books was at the following rate-1878, 77729 per Cent.; 1879, 79,180 per cent.; 1880, 79,209 per cent. Applications had, been made to the Guardians by the inquiry officers for payment of fees of 348 children, and orders were granted in 243 cases, the tote,l cost amounting to £31155.11d. The expenses of the committee during the year ended 31st December last amounted to £lO3 165., which amounted to nearly fd. in the £ on the rateable value of the district, but the sum of £1 16s, had been repaid on account of costs since the 31st December, 1880. On the motion of the VICE-CHAIRMAN the report was adepted, and the officers re-elected at their former salaries.

TIfE ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE. The Assessment Committee recommended that the salary of the clerk, for the year be £75. Mr. BRUNDRIT, in proposing that that sum be paid, said at a meeting which they held that morning the recommenda- tion was unanimously adopted and every Guardian ex- pressed himself in terms of the highest praise of the way in which Mr. Linaker had discharged his duties during the year. He could cordially endorse the remarks and hoped the clerk would long be with them to render such valuable services to the Union. Mr. NIELD seconded the proposition. Mr. DARBYSHIRE asked if the amount was increased.
Mr. BRIINDRIT said it was the same as in 1872 and 1873. There had been no extra work this year and there was there- fore no honorarium given to the clerk as was the case last year. . _ _
„ .._. The proposition Was unanirnously carried.

the cheese had been won at a raffle, and asked him to ' irQ him fivepence per pound for it. He told him he did not care for buying a whole one, as he could get what would suit him in Liverpool for fourpence per pound. Millington then said that if he would purchase the cheese he might have it at fourpence per pound. He agreed to do so, and Millington then went away. In about an hour he returned with the cheese, and Ball accompanied him. The cheese was weighed, and found to be 46Ibs. He gave Millington 15s. for it, the other fourpence being thrown off as discount. He paid Millington 48. that night, and on the following evening another ss. He had not !riven him any other money. A few nights after he had paid the 55., Ball came to his shop and said Millington had sent him up for the balance of the money owing for the cheese. He told him that the article had been purchased from Millington, and he must come for the money—Ser- geant 'landlord said he apprehended the prisoner on the previous day.—On being formally charged, the prisoner said : I know no more about the cheese than the cheese knows about me.—ln answer to the Bench, the Superinten- dent of Police said that there were no previous convictions against the man, who, when he was a boy, was sent to an industrial school for five years.—Prisoner was committed to gaol one month, with hard labour.—The Chairman said the magistrates were of opinion that the man Williams had behaved very bully in the matter, as he must have known that the cheese could not have been coins by honestly to be sold at such a price.—Williams said the prisoner and Mil- lington gave him clearly to understand that it had been obtained in a lottery.

A DRUNKEN DRIVER.—JOIIR Woellaston, a boatman, was convictetl, on the evidence of Sergeant Cashin, of having been drunk whilst in charge of a horse belonging to the Bridgewater Navigation Co., in Bridge-street, on the pre- vious day.—The Chairman said he and Mr. Bankes can:
.. sidered the case a very serious one, and defendant would have 205. and 59. 41. costs to pay, or be sent to gaol one month.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Ih undrit and Mr. R. M. Brooke. CHARGE OF MAEHING A DOG AT HALTON. John Trimble, a Halton labourer, was charged with having, on the 6th inst., unlawfully and maliciously maimed and wounded a dog, by striking it on the head with an axe. The case occupied considerable time.—The evidence showed that

. _ the animal was the property of Mr. Henry Reynolds, J.P., who, last week, left his house at Halton, and went to reside at another, situated at Netherton, near Frodsham. The , former residence was left in charge of an old man named Woods. On Sunday, about midday, the 'dog was noticed to be all right, and about four in the afternoon it was found by P.C. Lowndes to have been severely wounded on the head. The wound was about four inches in length, a con- siderable depth, and much blood appeared to have been lost by the animal. It was supposed that some person had been in the yard, where there was a heap of slack, with the ob- ject of stealing some of it, and the dog had set upon the man, who bad struck it with the axe, which was lying near, , and found to be smeared with blood. Evidence was given to the effect that the prisoner was Seen in the immediate neighbourhood of the house about the time that the injury must have been done, and that he lived at the other end of the village. Also that the footprints were found in the garden which exactly corresponded in shape with the boots which the prisoner was found wearing. The footprints were traceable in the direction of the back premises, but it was impossible to follow up any tracks in the yard, or the ap- proach to it, on account of the paving.—Trimble• pleaded not guilty, and called a witness, who stated that he was in his company from about noon on the dav of;the alleged offence to six at night, and he never left him.—Mr. Brun- drit said the magistrates did not consider the evidence suffi- cient to convict, and the prisoner would be discharged. YEsrunnev.—Before Mr. R. M. Brooke.

ALLEGED THEFT OF Pon,—Win. Henry Dunbavand was charged with stealing 61bs. of pork, the property of Mr. S. Crosby, provision dealer, High-street—From the evidence of the prosecutor's son, it appeared that the prisoner was noticed loitering about the shop, on the previous night, and about eight o'clock he entered the place and walked away with the piece of pork. Witness followed and gave him into custody.—Prisoner was remanded until Monday. ALLEGED FRAI7D BY MEANS OF A BANK 800%. Michael Ryan, a labourer, whose wife keeps alodging-house, and who was some time ago sentenced to a rather long term of hnprisonment for unlawfully wounding her, was charged with having, on the 28th ult., and on divers other days, obtained from Mr. James Percival, vations goods, consisting of bacon, sugar. beef, dic., value £1 65. 7d., and certain money, viz., Bs. 3d. and £1 ss. 2d., by means of false rat- tences. The prosecutor, who keeps a shop in Church-street, said he had known the prisoner about twenty years. On the 18th January, the prisoner came to his shop, said he was going to work in the town, and asked if he would take charge of his bank book. He knew at that time that Ryan ' had been out of Runcorn for some time. Prisoner handed him a book purporting to be an account between himself and Parr's Bank, Wigan. He examined it, and found entered to the credit of the prisoner a sum of £l5O, which appeared to have been deposited at one time, and on the debit side the withdrawals seemed to be £5O, showing a' 'balance in his favour of £lOO. ' Ryan' asked him to let him I have acme goods on credit, and he agreed to do so upon his depositing with him the bank book as security. The, same day he let him have groceries to the value of 24 11d. He kept the bank book, and the prisoner came at various times between that day and the 28th February, for other goods. He let the man have things to the amount of £1 61. 7d., and also advanced him Bs. 3d. in small sums. He should not have allowed him to have the goods if he had not left the book with him as security. On the 28th Feb., as the prisoner owed him £1 14s. 10d., he sent for him and toll him he wanted the money. On Ryan stating that he could get some cash on the book, he went with him to Barr's branch bank, Runcorn and saw Mr. Chorlton, the manager. Prisoner asked for a cheque for £3, and on his (witness) I producing the bank book, Mr. Chorlton drew out a cheque for £3, on Parr's branch bank, Wigan, in the name of Ryan, who signed the cheque, and he (wit- ness) endorsed it. The mana;er cashed it. He (witness) kept £1 145., and handed Ryan the balance. He did this believing that the prisoner had an account with the bank The cheque was returned to him on the 2nd inst. marked, "Account closed." He again saw the prisoner, who still maintained that he had an account with the Wigan Bank Prisoner, on being asked for the bank book (which ha l been given up to him in the meantime), told two or three stories as to where it was, and ultimately admitted he had not got I it. on which a warrant was taken out for his apprehension. Witness had had to refund the bank the money.—Mr. Jas. Robertson Thomson, manager of Chester Parr's branch bank, said he was assistant manager at Wigan en October Ist,. 1879. when the. prisoner opened an account there by deposit-1 £so—£4o is notes and £lO in, gold.—Mr. Jo'm Browne., chief cashier at Parr's Bank, Wigan, produced the copy of the account with the prisoner at the Wigan branch.—Mr. Edward Ambrose, Chorlton, manager of the Parr's Runcorn branch corroborated the statement of the prosecutors as to what took place at the bank.—Sergeant Handford proved apprehending the prisoner on Tuesday afternoon. Ryan,on being formally charged, said he had no statement to make. He was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. STEALING ROPE.—William Randle, alias Smoker, who had been previously convicted of felony, was charged with stealing 801 b of rope, the property of the Bridgewater Navi- gation Co., Runcorn, on the previous day.—The evidence was to the effect that the prisoner and another man were seen to cut the rope from a flat which was tied up at the Old Quay, and afterwards take it to Lavelle's marine store, 3/ersey-street, for sale. On being questioned, the missing man ran off, and the other was taken into custody.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The, usual meeting of this Authority was bold in the Board-room, at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday, when Mr John Ashton presided. There were also present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner. Messrs. W. Pickering., J. Weir, J. Midwood, J. Mclntyre, J. ChMloner, James Darbyshire, and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). CLAIM AGAINST THE AUTHORITY, The DEPUTY CLERK laid before the Authority a claim which bad been received from the Warrington Corporation (gas department) for £1 18s 9d, for repairs to main and sur- face darn.,ged by Messrs. A rate of one farthing in the £ would produce £l5B 16s 9d; and at the present rate of expenditure would provide the Authority with funds to Lady Day, 1882. The report, which was thought by the Authority to be highly satisfactory, was adopted. THE CLERK'S SALARY. The DEPUTY CLERK stated that the Authority would have to fix the amount of the clerk's salary for the ensuing y Mr. WEIR: What is the present salary ? The DEPUTY CLERK: £6O per annum. The CHAIRMAN: I take it that we could hardly increase the salary without giving special notice to the members. The DEMITY CLERK said if the Authority wished to do SO it could be settled at once. Mr. WEIR said it wou'd perhaps he as well to go on for another 12 months at the same salary, awl proposed that he present amount be paid. The proposition was agreed to. ' ST. RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of the Runcorn School Board was held on Wednesday. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were also present the Rev. Win. Pennelly, Messrs. Simpson, Lea, Briacoe, Pritchard, Norman, and Rigby (clerk.)

SCHOOL CENSUS. The CLERK read the following document-_I have the honour to report that, in compliance with a resolution of the 12th Janury, ;1881, I have caused an educational census of the school district to be taken, and I now beg leave to submit the results arrived at for the consideration of the Board. As in 1875, the school district has been divided into eleven sub-districts. An exhaustive house to house visitation has been made by the enumerators, who have carefully recorded the age of each child under 13 years. These figures I have verified and submitted to several tests, and I think I may venture to say that the returns are worthy of complete confidence. In the cases of absentees-there were twenty-six families absentee, against 16 in 1875 - allowance has been made upon the lines of the previous census. Al- though enquiries were frequently made as to the object of the Board in taking a second census, information was not withheld by any householder, save in one solitary instance; but in this caee a reference to the records has supplied the answers needed. It has been determined that the aggregate! number of children of all classes under 13 years of age in the school district is now 5,076. In 1875 there were 4021, or 1,055 less than at present. The 5,076 are made up in this wise :-520 under one year. In 1875 there were 425. In- crease, 95. 443 between one and two years. In 1875 there were 400. Increase, 43. 461 between two and three years. In 1875 there were 367. Increase, 94. 444 between three and four years. In 1875 there were 324. Increase, 120.1 431 between four and five years. In 1875'there were 359. Increase, 72. 426 between five and six years. In 1875 there were 314. Increase 112. 396 between six and seven years. In 1875 there were 325. Increase, 71. 364 between seven and eight years. In 1875 there were 289. Increase, 75. 364 between eight and nine years. In 1875 there were 284. Increase, 80. 328 between nine and ten years. In 1875 there were 260. Increase, 68. 312 between ten and eleven years. In 1875 there were 251. Increase, 61. 297 between eleven and twelve years. In 1875 there were 237. Increase, 60. 290 between twelve and thirteen years. In 1875 there were 186. Increase, 104. Total, 5,076. In 1875, 4,021. 'lncrease, 1,055. This increase has taken place for the most part in Mill- brow district (258) ; in the Duke's-field district (531) and Newtown (141). The remaining districts, situated in the centre of the town, have fluctuated but little, Mersey-street district, now containing 18 children less than it did in 1875, and Nelson-street district 43 less. In 1875 there were 2,829 children between three and thirteen years; now there are 3,652, or 823 more than in 1875. As my Lords insist upon school accommodation being provided for all children be- tween the ages of three and thirteen years, after making certain deductions which will be taken into account hereafter, it follows that the increase of eight hundred and twenty-three will beof greater immediate interest to the Board than any increase which has taken place in the number of children under three years of age. I propose, therefore, to show the nett number of children between 3 and 13 years of age for whom public school ac- commodation must of necessity be provided, and to com- pare it with the existing accommodation. Of children of all classes over three, but under 13 years, there are 3,652. From this number 522 must be deducted, being one- seventh, as representing the proportion of the middle and upper classes, leaving 3,130. 'A further reduction of 313, or ten per cent, is allowed in respect of those who will be absent from school from unavoidable causes, and 83 should be added for the absentees not accouated for in the census After making this addition, and the two substractions, the nett number of children between 3 and 13 years requiring public elementary school accommodation will stand at 2,905. The nett number in 1875 was 2,233, or 672 less than in 1881. Already there is in Runcorn ample accommoda- tion for 2,289 children; but there are 2,905 wanting space -a deficiency in the existing accommodation of 616 places. In the district of Newtown, taking the Duke's canal as its northern boundary, there are 606 children in need of schools, while Newtown infant school supplies the wants of 100 only. Hence there is a deficiency here of 506. In Mill Brow district, again taking the Duke's canal as a boundary! (if the Roman Catholic School be accepted as drawing the bulk of its scholars from the heart of the town) there is also a large deficiency. The Board school finds room for 90 chil- dren, but there are 466 needing it. There, again, is a deficiency of 376. If Mill Brow and Newtown districts be separated from the remainder of the school district, there would then be a redundancy of school accommodation in the lower parts of the town. I have ascertained that there are 1,333 children (after deductions) in these parts requiring schools, and that the National, Trinity, Wesleyan, and Roman Catholic schools are available for 2,099, or for 266 I more places than are at present required. If, therefore, the deficiences of Newtown District (506) and Mill Brow Dis- trict (276) be added together, there will be a total deficiency' of 882 places. Against this must he set the accommodation! of 266 more than required in the lower parts of the town, and the nett deficiency will stand at 616, a number which coincides with the figures given before, as between 2,289 places, and 2,905 children to occupy them. I have deter- mined the number of children amenable to the bye-laws of the Board to be 2,777, as against 2,146 in 1875. F. RIGBY, Clerk to the Board. The Cularraurr thought the report pointed to the de- sirability of a site for the new schools being chosen so as to be convenient for children living in Mill Brow and New- town. The CLERK said he had no idea that there were 1,000 more children in Runcorn at present than there were six years ago. Mr. PRITCHARD had for some time been under the im- pression that owing to the great increase of buildings in Duke's-field and other parts of the town the number of chil- dren must have been considerably augmented. Mr. Nonstate was of opinion that the Board had adopted a wise course in having an educational census taken. It appeared that they would have to provide for 616 more children. The CLERK: That is the result of the enquiry. The CHAIRMAN thought the state of matters revealed by the census returns could only be met by the erection of two schools-one for boys and the other for girls. The CLERK remarked that there were 250 empty houses in Runcorn, which, of course, were not included in the returns he had laid before the Board. Whether this was owing to bad trade or the fact that the town was over-built, Lie could not say. Mr. PRITCHARD remarked that if they were to build a school in Newtown to accommodate 250 children, the Educa- tion Department would no doubt call upon them to erect one for Mill Brow. He was of opinion that it would be well if they could erect a central school for Mill Brow and Newtown which would satisfy the requirements of the Education De- partment. It was just possible that if they decided to put ups building for 500 children, it would satisfy the members of the Board and the Government inspector also. Rev. W. FENNELLY : All that the department require is sufficient accommodation. The CLERK: In two or three months time w% shall have the national census. Mr. PRITCHARD moved that a central school be erected for 500 children-say 300 boys and 200 girls-to meet the present deficient accommodation. Mr. Nouatax considered the suggestion of Mr. Pritchard la good one, and said he would second the motion. It would be well if they could get a site on which they could extend the building they put up, should circumstances at any time require them to adopt such a course. Rev. W. FENNELIY had been informed that the foundation of the land near Mill Brow school, was of a good character, and that, if necessary, the buildings might be enlarged to accommodate 300 more children. Mr. NORMAN said the foundation was solid clay. The resolution was passed unanimously. REPORT OF THE SITES COMMITTEE.. .

Mr. PRITCHARD read the following report of the Sites Committee :—" On the 9th inst., the Sites Committee met by appointment at Newtown and after a general view of the position of the neighbourhood, they proceeded to inspect several sites of land, which in their opinion might be available for the erection of the proposed new schools. They first inspected the plot of land near the railway, belonging to Mr. J. Johnson, leading out of the short street called Eaton-street. 'fhencethey proceeded to view the land at the top of Spring Gardens, and also looked at that in the , Holloway, near to the station, and Mr. Savage's farm. They afterwards examined the vacant land between Lowland's road and the canal, and then proceeded to that in Albert- street, which they had been corresponding about with Major tirted's agsnt. They went to the Greeuway fields, and, with the aid of a plan, examined the various building sites. The result they came to was to recommend to the Board three sites for consideration,which were, in their opinion, thomlost suitable for the purpcse, as follows :-Ist. The land belong- ing to Mr. J. Johnson, junr., situate at the end of the street near the railway.-2nd. The Albert-street site, which they had already enquired about.-3rd. The plot immediately behind the houses belonging to Mr. Tonks, and the residence of the Wesleyan minister, which was situate on the left hand side of the newly made street on the Greenway-field." The Board then proceeded to discuss, briefly, the various sites proposed. In answer to several members the clerk stated that the various schools belonging to the Widnes School Board, had been erected by Messrs. F. and J. Holm, and Her Majesty's inspector had reported upon them as pattern schools. Mr. NORMAN proposed that Mr. Charles Linaker, architect, should be instructed to prepare the plans. The CHAIRMAN : Don't you think, Mr. Norman, that we are Linakered enough in Runcorn ? A very brief discussion took place upon Mr. Linaker's merits, in which several of the members, including Mr. John Simpson, took part. The general opinion appeared to be that it would be a prudent course to select some architect whorhsadimpso badas spokelargeexpie n veryrienc complimentaryeine terms erecting serhmoosis. mof Messrs. Holm. • the Board rather thatr m more r tob ornamental r nscahmoooolstaltothboonerseoctmede by f the denominational schools were. (Laughter.) r. PEr TwCoEut would be Mr. SIMPSON proposed, and Mr. BRISCOE seconded, that Messrs. Holm be requested to look at the two sites recom- mended by the Sites Committee, and prepare alternative Plans of schools to accommodate 500 children, showing what the cost would be if a building of more than one floor was trected, as compared with one on the ground floor. Also that the decision on the question of sites be deferred, REV. W. PRESTON, M.A.., AS A. BADOAINE The CLERK read the following copy of latter from the Rev. W. Preston:—

Trinity Parsonage, Feb. 24. —Gentlemen,—At the special re- quest of my mission worse's in connection with the Ragged school, I write to ask if you will be so kind as to give there permission to use only the parlour, or class-room, in the above school, on Wednesday evenings, from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m., 1r the holding of a sliw t week day service, as the cottage where they now bold suoh is not convenient. They are willing to pay you something for its use. Would ten shillings per annum be too little. They undertake not to use either the schoolroom or any of its furniture. Previous to your possession of the school, a week day service was held in it.—l am, gentlemen, yours faith- fully, yym. PRESTON.—To the Runcorn School Board. The following estimate of the amount which would have to be expended in various items to brim" the cost of using the rooms within 10s. was also read, alter having been handed in by Mr. Lea :—" Ragged School class-room on ground floor : Every Wednesday evening for two hours from 6to 8. First hour for choir practice; second hour for prayer meeting or cottage lecture. Coal, 6 months, 26 nights, at ± cwt. per night; 61. cwt. at 11d., ss. 1113. Gas , (1 four feet burner), 26 nights at 2 hours, 52 hours at 4 feet per hour, 208 feet of gas at sd. per 100 feet, 10d. ; extra cleaning for old woman (very light) say 2s. 6n1.; labour of removing forms from next room and replacing them, iti/ ; use of forms (our own) nil, equals 9s. 31a. per annum. No gas or coal would be used during six summer months; and the wear and tear would be very slight." (Laughter.) The reading of the calculation caused considerableamuse- ment, and the Board seemed to be under the impression that it originated from Mr. Breston, though Mr. Lea was afterwards understood to say that another gentleman had drawn it up. Mr. NORMAN said it appeared that the "old woman" would have to attend 52 times for the sum of 2s. 6d.

(Loud laughter.) Surely it would not do to sanction such a small amount as that as payment for a whole year's extra cleaning. The CHAIRMAN: Are the seats free and open, or have the sittings to be paid for? (Renewed laughter.) The CLERK: At least you cannot accuse them of extrava- gance. Even 2d. per week for the use of the rooms would he 85. Bd. a year, and the total amount of the bill is only 9s. ! Mr. NORMAN said they must take into account wear and tear.
Mr. LEA said it.was nonsense to talk ab,,mt wear and tear

in such a case, as the people would use their own forms, dre. Mr. NORMAN said, suppose they knocked the jamb" off the door in removing the forms, the Board would have to do the repairs. They ought to make some estimate for wear and tear. He thought it a singular idea that a'rich congre- gation like that of Trinity church, should come to the School Board and make such a request. Sooner than let them have it at the price named, he would give a shilling towards the expenses himself. Some discussion then took place about the sum of 2s. 6d., which was proposed to be allowed to the "old woman" for cleaning the place; and the Chairman suggested that the matter be left in the hands of Mr. Preston as he would drive a better bargain than any other member of the Board. Mr. NORMAN suggested that they had better send the bill _ .

back for amendmea (Loud Laughter.) A sovereign per annum would be little enough for the use of the room, and they might let Mr. Preston arrange as to the payment for the cleaning. The CHAIRMAN : Shall we take the responsibility for the cleaning? Mr. NORMAN: I would take no responsibility at all. Mr. PRITCHARD : We could not offer the "old woman"

2s: 6d. for 59 attendances. Mr. NORMAN : I move that we let them have the room for 15s. a year, and that they arrange for the cleaning. The CHAIRMAN: That would be a sort of splitting the difference. Everything in England is a compromise, and it appears that School Board proceedings are no exception. (Laughter.) The resolution was then put and carried amidst slight laughter.

div.head: FINANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: FINANCE COMMITTEE.

Mr. NORMAN said they had gone very carefully over the estimates and the estimated rates was a farthing in the £ less than that in the corresponding half of last year. It was, as Mr. M,lntyre had said, a very serious thing that 3d on a rate of 62 l in the £, should go to the county rate, and he thought the committee that had been appointed might do very good work for the Union. The CLERK real the estimate of the committee which states that the total amount required during the ensuing half year was £8,262, and after taking credit for the prob- able balance at Lady Day 1881, the amount required by con- tribution orders from the overseers was £5,652. The rate- able value of the Union on 3rd March, £200,357, being an increase of £1,820 as compared with the corresponding period of last year. A rate 61d on the £ would produce time sum of £5,635 or t decrease of about id in the as com- pared with the calls required for Michaelmas half year, 1680. DEFAULTING OVER SEERS.

The Clerk was instructed to take proceedings against the overseers of the following townships for not having paid their calls:—Acton Gramre, Antrobus, Aston Bridge, Frod- sham Lordship, Halton. Kingsley, Moore, Norton, Preston- o'-th'-Hill, Sutton, Walton Superior, Walton Inferior, and 1 Whitley Superior.

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
MONDAY.—Before Mr. Henry Reynolds and Mr. C. W. Hazlehurst.

ALLEGED ASSAULT.-7Thomas-YOhnson was charged with assaulting Edward Goodall, at Weston, on the 3rd inst.— Complainant said that just after he had had dinner the defendant came up to him and struck him. He asked that the case might be adjourned, as he had witnesses who could not possibly be present that morning.—The Bench granted the application. TRESPASSING ew PURSUIT OF GAME AT SIITTON.—Three men, named William Snape, William Cook, and John Hobby, were charged with trespassing in pursuit ef game on the 25th ult.—Mr. Graham, of Warrington, appeared on behalf of the prosecution, and said that on the slay in ques- tion a keeper named Kenyon, who was in the employ of Mr. Daglish. was on land belonging to Mr. Acton, at Sutton, with a man named Lightfoot, who called his attention to the defendants. They went up to the men, and found they had ferrets, nets, and a spade with them. They had been digging, and said they had permission from Mr. Acton, the tenant, to go upon the land. Defendants declined to give their names, but they were afterwards ascertained from a policeman.—Kenyon was called, and corroborated Mr. Gra- ham's opening statement.—ln cross-examination, Snape said be did not refuse to give his name.—Evidence in sup- port of the case was also given by Samuel Lightfoot, under keeper to Mr. Dagl iSh.—Snape called Mr. Acton As a witness for the defence. He altnitted that he had told Snape "he might go on the land for anything that he cared ; but he had better ask permission from Mr. Kenyon."—John Barrow, another witness, said that Acton had been asked if they mig,ht go on the land.—Snape and Cook were each fined 409 and costs, or in default of payment one month's imprison- ment. Helsby, who had not been previously convicted, as was the case with the other men, was fined lOs and costs, or in default 14 days' imprisonment. USING PROFANE LANGUAGE.—For having been guilty of this offence, on the 20th ult., Julia Hushing was fined 10s and Os 6d costs, or 14 days' imprisonment, on the evidence of P.C. Bossons. POOR RATE DEFAULTERS.—Twenty-five people were sum- moned by Mr. Sutton, assistant overseer, for non-payment of poorsi. rates.—Orders were made for payment in each case. TRANSFER Dia.—The following transfers were made:— Castle Hotel, Halton, from John J. Scott to Bartholel Rob- berg; the Feathers Inn, Runcorn, from George Green to Daniel Crows; and the Dog and Partridge, Runcorn, from Thomas Wood to Thomas Hill. TuEsoay.—Before Mr. R. M. Brnok3 (chairman) and Mr. Wm. Bankes. STEALING A CHEESE FROM A SI-10P Doon : CENSURE ON A SHOPIKEEPER.—Edward Ball, a man about 26 years of age, was charged with stealing a cheese and a box, the property of Samuel Tomlinson, grocer and milk-dealer, of Albert-street—From the evidence of the prosecutor and his father-in-law, Wm. Bouketn, shoemaker, it appeared that on the afternoon of the 17th ult., the cheese was received ins box by .Boukein. The box was left at the door of the shop. and seen safe between seven and eight in the evening by the prosecutor. It was missed about nine o'clock, and shortly hefore that time the prisoner and some companions were seen near the place. The cheese was worth £1 Hs. 9d., whole- sale price, and the half of 'one now produced was similar to the stolen one. The bax had not been recovered.—Thomas Williams, provisisn dealer, Canal-street, stated that about three weeks en'v a Imo named Millington came to the shop to see him about buying the stolen cheese, and at the time of his visit the prisoner was standing at the door. Milling- ton, who is now in custody for stealing ducks, stated that

div.head: NEW PRECEPT.
div.p: NEW PRECEPT.
It was resolved by the Board to sanction a precept on the overseers for £2OO to meet the current expenses up to the 29th of September. This terminated the business.

WIDNES LOCAL BOAO. This Board held their monthly meeting on Tuesday. Major Cross presided, and there were also present—Messrs. E. Carey, H. Gaskell, jun., J. Knight, J. W. Carlile, F. Heyes, B. Brown, F. H. Gossage, G. I. J. Well s, J. Matthews, and Dr. O'Keeffe ; Mr. Oppenheim (who acted as law clerk), Mr. Allen (accountant), Roberts (engineer), Higginsen (surveyor), and Dickson (inspector of nuisances).

GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. These minutes showed that the Netherley engine house was ready to receive the machinery, and the contractors had been requested to proceed with its erection. The roofs of all the buildings were now el ted. Telegraphic communication was being established between Pex Hill and the offices. The water in stock on the 16th ult. was 7,204,743 galls. There had been a decrease of 3.54 per cent, in the gas sent out for the four weeks ending February 16th, as compared with the similar period last year. Resolved that the committee could not recommend any further payment on Messrs. Daglish ani Co.'s account until the whole of their work was delivered.

Messrs. Kershaw and Co.'s tender to supply pitch pine for beams for the pumptrees in the Netherley well, at the sum of £8155.' or 2s. 41. per cubic foot, had been accepted. The Stocks well heading question had been referred to a speclal meeting of the committee. The letter from Mr. Danby, clerk to the School Board, as to the supply of coke, had been left in the hands of the engineer to reply. The same official had been authorised to offer the Cameron engine and pumps at the trial bore hole, Stocks well, to Mr. Timmins, for £125 cash. A minute had been passed referring to the Board for determination an application made by Messrs. Lea and Sons for an allowance on ccount of loss sustained by them in connection with the supply of fuel under their contract, in consequence of the recent strike, together with the Board's claim against them for damiges in respect of short deliveries. A minute had been passed approving of the draft agreement with the Sheffield and Midland Railway Company's Corn- mittee with respect to their proposed new branch, subjzct to ' the land being conveyed to Rib Board being that portion which immediately abutted upon the easterly side of the Board's present property, the amount of land to be the same as that given up by the Board, plus the additional acre agreed to be given by the committee, and subject to the agreement providing that the committee shall lay a sewer along the northerly side of the Board's land, the Board having the right to connect any of their drains with such sewer.—Recommanded, that the rent of offices, yard space, and stables, charged to the Highway to £4O per annum. Committee, be reduced Mr. CARLILE moved the adoption Of the minutes, and said that the agreement with the Sheffield and Midland Railway would be carried out in due course. Mr. GASKELL seconded the motion, which was passed. It was agreed that the application by Messrs. Lea and Sons should be left to the committee to report at the flet riveting. THE EXCESSIVE EXPENDITURE OF THE lIIOIII,VAY COMMITTEE.

The minutes of the Highway Committee stated that the agreement with the owners of the land in Derby-road (late Marsh Hall-lane) had been completed. Mr. Kershaw having obstructed the footpath leading to Appleton village, the Surveyor had written him and the Rev. T. Finegan on tha subject, and the obstruction had since been removed, but the quarry fence was insufficient to prevent risk of acoi- dents. The fence between Deacon-road and the old quarry being dangerous, the Surveyor had written to Mr. Sayer, calling upon him t put the fence in order, but had received -no reply. The Surveyor was preparing a plan and estimate for the flagging,. ,s/c., round the Warrington-road Board Schools. Major gross's plan of building land in Moor and Lower-house lanes had been approved. Mr. H. L. Riley had been written to requiring him to carry out his under- taking of August, 1877, with respect to Egypt-street. After lengthened consideration of the matter by the committee, the Surveyor had been given instructions to go through the highway accounts with the accountant, and report to. the chairman on that day (Tuesday) as to the committee's ex- penditure. Mr. KNIGHT, chairman of the committee, moved that the minutes be pessed. The members would see from tho Finance Committee's minutes that the accounts of the High- way Committee to be passed this month were £935 be. This sum might appear very large to them and the public, if he did not give them some explanation. He might, first of all, say that the members of his committee were going to turn over a new leaf. [Mr. Carey: Do you mean in the cheque book? (Laughter.)] In previous years there ap-i peared to have been no regard paid to ' discharging all debts at the end of the year. As far as he knew, the committee had brought into that year's accounts every liability with which they were acquainted. Of the £035, £162 10s. div.p: I BEG to EXPRESS MY REGRET for having re- peated statements reflecting upon the character of Mr. PLACE, and calculated to do him serious injury, and which 1 now believe to be entirety devoid of foundation. JOHN WOOLFALL. March 11th. 1881.

NOW COMPILING KELLY'S DIRECTORY OF LANCASHIRE with Maps engraved for the Work. Pace to Subscribers, 405.; Non-Subscribers. 50s. The Pub- lishers, in submitting the Prospectus of the Fourth Edition of the Directory of this County, respectfully hope for a con- tinuance of the patronage of their former Subscribers. The work will contain a topographical account of each Parish, Village, Hamlet, and Township, with its distance from London and other ohief towns, its position in the division of the County, Hundred and Union, and County Court District, and also the Diocese, Archdeaconry and Rural Deanery; Des- cription of the Churches, with the Value of the Living, and the names of the Patron and Incumbent, the chief Landowners; the Acreage, notice of Soil and Crops, Local Chariti-% and des- cription of the Principal Seats. In the towns are also given a short historical account. paiticulars of the Local Government; an Architectural Description of the Churches and other Public Buildings, Chapels of different Denominations; Public Schools, a full account of the Principal Manufacturies of which each town is the seat; the Markets, Fairs, and Paces; .4 gricultui al and Scientific Societies and Meetings, Ac.; Objects of Natural Curiosity and Antiquities; Hospitals, Almshouses and Charities. The Directory of each town comprises Lists of the Resident Nobility, Clergy, and Gentry, and also a list of all engaged in Professional and Mercantile Pursuits. in Alphabetical Order. Information relating to Law and Public Offices, Churches and Chapels, the arrival and departure of the Mails and Coaches, Posting Houses, Commercial Inns, together with particulars respecting Conveyance by Railway, ‘1 ater or Land Carriers. will also be included. Immediately following will be given an Alphabetical Arrangement of Names of the Nobility, Clergy, and Gentry. and a General Classification of Trades, which wilt exhibit all the Persons engaged in any Trade throughout the County. The Proprietors respectfully request the favour of the gentlemen in their employ being personally seen on their applying for infor- mation, and that the precise melting •of the Name, 4-c., may be given te them. London : KELLY S; Co., 51, Great Queen Street, Lincoln's Inn Fields, W.C.
